issues.title: Severe CLI reliability failure: 63.8 MB image-history requests before any compaction, WebSocket fallback, and prolonged stalls on Windows

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: context
labels.description: Issues related to context management (including compaction)

labels.name: connectivity
labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

issues.body:
## Summary and urgent request

Please urgently investigate aggregate image-history byte growth and the repeated full-request cost after WebSocket fallback, and provide a supported recovery path for affected sessions.

In a real image-assisted coding task, Codex accumulated **63,759,837 bytes per request**, still **45,853,691 bytes after zstd compression**. At the corresponding history snapshot, **38 typed image occurrences accounted for 61,279,872 ASCII data-URL characters**. This happened **before any compaction**, not only through images retained in an old compacted replacement history.

The failure had a serious practical impact: repeated stream errors, five-attempt retry batches, HTTPS fallback, and prolonged periods in which the primary task did not advance. One failed sequence on 0.153.2 lasted approximately **88 minutes without new effective model output**. Updating to **0.153.4**, the latest stable release when checked on September 5, did not remove the accumulated payload or prevent the observed WebSocket fallback.

**I am extremely dissatisfied with this experience. These failure periods made Codex CLI effectively unusable for my paid development workflow. Waiting through prolonged retries without an actionable explanation or reliable recovery procedure is unacceptable. Users should not need to inspect SQLite databases, count Base64 payloads, or study client source code merely to keep an image-assisted coding task usable. I am asking for urgent maintainer triage, a supported mitigation, and a prioritized fix—not merely another generic reconnect warning.**

The report also includes a later partial recovery: a successful compaction removed the old tool-image payloads from active replacement history and work resumed. I am not claiming permanent data loss or that every use of `view_image` fails.

## Related reports and the additional evidence here

This is closely related to [#41338](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/41338) and [#24550](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/24550). Please consolidate this evidence into an existing tracker if that is the preferred triage path.

The distinguishing measurements are:

- Windows, the built-in OpenAI provider, ChatGPT authentication, and current stable 0.153.4—not a Responses-to-Chat bridge.
- **Zero compaction records** at the failure snapshot: ordinary current-window image outputs can already create the large-request condition.
- **37 distinct data URLs across 38 occurrences**. Exact deduplication would remove only **1,119,846 bytes, or 1.83% of the image data**.
- The largest individual data URL was **5,183,170 bytes**. **None exceeded 10 MiB**. A per-image 10 MiB ceiling alone would not address this workload.
- Actual pre/post-compression request measurements, separately from rollout file size and token accounting.
- A subsequent compaction that can be inspected structurally: tool-output images were removed, while the original user-message images remained.

## Environment

| Field | Observed value |
|---|---|
| Codex CLI | 0.153.2 during the original long failed sequence; upgraded to 0.153.4 before the later resumed failure |
| Current stable release checked | `rust-v0.153.4`, published September 4, 2026 |
| Source version audited | `3d2ee51ca2d5db578f328aa75e20aa22c0197c9a` / `rust-v0.153.4` |
| Platform | Windows x64, OS build `10.0.26100` |
| Shell | PowerShell 7.6; terminal-emulator version not collected |
| Subscription / authentication | ChatGPT Pro; ChatGPT authentication |
| Provider | Built-in OpenAI provider, Codex Responses endpoint |
| Model | `gpt-6-astra` |
| Reasoning selection | Initially `xhigh`; the resumed pre-compaction and post-compaction turns both used `ultra` |
| Service tier | `default` |
| Network | Explicit HTTP/HTTPS proxy variables pointing to a local v2rayN proxy; TUN/routing changes are disclosed below |

Relevant **non-default** context settings were:

```toml
model_context_window = 1000000
model_auto_compact_token_limit = 900000
```

The session reported a `model_context_window` of **828,400**. I am disclosing the configured values without asserting that they were the effective runtime limits. This is not a claim of reproduction with an untouched default configuration. It is a supported long-context workflow that lacked an effective safeguard against its much larger serialized image payload.

### Codex doctor report

A new full `codex doctor --json` report was not collected for this investigation. The evidence below comes from targeted read-only inspection of the affected rollout, retained client logs, process/network state, and the pinned client source. I am not substituting an older doctor report or claiming that doctor passed.

## What happened: measured request and history sizes

The HTTP client recorded the following at **2026-09-05 11:12:14 UTC**:

```text
Compressed request body with zstd
pre_compression_bytes=63759837
post_compression_bytes=45853691
compression_duration_ms=78
```

Several earlier requests in the same resumed task were almost as large:

| UTC | Before compression | After compression | Compression time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 10:55:20 | 63,721,050 B | 45,827,415 B | 70 ms |
| 10:57:42 | 63,740,637 B | 45,841,192 B | 76 ms |
| 10:58:22 | 63,742,371 B | 45,842,100 B | 70 ms |
| 10:59:43 | 63,742,371 B | 45,842,094 B | 98 ms |
| 11:12:14 | 63,759,837 B | 45,853,691 B | 78 ms |

These are **application-recorded request-body sizes**, not inferred wire traffic, billing totals, or the size of the JSONL file. Compression itself was fast; the measurements do not justify blaming local zstd work for multi-minute delays.

The corresponding history was inspected through **11:12:15 UTC**, counting only `response_item` records:

| Typed image location | Occurrences | Data-URL characters / ASCII bytes |
|---|---:|---:|
| User-message `content[].image_url` | 7 | 4,307,974 |
| Function/custom-tool `output[].image_url` | 31 | 56,971,898 |
| Total | **38** | **61,279,872** |

All counted image values belonged to typed `input_image` objects. UI/event duplicates were not included in these totals. The main sources were generated images and image-viewing tool outputs; this is not a claim that the whole total came from `view_image` alone.

The last completed request recorded at **10:58:22 UTC** reported **482,479 input tokens**, of which **480,000 were cached**. That is the last completed-request usage record, **not** a new usage measurement for the 11:12 submission. It demonstrates that high token-cache reuse coexisted with repeated large requests; unchanged usage counters do not prove the backend performed no work or incurred no cost.

## Failure chronology and severity

All times below are September 5, 2026, UTC.

| Time / interval | Observation |
|---|---|
| 08:53:15–10:21:18, CLI 0.153.2 | After the last productive tool result, repeated response-stream failures produced no new effective model output for approximately 88 minutes; the turn eventually failed. |
| 09:08:19, 09:23:24, 09:38:29, 09:51:07, 10:06:11 | Five recorded retries in that failed sequence. The roughly 15-minute spacing is observed behavior, not a claim about a proven timeout setting. |
| 10:51–10:52 | CLI upgraded to 0.153.4 and restarted; the original session was resumed. |
| 10:53 | Multiple WebSocket handshakes succeeded; actual request sends then failed with Windows error 10054 and exhausted five retries. |
| 10:54:01 | HTTP fallback was activated. |
| 10:55–10:58 | Some productive tool activity resumed, including starting two subagents. |
| 10:59:43 | A separate manual route change restarted the proxy and caused a known disconnect. This event is treated separately, as explained below. |
| 11:00:19 and 11:12:44 | HTTPS requests received HTTP 200; SSE keepalives were also observed during long waits. |
| 11:07:35 and 11:08:44 | The two subagents completed; their progress must not be confused with the primary thread's progress. |
| 11:31:23–11:36:38 | The running turn was interrupted, then a compaction ran and completed. |

The errors included:

```text
stream disconnected before completion:
failed to send websocket request: IO error: ... (os error 10054)

Falling back from WebSockets to HTTPS transport

stream disconnected before completion:
Transport error: network error: error decoding response body
```

The original 88-minute terminal failure occurred on **0.153.2**. The later handshake/send failures, fallback and large requests were observed on **0.153.4**. I am not attributing the earlier 88-minute sequence to the newer binary.

## Later recovery: important evidence, not omitted

At **11:36:38**, the completed compaction installed a replacement history containing:

- 36 items: 35 messages and one compaction item;
- **7 embedded images totaling 4,307,974 characters**;
- approximately **4,378,186 bytes** when serialized as compact UTF-8 JSON by the inspection code.

The retained image multiset exactly matched the earlier user-message image multiset. The old raw tool outputs were no longer present in the replacement history. Relative to the earlier snapshot, embedded image bytes decreased by approximately **92.97%**.

Subsequent retained HTTP logs showed requests around **9.8–10.9 MB before compression**, substantially below the earlier 63.8 MB, and the primary thread again performed commands and file edits. Those later requests already included additional post-compaction work, so they are not the size of the first untouched compacted request.

This is a **natural before/after observation**, not a controlled benchmark. The model selection remained Astra/Ultra and the same CLI process continued, but the workload changed and upstream conditions were not controlled. Long waits were not eliminated: one later parent-thread tool-result-to-next-tool-call interval was still about **11 minutes**.

The observed recovery supports treating active-history size as an important contributor. It does **not** prove that compaction alone fixes every affected thread, or that every minute of delay was upload time. It also matches an important implementation distinction: current compaction can discard original tool outputs while retaining user images.

## Reproduction conditions

The observed workload was:

1. Run a long image-assisted coding session using the built-in OpenAI provider and the environment described above.
2. Generate and inspect multiple images through normal tools. Retain several dozen prepared images in active history; individual images need not exceed 10 MiB.
3. Continue model/tool iterations without a compaction having reduced that history.
4. Resume the same history after a CLI restart.
5. Compare request-body byte measurements with token accounting, and observe whether the actual resumed WebSocket request succeeds after the handshake.

This describes the real failure conditions. **A standalone minimal deterministic network reproducer and a sanitized-copy A/B test have not been run.** The private workload cannot be pasted into a public issue. The report is not evidence that every image, network, model, or default configuration reproduces the transport failure.

## Technical assessment: what is proven, and what is most likely

**Confirmed:** this workload retained tens of megabytes of typed image data and repeatedly constructed very large requests. The current source explains how that payload survives truncation and is resent when the full-history path is used.

**Most strongly supported explanation of the amplification:** accumulated inline images become expensive repeatedly when incremental WebSocket continuation is unavailable and the client submits the full active prompt over HTTP. Additional images can enlarge subsequent submissions again. The natural compaction observation and related community controls support this explanation.

**Not established:** the exact origin of the first TCP reset, a particular server/proxy message-size ceiling, or a universal causal relationship between image size and every observed stall. Payload size or multimodal replay shape may trigger a transport/endpoint limitation, but local/upstream proxy behavior and backend processing are still possible contributors. High reasoning effort also contributes to ordinary model latency.

<details>
<summary>Pinned source evidence and the conditional byte-amplification argument</summary>

The following code was checked at release commit `3d2ee51ca2d5db578f328aa75e20aa22c0197c9a`:

| Component | Relevant behavior |
|---|---|
| [Image-viewing handler][src-view] | Produces a data URL and a typed image output. Omitting the image from the log preview does not remove it from model input. |
| [Tool-output truncation][src-trunc] | Text is budgeted/truncated while `InputImage` URLs are copied in the inspected paths. |
| [History/token estimation][src-history] | Replaces the actual Base64 byte contribution with an image-token estimate. Correct token estimation still requires a separate serialized-byte safeguard. |
| [Request construction and transports][src-client] | HTTP constructs a request from the formatted active prompt. WS may use incremental input when prior-response state and prefix matching permit it; otherwise it uses full input. |
| [Compacted-history retention][src-compact] | Filters ordinary raw tool outputs; retained user images can remain. Thus compaction outcomes depend on the history's shape. |
| [WebSocket response stream][src-ws] | The ordinary `Message::Close(_)` branch discards close details and returns a generic stream error. This does not imply that our 10054 included a close frame. |

The deterministic part can be stated narrowly. Let `b_i` be the byte length of each prepared inline image URL retained in a history that is serialized in full. These strings must contribute at least `sum(b_i)` bytes to that uncompressed request, before surrounding JSON and other inputs. If the same image strings are retained across `k` such requests, they contribute at least `k * sum(b_i)` bytes across the constructed request bodies.

That is a serialization consequence under stated conditions. It is **not** proof that all requests reach the network in full, that those bytes are billable tokens, or that a connection must fail at a particular size. Compression and WS incremental continuation change transfer costs; the recorded zstd sizes establish the substantial cost in this case.

For this workload, a single-image ceiling and exact deduplication are insufficient on their own: no image exceeded 10 MiB, and 37 of 38 encoded images were distinct. The safeguard needs an aggregate/lifecycle dimension.

</details>

## Confounders and limits explicitly checked

- **Proxy route change:** at 10:59:43, changing routing restarted Xray/sing-box and disrupted both the affected session and another active session. That disconnect is not used as proof of image-induced failure. Earlier failures predated it.
- **Proxy configuration was present:** explicit HTTP/HTTPS proxy settings were active and actual WebSocket handshakes succeeded. This differs from an older missing-proxy/handshake-timeout problem.
- **Connection versus progress:** HTTP 200 and periodic SSE keepalives demonstrate some established stream activity, not completion of model work. I am not calling every long wait a deadlock.
- **Local resource evidence:** the inspected snapshots did not show CPU/memory exhaustion; local request compression was measured in milliseconds. These snapshots do not exclude every possible local bottleneck.
- **Billing:** no monetary loss, duplicate model billing, or precise quota waste is claimed from the byte counts or unchanged usage counters.
- **Recovery:** a compaction later succeeded and work resumed. No permanent data loss or permanently unrecoverable session is claimed.
- **Log retention:** older retained-client-log rows rotated during the investigation. Their measurements were captured while present; the persistent rollout and saved diagnostic observations were cross-checked. No unrestricted packet capture or server-side trace was obtained.

## Existing fixes and reports have been considered

| Reference | Relevance and boundary |
|---|---|
| [#41338](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/41338) | Directly reports the byte/token mismatch from local image viewing; open when checked. |
| [#24550](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/24550) | Reports WS retries/fallback with retained images. Its original compaction-specific reproduction differs from this pre-compaction case. |
| [#30441](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/30441) | Related image-history size failures; this local report does not claim a 413 was observed. |
| [#24388 and closure response](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/24388#issuecomment-4835137176) | Acknowledges an earlier compaction issue and explains a change in compaction implementation. This should not be read as confirmation that every image-byte retention problem is fixed. |
| [Merged PR #38681](https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/38681) | Preserves parent HTTP fallback for delegated sessions. Its commit is an ancestor of 0.153.4 and the relevant code is present. I am not claiming that this specific fix is absent. |

In particular, I am not requesting that maintainers redo #38681. Please assess the remaining current-window byte growth and repeated full-history submission separately from already-addressed delegated-session fallback behavior.

## Expected behavior and urgent requested action

Image viewing is a core, legitimate workflow. The expected solution should preserve useful visual capability rather than requiring users to avoid images altogether.

Please:

1. **Urgently triage and assign ownership** for the aggregate image-history/request-byte problem, clarify which existing tracker owns it, and provide a current supported mitigation and expected fix/release path.
2. Add an **aggregate serialized-byte safeguard**, independent of token budgeting, covering ordinary tool outputs before compaction as well as continuation, resume/fork and compacted history. Many individually small images must be covered.
3. Provide a bounded lifecycle or out-of-band representation for older image artifacts, with explicit references and on-demand retrieval. Do not silently discard task-critical current images or the user's original files.
4. Avoid repeatedly resubmitting a deterministically rejected large request unchanged. Preserve actionable close/status details when available; do not infer an oversize error solely from a generic TCP reset.
5. Provide a **supported recovery procedure for existing affected sessions**, with preservation of project files and useful task context, instead of requiring manual JSONL/SQLite surgery or abandoning a long task without a reliable handoff.
6. Make the UI distinguish connection attempts, accepted requests with heartbeats, actual model progress, and repeated request-size failure. Surface the relevant byte measurements and a useful recovery action.

Suggested regression coverage should include multiple sub-10-MiB images, current-window tool images before any compaction, high token-cache reuse with large serialized bodies, both user and tool images after compaction, and repeated continuation after fallback. Please verify both the **request bytes** and successful follow-up behavior; a low token count or a successful compaction notification alone is insufficient.

**This is a serious interruption to paid, real development work, not a cosmetic warning. Please provide an actionable official response as soon as possible.**

## Privacy and supporting material

Only sanitized measurements and code references are included. Raw rollouts, images, prompts, project paths, credentials, cookies, account identifiers and private request IDs are intentionally omitted. Please specify an appropriate secure channel if additional private diagnostic material is necessary for triage.

issues.title: Codex should not resend large base64 image tool outputs in subsequent context

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: context
labels.description: Issues related to context management (including compaction)

labels.name: tool-calls
labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

issues.body:
## Summary

When a user submits an image to Codex, sending the image in the immediate request is expected. However, after that turn is processed, Codex appears to persist the full base64 image payload in conversation/tool history and resends it in later `/v1/responses` requests.

This causes unbounded context growth. In one observed case, a later request included multiple base64 image payloads in `tool` messages, producing an upstream Chat request of about 8.34 MB and about 5.7 million prompt tokens. Several OpenAI-compatible upstream providers then failed with 502/524 or HTTP 200 streams with no valid output.

## Expected behavior

- User-submitted images can be included in the current request.
- After the image has been processed, Codex should not keep resending the full `data:image/*;base64,...` payload as ordinary conversation context.
- Large image payloads should be replaced by a compact reference, digest, placeholder, or omitted from subsequent context unless explicitly required again.
- Tool outputs containing large binary/base64 data should be aggressively pruned or summarized before being stored in long-lived conversation history.

## Actual behavior observed

A later Codex request contained full base64 images inside historical `tool` messages. The largest tool message was a PNG data URL of about 7.68 million characters. Another JPEG data URL was about 426k characters.

The request shape after being converted to OpenAI Chat format was approximately:

```text
messages = 77
roles:
  system    4
  user      9
  assistant 39
  tool      25
tools = 10
upstream_body ~= 8,343,294 bytes
prompt_tokens ~= 5,722,717
completion_tokens = 0
```

Largest historical message contents:

```text
tool message[36] ~= 7,681,241 chars
  [{"type":"input_image","image_url":"data:image/png;base64,..."}]

tool message[23] ~= 426,314 chars
  [{"type":"input_image","image_url":"data:image/jpeg;base64,..."}]
```

This was not caused by the proxy duplicating request data. The actual upstream request body did not include the proxy diagnostic raw request field; the large payload was already present in the conversation messages submitted by Codex.

## Failure mode

Observed downstream/upstream behavior included:

```text
I-智枢云桥/gpt-5.5 -> 502 after about 203s
https://vsllm.com/gpt-5.5 -> HTTP 200 stream, first token after about 84.8s, then dropped
prompt_tokens = 5,722,717
completion_tokens = 0
```

Other OpenAI-compatible providers also failed for similar Codex `/v1/responses` requests with large historical context, usually as 502/524 or stream dropped/no valid output.

## Why this matters

This makes long-running Codex sessions unstable after image/tool interactions:

- Context can grow by several MB from a single image.
- The same large image data can be resent repeatedly in later turns.
- Prompt token counts can explode into millions.
- Upstream providers may fail, timeout, or return incomplete streams.
- The failure is confusing because the user is not submitting a new image in the later turn.

## Suggested fix

Codex should treat large image/base64 payloads as ephemeral request data rather than durable text/tool history.

Possible mitigations:

1. Strip or replace `data:image/*;base64,...` payloads from historical messages after the turn that consumes them.
2. Store a compact placeholder such as `[image omitted: sha256=..., bytes=...]` in later context.
3. Apply max-size limits to tool outputs before persisting them into conversation history.
4. Avoid serializing image payloads into `tool` messages that are replayed to the model in subsequent requests.
5. Add diagnostics/warnings when a request context contains very large base64 payloads.

The key point: submitting an image in the current user turn is fine, but resending the full base64 image in all later turns should be avoided.

issues.body:
# Codex CLI pre-process policy rejection without a rule or justification

## Observed behavior

On Windows, Codex CLI 0.164.0 rejected an authorized local maintenance command before creating the PowerShell process. At 2026-10-28T01:21:29.211544Z, the tool reported `exec_command failed: CreateProcess ... rejected: blocked by policy`. The returned error did not name the policy source, matching rule, or justification. The long command was truncated in the error, so we do not have a complete command input from that error for a faithful policy replay.

The invocation header reported model `glm-5.3`, provider `ZAI`, approval `never`, sandbox `danger-full-access`, and reasoning effort `max`. These header values are observations, not proof that the rejected action was permitted by every effective policy layer. The executable reported `codex-cli 0.164.0`; SHA256 was `6f267830b029ee25d9339864aa867cd45de9f8fd4c5ea007d2e63c13a0c66d36`.

## Existing evidence and limits

The intended command would acquire maintenance locks, stop selected services, take a cold backup, and install a prepared package. The rejection occurred before service mutation. Independent read-only checks found all original runtime files unchanged and the original service processes still running. The CLI subsequently exited normally after writing its failure report; this exit did not mean deployment succeeded.

A static `codex execpolicy check` using the existing user rule file and only the observed PowerShell executable/`-NoProfile`/`-Command` prefix returned no matching rules. It did not include the full command body or all managed layers, so it does not establish permission or identify this refusal's source. A presence-only check found no Windows system `requirements.toml` at the documented ProgramData location. Other policy sources have not been excluded. No configuration or rules were changed, and no denied maintenance command was retried.

No minimal reproduction has been established. The retained private evidence can identify the original UTC event and thread through an appropriate private support route, without uploading the raw session by default.

The verified original executable also completed `--help`, `doctor --help`, and `debug --help` with exit code 0. Those help surfaces did not document an exact refusal-event selector or decision-audit export. The doctor help described broad installation, configuration, authentication, and runtime diagnostics; the debug help listed `models`, `app-server`, `prompt-input`, and `help`. We did not run a doctor report or any debug subcommand. This limited help inspection does not establish that no other host interface exists.

## Requested help

What supported diagnostic or audit entry point can identify the policy source, matching rule, and justification for this original pre-process refusal? If this event belongs to a different host component, please identify the supported intake for that component. We need the documented resolution path for the actual denial before scheduling another installation attempt.

## Official reporting references

The official [Troubleshooting documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/reference/troubleshooting) describes feedback from an existing chat and Codex GitHub issue reporting. The official [Open Source documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/open-source) identifies `openai/codex/issues` as the Codex bug-report channel and asks for the component and version.

These are general reporting channels. They do not establish that the Codex maintainers own this machine's effective policy, that a support case has been accepted, or that any deployment retry is allowed.

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: iOS
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex iOS app

issues.body:
### What feature would you like to see?

Please add a “phone use” capability, similar to computer use, that lets the assistant operate my phone with my permission.

I would like it to understand the current screen, open supported apps, tap, swipe, type, and complete tasks across mobile apps. This would help with tasks that currently require me to perform every step manually on my phone.

The phone itself should be the device being operated, rather than only a remote client for controlling Codex on a computer.

### Requested platforms and scope

iOS and Android. Please document supported devices and apps, whether a paired computer is required, and differences in OS permissions or app-store restrictions.

Please distinguish visual screen control from narrower app actions or Shortcuts integrations. Those may be useful fallbacks but are not equivalent capabilities.

Android's [Computer Control preview](https://developer.android.com/ai/computer-control) demonstrates screenshot-based app operation, but currently requires an OEM-preloaded assistant and privileged permission. Apple's [App Intents](https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2025/244/) provides app-defined actions rather than unrestricted screen control. Please use supported mechanisms rather than bypassing platform protections.

### User control and safety

Access should be opt-in, with a visible active-session indicator, an immediate stop control, and a way to revoke access. Sensitive actions should require confirmation, and authentication or protected screens should be handed back to the user.

Please allow per-app access control, explain how captured screen content is processed and retained, and keep credentials, biometrics, security permissions, and protected confirmations under the user's direct control.

### Related requests

#24177 concerns controlling a desktop environment from mobile; this request is for operating the mobile device itself. #37491 proposes a mobile OS, while this request is for a capability on existing iOS and Android devices. #33663 and #45198 concern Mac-mediated iPhone Mirroring interactions, rather than a first-class cross-platform phone-use workflow.

issues.title: app-server: thread/unarchive does not restore the spawned subagent threads that thread/archive archived

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: subagent
labels.description: Issues involving subagents or multi-agent features

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

issues.body:
## What version of Codex are you using?

0.165.0-alpha.1 (app-server)

## What happened

`thread/archive` archives the thread together with its whole spawn subtree (`state_db_spawn_subtree_thread_ids`, then `archive_threads` with every descendant), and the descendants' rollouts move to `archived_sessions`. `thread/unarchive` on the same thread restores only that thread. After an archive and unarchive of a parent thread, every spawned subagent thread stays archived.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start a thread that spawns one or more subagent threads.
2. Call `thread/archive` on the parent, then `thread/unarchive` on it.
3. `thread/list` with `ancestorThreadId` set to the parent: the children are still archived.

## Expected

`thread/unarchive` restores the descendants that the matching `thread/archive` archived, or the asymmetry is documented and an option restores the subtree.

I cannot confirm whether this Electron/module error is the direct root cause, but it seems related because the Chrome extension says it is connected while Codex cannot use the Chrome extension backend, and Computer Use cannot determine the current Chrome URL.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Use Codex Desktop on Windows with Computer Use enabled.
2. Install and enable the Codex Chrome Extension.
3. Open Google Chrome.
4. Keep Chrome on `chrome://newtab/` or `about:blank`.
5. Ask Codex to use Computer Use to inspect or operate the Chrome window.
6. Computer Use detects the Chrome app/window successfully.
7. Attempt to acquire the Chrome screen/window state through Computer Use.

Expected reproduction result:

```text
Computer Use has been stopped for this turn because it could not determine the current browser URL on Windows with enough confidence to enforce policy.
```

Baseline checks that succeeded:

- Computer Use + Windows Calculator: success
- Computer Use + Notepad: success
- Computer Use + Chrome app/window detection: success

Failure:

- Computer Use + Chrome screen-state acquisition: failure

Versions observed:

- Computer Use plugin: `openai-bundled/computer-use/26.527.31326`
- Chrome plugin: `openai-bundled/chrome/26.527.31326`
- Browser plugin: `openai-bundled/browser/26.527.31326`
- Codex Chrome Extension: `1.1.5`
- Chrome: `148.0.7778.217`

### What is the expected behavior?

Computer Use should be able to determine the current URL for a Chrome window on Windows when the tab is on `chrome://newtab/` or `about:blank`, and then continue with the requested browser GUI operation.

If the URL cannot be determined, Computer Use should provide a more specific diagnostic message, such as whether the problem is caused by:

- Chrome extension connection failure
- Chrome profile mismatch
- Native messaging host issue
- Windows UI Automation / address bar URL detection failure
- inability to map the detected Chrome window to a known Chrome tab

If possible, Computer Use should use the same Chrome extension / Chrome plugin connection information to map the detected Chrome window to the current tab URL.

### Additional information

I tried the following before filing this issue:

- Retried in multiple Codex threads
- Rebooted the PC
- Reinstalled the Codex Chrome Extension
- Verified that the extension is enabled
- Verified that the extension popup shows `Connected`
- Verified that Chrome is detected by Computer Use
- Verified that Computer Use works with non-browser Windows apps

The extension settings gear produces this error, which may be related:

```text
Error launching app

Unable to find Electron app at
C:\Program Files\WindowsApps\OpenAI.Codex_26.527.3686.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0\...\google-chrome

Cannot find module
'C:\Program Files\WindowsApps\OpenAI.Codex_26.527.3686.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0\...\google-chrome'
```

The Chrome extension UI says `Connected`, but Codex reported:

```text
Browser is not available: extension
```

This may indicate that the extension UI, the Chrome plugin backend, and Computer Use's Chrome URL safety check are not all using the same working connection path.

issues.title: Automatic compaction loses active task: continuation receives environment-only user context despite preserved rollout

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: extension
labels.description: Issues related to the VS Code extension

labels.name: context
labels.description: Issues related to context management (including compaction)

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

issues.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

A long-running Codex session lost its active task immediately after automatic compaction. The assistant stopped and asked the user to resend the task, despite the original conversation and a task checkpoint still existing locally. When the user pasted the recent transcript and asked to locate the chat, the assistant located the very same session but presented it as a separate chat to resume.

This is an observed continuity failure; the precise client/server root cause is not established.

### Environment

- Session metadata: Codex 0.164.0; source `vscode`, originator `codex-tui`.
- macOS 15.7.7, arm64.
- Model recorded at the affected boundary: `gpt-6-astra`, medium reasoning.
- Occurred 2026-10-27 at 22:16:27 UTC during ongoing work.

### Evidence from the saved rollout

At the affected `compacted` record:

- `message` was an empty string.
- `replacement_history` contained seven entries: one additional-tools entry, five developer-message entries, and one user-message entry.
- The sole user message was environment context, not the user's task.
- No assistant summary or substantive user task message was present in that replacement history.
- `retained_context` separately recorded eight user messages and eight assistant messages, with both corresponding incomplete flags true. This establishes that retained metadata existed; it does not establish that its contents reached the continuation model.
- The original earlier transcript remained readable in the same local session file. This was not deletion of the on-disk transcript.

At 22:16:49 UTC, the assistant responded:

> I have the workspace context, but the active request isn’t available. Please resend the task you’d like me to continue.

Later, reading the original session file and an existing filesystem checkpoint recovered the authorized task and progress.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed sequence (not yet a deterministic minimal reproduction):

1. Run a long, multi-stage coding/validation task in one session across several automatic compactions.
2. Let another automatic compaction occur while the task is unfinished.
3. Inspect whether the continuation retains the active task, prior decisions, and pending work.
4. In this occurrence, it instead stopped and requested the task again; inspecting the compacted rollout showed the replacement-history shape above.

Earlier compactions also had empty `message` strings, so an empty string alone is not claimed to be sufficient to reproduce this failure.

### What is the expected behavior?

Compaction should preserve enough usable task state for continued work, or explicitly surface a failed handoff and recover the prior state before continuing. It should not silently resume with only environment context and then abandon an active authorized task. The continuation should also recognize its own current session when locating the transcript.

### Additional information

Related: #54584 and #55508 concern invalid or stale local-compaction summaries with other providers. This report does not establish that the same code path is responsible: this occurrence used the model listed above and includes separate retained-context metadata.

Please investigate validation of the replacement context and delivery of retained task state at this boundary. A regression test should verify that a continuing long-running task can recover its objective and pending operation after compaction.

Project names, repository details, credentials, source code, private task content, and full session logs are intentionally omitted.

### What platform is your computer?
macOS; environment settings inspected in Chrome.

### What issue are you seeing?
A private cloud environment remains in “Publishing” for over six hours according to the UI, with no confirmed published version, terminal error, or actionable operation status.

The affected environment has no OIDC attachment and no supplied credentials. This blocks setup before any authenticated workload can run.

### Observed sequence
These are steps observed on this account, not a minimal reproduction verified on a second account:

1. Prepare and validate an environment draft. The setup runtime can run the public tooling and an offline validation check.
2. Save the configuration. Verify the saved fields by readback.
3. Attempt publication. After a newer-settings conflict, reconcile the saved state and verify the same intended settings.
4. The UI reports **“Draft saved · Not published”** and enables **Publish**; the catalog reports **Unpublished / Private**.
5. Submit one recovery Publish of that saved state at approximately **2026-10-27 21:03 UTC**.
6. The UI continues showing **Publishing** with settings controls locked. It later displays:
   > Couldn’t confirm publishing status  
   > Publishing may still be running. Check its status to continue.
7. **Check status** returns to the Publishing display rather than producing a terminal result. At **2026-10-28 03:08 UTC**, the UI displayed **“Publishing… 365:13 elapsed.”** No subsequent publication was submitted during that interval.

The catalog continued exposing the earlier/base version rather than a confirmed newly published version. Supported inspection did not expose a publication operation/correlation ID, backend error, or background-build progress. No active installer command was shown in the setup task. That does not prove whether a backend job was still running.

### Expected behavior
Publish should either complete and expose the resulting version, or return an actionable failure. If the UI loses track of an operation, Check status should reconcile it and provide a supported recovery path without requiring users to guess whether another Publish would overlap.

### Additional context
- An earlier, separate published environment had successfully executed work. This is not a claim that all cloud environments are unusable.
- A separate OIDC investigation exists, but this report concerns publication of an environment with **no OIDC attachment**. We have not established a common cause.
- The work is now paused. No service-account key or authenticated test was created for this pilot.
- The publication status has not been confirmed canceled.
- The issue has also been reported through the existing Help Center conversation. No human reply or reference number was visible at the last check.
- Private configuration IDs, repository details, local paths, credentials and transcripts are intentionally omitted from this public report.

### Related reports
- #54764: closest symptom match, including unconfirmed publishing status.
- #49568: save/publish problems in the legacy-to-current environment migration workflow.
- #55695: save/publish rejection with a reported executor-capability error.

These are related symptoms, not evidence of a shared root cause.

Could the team clarify how to obtain the publication operation ID/status and recover the saved environment without losing its configuration or creating overlapping publication requests?

### Additional startup observation
Shortly after filing, the separate credential-free probe against the earlier published environment reported `failed to query executor configuration capabilities` (runtime identifier omitted). No executor capability checks or commands ran. This is a concrete startup error from that separate probe, not proof that the publication stall has the same cause. The earlier historical successful execution remains distinct from this new failed startup.

issues.title: MCP Auto discovery timeout consumes a late HTTP discover response as initialize response (expected 1, got 0)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: mcp
labels.description: Issues related to the use of model context protocol (MCP) servers

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

issues.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

Official unmodified `codex-cli 0.165.0` and `codex-cli 0.161.0` macOS arm64 release binaries. Both reproduce. Each downloaded release archive was checked against its GitHub release asset SHA-256 before extraction.

### What subscription do you have? Which model were you using?

No subscription, account credentials, or model request is required. The reproducer only uses app-server initialize, thread/start, and mcpServerStatus/list. It never starts a turn; the configured provider is an unused local fixture.

### Platform

macOS arm64, local Python standard-library HTTP server, app-server JSONL over subprocess pipes. No terminal/multiplexer dependency. An isolated HOME, CODEX_HOME and TMPDIR are used for each case.

### What issue are you seeing?

With `features.mcp_2026_07_28=true`, a modern-only HTTP MCP server connects and exposes its echo tool when server/discover responds immediately. If its correctly correlated successful discovery response is intentionally held for 12 seconds, the same official clients fail with:

```text
MCP startup failed: handshaking with MCP server failed: conflict initialized response id: expected 1, got 0
```

The client sends initialize after the outstanding discover response. The fixture advertises only 2026-07-28 and deliberately rejects legacy initialize; it echoes every valid request ID. This occurs with both application/json and text/event-stream. A separate wrong-ID negative control is rejected without initialize fallback.

| Fixture | 0.161.0 | 0.165.0 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Immediate JSON discovery | Connected; echo discovered; no initialize | Same |
| Immediate SSE discovery | Connected; echo discovered; no initialize | Same |
| Discovery success delayed 12 s, JSON | expected 1, got 0; initialize observed; no tools | Same |
| Discovery success delayed 12 s, SSE | expected 1, got 0; initialize observed; no tools | Same |
| Immediate JSON, response ID intentionally 99 | expected 0, got 99; no initialize | Same |

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Download the unmodified `codex-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz` assets from [0.161.0](https://github.com/openai/codex/releases/tag/rust-v0.161.0) and [0.165.0](https://github.com/openai/codex/releases/tag/rust-v0.165.0). Check each archive against GitHub's asset digest. The tested archive SHA-256 values were:
   - 0.161.0: `bd83479f3ae21474c407ec2164fbc2a63fa763f7afbbd123fb6a69c5201cfd38`
   - 0.165.0: `78ea9c178d2dc8fde71d6494df3b9eab902fd6d6de0a84e65234220d93bb6144`
2. Save the script below as reproduce.py. Place the extracted native executables beside it as `assets/codex-0.161.0` and `assets/codex-0.165.0`; verify --version.
3. Run with Python 3.13+ (the script uses no third-party packages):

```sh
python3 reproduce.py --output runs/control --cases fast-json fast-sse
python3 reproduce.py --output runs/late --cases slow-json slow-sse wrong-id
```

Output directories must be new. Ten total observations were recorded. Each case closes its app-server process group and local listener. Script output contains selected method/ID/timing and server-status fields, not raw request bodies or arbitrary stderr.

<details><summary>Self-contained reproduce.py</summary>

```python
"""Stock Codex app-server against an isolated HTTP MCP boundary; no model turn.

Only method, request id, response type and elapsed times are recorded.
The delayed cases deliberately withhold discovery for 12 seconds to cross the
SDK's internal 10-second Auto probe deadline. This is fault injection, not retry.
"""
import argparse
import concurrent.futures
import hashlib
import http.server
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import queue
import re
import signal
import subprocess
import threading
import time

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
TOOL = {"name": "echo", "description": "Synthetic echo", "inputSchema": {"type": "object", "properties": {}}}


class Fixture:
    def __init__(self, delay, sse, wrong_id=False):
        self.delay, self.sse, self.wrong_id = delay, sse, wrong_id
        self.started = time.monotonic()
        self.events, self.lock = [], threading.Lock()
        self.stop = threading.Event()
        self.model_requests = 0
        fixture = self

        class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
            protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1"

            def log_message(self, *_):
                pass

            def do_GET(self):
                self.send_response(405)
                self.send_header("Content-Length", "0")
                self.end_headers()

            def do_POST(self):
                if self.path != "/mcp":
                    fixture.model_requests += 1
                    self.send_response(503)
                    self.send_header("Content-Length", "0")
                    self.end_headers()
                    return
                body = json.loads(self.rfile.read(int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", 0))))
                method, ident = body.get("method"), body.get("id")
                fixture.record("received", method=method, id=ident,
                               protocol=self.headers.get("MCP-Protocol-Version"),
                               methodHeader=self.headers.get("Mcp-Method"))
                if method == "server/discover":
                    if fixture.stop.wait(fixture.delay):
                        return
                    result = {"resultType": "complete", "supportedVersions": ["2026-07-28"],
                              "capabilities": {"tools": {}}, "ttlMs": 0, "cacheScope": "private",
                              "_meta": {"io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo": {"name": "modern-only-fixture", "version": "1"}}}
                    reply = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": ident + 99 if fixture.wrong_id else ident, "result": result}
                elif method == "initialize":
                    reply = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": ident, "error": {"code": -32022,
                             "message": "Unsupported protocol version", "data": {"supported": ["2026-07-28"]}}}
                elif method == "tools/list":
                    reply = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": ident, "result": {"resultType": "complete", "tools": [TOOL]}}
                elif method == "tools/call":
                    reply = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": ident, "result": {"resultType": "complete", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "pong"}]}}
                elif method in ["resources/list", "resources/templates/list", "prompts/list"]:
                    key = {"resources/list": "resources", "resources/templates/list": "resourceTemplates", "prompts/list": "prompts"}[method]
                    reply = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": ident, "result": {"resultType": "complete", key: []}}
                else:
                    reply = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": ident, "error": {"code": -32601, "message": "Method not found"}}
                raw = json.dumps(reply).encode()
                if fixture.sse:
                    raw = b"event: message\ndata: " + raw + b"\n\n"
                try:
                    self.send_response(200)
                    self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/event-stream" if fixture.sse else "application/json")
                    self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(raw)))
                    self.end_headers()
                    self.wfile.write(raw)
                    self.wfile.flush()
                    fixture.record("responded", method=method, id=reply["id"], result="error" if "error" in reply else "success")
                except (BrokenPipeError, ConnectionResetError):
                    fixture.record("client_closed", method=method, id=reply["id"])

        self.server = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
        self.server.daemon_threads = True
        self.base = "http://127.0.0.1:" + str(self.server.server_port)
        self.thread = threading.Thread(target=self.server.serve_forever, daemon=True)
        self.thread.start()

    def record(self, kind, **fields):
        with self.lock:
            self.events.append({"seconds": round(time.monotonic() - self.started, 4), "event": kind, **fields})

    def close(self):
        self.stop.set()
        self.server.shutdown()
        self.server.server_close()
        self.thread.join(timeout=3)


class Rpc:
    def __init__(self, binary, case, fixture):
        self.pending, self.sequence, self.lock = {}, 0, threading.Lock()
        self.errors = []
        self.notifications = []
        home, project, temp = (case / x for x in ["home", "project", "tmp"])
        for d in [home, project, temp]:
            d.mkdir()
        (home / "config.toml").write_text(f'''model="gpt-5.4"
model_provider="fixture"
approval_policy="never"
sandbox_mode="danger-full-access"
cli_auth_credentials_store="ephemeral"
[features]
shell_snapshot=false
mcp_2026_07_28=true
[model_providers.fixture]
name="Unused local fixture"
base_url="{fixture.base}/v1"
wire_api="responses"
requires_openai_auth=false
[mcp_servers.probe]
url="{fixture.base}/mcp"
startup_timeout_sec=30
tool_timeout_sec=5
''')
        env = {"PATH": "/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin", "HOME": str(case), "CODEX_HOME": str(home),
               "TMPDIR": str(temp), "LANG": "C.UTF-8", "NO_PROXY": "127.0.0.1,localhost", "RUST_LOG": "off"}
        self.proc = subprocess.Popen([str(binary), "app-server", "--strict-config"], cwd=project, env=env,
                                     stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
                                     text=True, bufsize=1, start_new_session=True)
        self.reader = threading.Thread(target=self.read, daemon=True)
        self.reader.start()
        self.stderr_reader = threading.Thread(target=self.drain, daemon=True)
        self.stderr_reader.start()
        self.call("initialize", {"clientInfo": {"name": "http-discovery-reproducer", "version": "1"}, "capabilities": {"experimentalApi": True}})
        self.write({"method": "initialized", "params": {}})
        self.project = project

    def drain(self):
        # Retain only the exact diagnostic of interest, never complete stderr.
        for line in self.proc.stderr:
            match = re.search(r"conflict initialized response id: expected \d+, got \d+", line)
            if match:
                self.errors.append(match.group())

    def read(self):
        for line in self.proc.stdout:
            msg = json.loads(line)
            if "id" in msg and "method" not in msg:
                q = self.pending.get(msg["id"])
                if q:
                    q.put(msg)
            elif "id" in msg:
                self.write({"id": msg["id"], "error": {"code": -32601, "message": "No interaction allowed in fixture"}})
            else:
                self.notifications.append(msg)

    def write(self, obj):
        with self.lock:
            self.proc.stdin.write(json.dumps(obj) + "\n")
            self.proc.stdin.flush()

    def call(self, method, params, timeout=40):
        self.sequence += 1
        ident, q = self.sequence, queue.Queue()
        self.pending[ident] = q
        self.write({"id": ident, "method": method, "params": params})
        try:
            msg = q.get(timeout=timeout)
        finally:
            self.pending.pop(ident, None)
        if "error" in msg:
            raise RuntimeError(json.dumps(msg["error"]))
        return msg.get("result")

    def close(self):
        if self.proc.poll() is None:
            os.killpg(self.proc.pid, signal.SIGTERM)
            try:
                self.proc.wait(timeout=5)
            except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
                os.killpg(self.proc.pid, signal.SIGKILL)
                self.proc.wait(timeout=5)
        self.reader.join(timeout=2)
        self.stderr_reader.join(timeout=2)


def run_case(version, name, delay, sse, wrong_id, output):
    case = output / version / name
    case.mkdir(parents=True)
    binary = ROOT / "assets" / ("codex-" + version)
    fixture = Fixture(delay, sse, wrong_id)
    rpc = None
    result = {"version": version, "case": name, "delaySeconds": delay, "responseFormat": "sse" if sse else "json",
              "wrongResponseId": wrong_id, "startupTimeoutSeconds": 30}
    try:
        rpc = Rpc(binary, case, fixture)
        tid = rpc.call("thread/start", {"cwd": str(rpc.project), "model": "gpt-5.4", "approvalPolicy": "never",
                                      "sandbox": "danger-full-access", "ephemeral": True})["thread"]["id"]
        status = rpc.call("mcpServerStatus/list", {"threadId": tid, "serverName": "probe", "detail": "toolsAndAuthOnly"})
        servers = status.get("data", [])
        selected = next((s for s in servers if s.get("name") == "probe"), {})
        result["runtimeStatus"] = selected.get("runtimeStatus")
        result["toolsError"] = selected.get("toolsError")
        tools = selected.get("tools", {})
        result["toolNames"] = list(tools) if isinstance(tools, dict) else [t.get("name") for t in tools]
        result["statusFields"] = list(selected)
        # Only the explicit local probe server error is retained from RPC output.
        # There are no credentials, model responses or user data in this run.
        result["connected"] = result["runtimeStatus"] == "connected" and bool(result["toolNames"])
    except Exception as error:
        result["driverError"] = str(error)[:1500]
    finally:
        if rpc:
            rpc.close()
            result["idConflictDiagnostics"] = sorted(set(rpc.errors))
        fixture.close()
        result["modelRequests"] = fixture.model_requests
        result["events"] = fixture.events
        result["methods"] = [e["method"] for e in fixture.events if e["event"] == "received"]
        result["initializeSent"] = "initialize" in result["methods"]
        (case / "result.json").write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2) + "\n")
        print(json.dumps({k: result.get(k) for k in ["version", "case", "connected", "initializeSent", "toolsError", "driverError"]}), flush=True)
    return result


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--output", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--cases", nargs="+", default=["fast-json", "slow-json", "fast-sse", "slow-sse", "wrong-id"])
    args = parser.parse_args()
    output = Path(args.output).resolve()
    output.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=False)
    cases = {"fast-json": (0, False, False), "slow-json": (12, False, False),
             "fast-sse": (0, True, False), "slow-sse": (12, True, False), "wrong-id": (0, False, True)}
    tasks = [(v, n, *cases[n], output) for v in ["0.161.0", "0.165.0"] for n in args.cases]
    with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
        results = list(pool.map(lambda task: run_case(*task), tasks))
    summary = {"scope": "Official macOS arm64 Codex app-server; synthetic loopback HTTP MCP; no model turn or authentication",
               "results": results, "sourceSha256": hashlib.sha256(Path(__file__).read_bytes()).hexdigest()}
    (output / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2) + "\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

```
</details>

### What is the expected behavior?

A successful modern discovery response should not be consumed as a response to a different initialize request. The client may fail at a documented discovery/startup deadline, or handle late response correlation correctly; it should retain an actionable error instead of misreporting the earlier ID as an invalid initialization result. This report does not request indefinite startup waits, weakened ID validation, or a legacy initialize bridge in a modern-only server.

A supported per-server modern-only lifecycle would also let managed modern-only configurations fail closed instead of falling back. Both inspected releases currently map the modern feature to ClientLifecycleMode::Auto; this is a possible API improvement, not a claim that changing lifecycle policy is the only correct fix.

### Additional information and evidence limits

Related SDK report: https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/rust-sdk/issues/1400. That report uses official Goose and a legacy stdio fixture; this reproduction uses official Codex and a modern-only Streamable HTTP fixture.

Source inspection shows an internal ten-second Auto discovery timeout and same-transport initialize fallback in the pinned Rust SDK. In the recorded HTTP server trace, the server receives discover ID 0, writes its correct success approximately twelve seconds later, then receives initialize ID 1 and returns a correctly correlated unsupported-version error. Server-side timestamps do not independently prove when the client internally chose fallback or sent a queued HTTP request; the native mcpServerStatus/list error is the directly observed result.

The overall MCP startup timeout is 30 seconds in every case. Intentional fixture delay is fault injection; there are no retries or timeout increases to mask the result. No production endpoint, OAuth, nono, private plugin, real account or user conversation is involved. Passing immediate-response controls demonstrate that the response shape is accepted by both tested clients. The discover response shape follows Codex's own rmcp-client modern_discover_result fixture.

Codex doctor output was not collected; this isolated, unauthenticated app-server protocol reproducer avoids importing personal client state. Codex agents assisted with source investigation and authored/executed this reproducer. No fix is claimed.

labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

issues.body:
## Environment

- Windows, Codex desktop app 26.1021.31345 (build 21828, prod).
- In-app update check returned `up_to_date` on 2026-10-27.
- Node reported v24.22.1 in the diagnostic output.
- Observed on 2026-10-27 at approximately 08:12 UTC in a local desktop chat.

## Reproduction and observed results

1. Invoke the Computer Use tool with the documented initial `await cua.getState()` call. The kernel exits before it returns UI state:

   ```text
   node_repl kernel exited unexpectedly
   Error: Cannot find module '<user Temp>\\.tmp<random>\\kernel.js'
   code: 'MODULE_NOT_FOUND'
   kernel_status: exited(code=1)
   reason: stdout_eof
   ```

2. Run the independent `node_repl` tool with `nodeRepl.write(1 + 1)`. It also exits with `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` for `kernel.js` in a different temporary directory.
3. Attempt a read-only shell command through `exec_command`. The command fails before executing, with:

   ```text
   Failed to resolve full path of the current executable [<user runtime cache>\\codex-primary-runtime\\dependencies\\native\\powershell\\pwsh.exe]
   exit code: -2147450747
   ```

   Specifying the system Windows PowerShell executable as the tool's shell still produced the same bundled `pwsh.exe` error.
4. Web search and the app's update-check tool worked. The workspace dependency discovery tool returned configured paths, but this does not verify that those files exist or are accessible.

## Expected behavior

Computer Use should initialize and return state, the minimal `node_repl` calculation should return 2, and a read-only shell command should start successfully.

## Scope and questions

The failures are observed in this chat; no fresh-chat or post-restart reproduction has been performed. Whether the `kernel.js` and PowerShell failures have the same cause is unknown. The error alone does not establish that files are absent, that access was denied, or that a staging race occurred. Similar symptom: #33958, but a shared cause has not been established.

Please investigate the runtime initialization and advise a supported, non-destructive way to collect additional diagnostics or recover. No permissions, security settings, application files, or temporary files were changed during this investigation. User name, full local paths, account details, screenshots, and private logs are omitted.

issues.title: GUI Remote: provide consistent desktop-app and web access to existing host sessions

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: codex-web
labels.description: Issues related to Codex Web

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

issues.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

ChatGPT/Codex desktop GUI and web GUI, specifically the user-facing Remote experience, with complementary Codex CLI interoperability. The request is for a supported first-party workflow, not a custom SDK integration or a user-maintained app-server gateway.

### What feature would you like to see?

Please make the existing Remote workflow consistently available from another computer through the official ChatGPT/Codex graphical interfaces, with the same core capabilities available from a phone or tablet.

**The primary request is computer-to-computer Remote access in the desktop GUI. Desktop-browser access is also requested, including for Linux clients; it is not intended to replace or narrow the desktop-app request.** Pairing and ongoing interaction should be possible entirely from computers, without requiring a phone or tablet.

The goal is to **change the device I work from without changing the session or its execution host**. This is not a request to migrate a repository to Codex Cloud, copy the environment to another computer, or stream the host's entire desktop.

#### Use case

For research and embedded-development work, a task may need to remain on a particular workstation because it has the required tools, compute resources, or hardware connections. For example, I want to start an ARM64 build on a workstation, then continue supervising the same task from a laptop: inspect errors and diffs, provide follow-up instructions, handle approvals, and retrieve the resulting files.

A phone is useful for a quick check, but a keyboard and a large screen are better suited to sustained technical work. Switching to a second computer should not require a new conversation, a separate environment, or a custom remote gateway.

#### Minimum useful behavior

- **Access through the official desktop and web GUIs:** expose a clear Remote entry point and an authorized-host picker, with pairing that can be completed between two computers. Make desktop controller availability and any platform, account, or rollout restrictions explicit rather than leaving the relevant controls absent without explanation.
- **Same-session continuity:** show the existing conversation, current task state, command output, diffs, and generated files. Reopening the session from another client must not fork the conversation or restart the work.
- **Full interaction:** send messages and attachments, answer questions, approve or reject actions, request a stop, and download authorized outputs.
- **Host-side execution and permissions:** keep tools, credentials, and execution on the original host or its configured remote environment. Preserve sandbox, workspace, and approval policies; do not require copying tokens or exposing an unauthenticated service.
- **Clear connection lifecycle:** display the execution host and connectivity state. Closing or disconnecting the controller should not cancel already-authorized autonomous work while the host remains available. Actions requiring new approval should wait, and reconnecting should restore the current state.

#### Complementary CLI interoperability

Prioritizing the GUI should not exclude Codex CLI. Two complementary workflows would be useful:

- **CLI as the host:** start work through Codex CLI on a workstation or headless Linux server, then open and control the same eligible session from the official desktop or web GUI, without requiring a desktop application on the execution host.
- **CLI as a remote client:** attach from another computer's terminal to the same host-backed session, as an alternative to the GUI rather than a separate conversation or execution environment.

Both paths should preserve session identity, running work, and host-side permission and approval policies. Switching clients should provide an explicit handoff where needed, without duplicate execution or conflicting approvals. This is an interoperability goal, not a claim that the CLI currently lacks all remote capabilities.

CLI support would complement the GUI request; a CLI-only solution would not satisfy the primary request for graphical access from a PC.

#### Acceptance criterion

Start a task on computer A. On computer B, open the official ChatGPT/Codex desktop GUI, select A under Remote, and reopen the same conversation. Review live progress and provide the next instruction or approval. Execution remains on A, with no environment migration or duplicated work. The same core workflow should also be accessible through the web GUI in a desktop browser.

For CLI interoperability, the equivalent handoff should also work for eligible sessions started on a headless CLI host, with an optional terminal client on computer B.

A full remote IDE or desktop-video stream is not needed for an initial version.

### Additional information

The [official Remote connections documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/remote-connections) already describes desktop-to-desktop control when the feature is available and notes that availability varies by rollout. This request therefore does **not** claim that Remote is universally mobile-only. It asks for consistent availability and discoverability in the desktop GUI, plus desktop-browser access to the same host-backed sessions.

Related: #30573 requests native Windows-to-Windows pairing and remote control. That issue overlaps with the Windows desktop part of this request; the broader scope here is consistent access across the official desktop and web graphical interfaces, including Linux browser clients, with complementary CLI interoperability.

**In one sentence: let me continue the same remote work from the computer and official interface of my choice, with full desktop-GUI access and no phone or tablet required.**

issues.title: macOS desktop Chat mode: Browser.list_tabs fails with "Browser access requires the originating browser context"

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?
ChatGPT desktop 26.1013.31256, build 20586, production channel. The macOS bundle identifier is `com.openai.codex`. The integrated update check reports `up_to_date`.

### What subscription do you have?
Not collected in the diagnostic report; this is a signed-in personal account. I can provide account-specific details privately if needed.

### What platform is your computer?
macOS 27.0.1 (26A434), Apple Silicon / arm64.
Microsoft Edge 155.0.4283.45.
Official ChatGPT extension from the Chrome Web Store, installed **inside Edge**: `hehggadaopoacecdllhhajmbjkdcmajg`, version 1.26.1005.11759.

### What issue are you seeing?
In the native desktop app's **normal Chat mode**, `Browser.list_tabs` is exposed but fails with:

```text
UNKNOWN: Error code: UNKNOWN; Error:
RuntimeException: Browser access requires the originating browser context.
Open ChatGPT in the browser with the connected extension and try again.
```

The same failure is reported in both the existing Chat and a **new normal Chat created directly in the desktop app**. Work succeeds in the same desktop app and is used below only as a comparison.

The extension/local bridge is healthy: the bundled extension-installation and native-host-manifest diagnostics both pass. Work in the same desktop app can discover Edge, list tabs, read a public page, follow its link, go back, reload, and read again.

| Surface / check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Normal Chat on ChatGPT Web in Edge | User previously confirmed successful tab listing |
| Bundled extension check | Installed and enabled |
| Bundled native-host manifest check | `correct=true`, no missing origins |
| Desktop Work: Edge discovery and tab listing | Pass |
| Desktop Work: public page read, navigation, back, reload | Pass |
| Existing normal desktop Chat: `Browser.list_tabs` | Fails with the error above |
| New normal desktop Chat: `Browser.list_tabs` | Same failure |
| Chat page reading | Not attempted after enumeration failed |

### What steps can reproduce the bug?
1. Install/enable the official ChatGPT Chrome Web Store extension in Microsoft Edge, and keep the desktop app running.
2. Confirm that both official bundled diagnostics pass:
   - `check-extension-installed.js --browser edge --json`
   - `check-native-host-manifest.js --browser edge --json`
3. Verify Edge access from desktop Work using only a public page. In this case, tab listing, reading `example.com`, following its IANA link, going back, and reloading all succeeded.
4. Create a new **normal Chat directly in the desktop app**, rather than on the web or in the extension sidebar.
5. Request an actual `Browser.list_tabs` call. In the test below it returned the originating-browser-context error, without returning a tab list.

**Test-method limitation:** the user created the new Chat directly in the desktop UI, then a local diagnostic Work task opened it with `navigate_to_codex_page` and submitted the test with `send_message_to_thread`. The Chat's response reports the real Browser call and exact error; `read_thread` exposes that request/response but not the raw internal Browser trace. A directly hand-typed desktop-composer A/B test was not independently captured. Please consider whether the cross-chat submission path is relevant. The receiving Chat also reported that it did not have sufficient metadata to independently identify its surface.

No web-search/fetch fallback was counted as browser success. No private tab contents were read. Private conversation IDs and account identifiers are omitted from this public issue.

### What is the expected behavior?
Normal desktop Chat should receive the authorized originating browser context when Browser tools are available, or clearly explain that the operation is unsupported on that surface. A healthy extension and native bridge should not lead to a tool being exposed that can only return a missing-origin-context exception.

### Additional information
#### Read-only inspection of the installed desktop bundle
The installed `webview/index.html` loads an entry point referencing:

```text
webview/assets/app-initial-3ccf4886957f.js
SHA-256: d6278b4127345cf6012fe969eea9f5a2d55a13225d1fcadc23db81ef5bab78fe
```

The following minified identifiers are specific to this build. Relevant excerpts:

```js
function ROt(){return VOt}
function zOt(e){VOt?.setLocation(e)}
function BOt(e){return VOt!=null&&(VOt.setAuthState(e),!0)}
var VOt;
function HOt(){return(HOt=t((()=>{})))()}
```

Within this module, the bridge variable `VOt` is declared but no assignment to it was found. Context preparation exits if that bridge is absent:

```js
function jqa(e){let t=ROt();if(t==null)return; /* ... t.prepareSubmit(...) ... */ }
```

The shared Chat submission pipeline calls `jqa(e)` and passes its optional `w?.context` as `sideChatContext` to the request builder. The only `browser_context` assignment found in this module is guarded by that context:

```js
function Mqa(e,t,n){
  if(t==null)return;
  e.client_contextual_info={app_name:`chatgpt.com`,app_surface:`browser_side_chat`};
  e.browser_context={instance_id:t.instanceId};
  // ...
}
```

The Chat fallback used by `send_message_to_thread` (`Gfo` → `Rfo`) reaches the shared `Hro` submission pipeline. Another UI submission call site also reaches `Hro`.

**Hypothesis, not a verified server root cause:** this native build appears to leave the side-chat context bridge uninitialized, causing `browser_context.instance_id` to be omitted. That is consistent with the returned exception. We did not capture the native outbound request or inspect the backend guard, so this does not establish every possible injection/routing path or prove that the cross-chat test is identical to a manually typed desktop request.

#### Follow-up: request construction, serialization, and available runtime evidence

**The native outbound HTTP request has not been captured.** The following findings combine read-only inspection of the distributed client with existing desktop logs; they are not a network trace or proof of the body received by the backend.

- The request preparation path described above passes the optional context from `jqa()` through `Hro()` to `UJa()` / `Mqa()`. In the inspected desktop module, no initialization assignment to the bridge variable `VOt` was found. With no bridge/context, `Mqa()` returns before adding `browser_context.instance_id`.
- Following the code further, `hqr()` constructs the POST to `/f/conversation` using `JSON.stringify(e)`. Its pre-dispatch path updates `client_prepare_state` and may add `app_attest_challenge`; the inspected branches do not add browser context.
- A scan of all distributed JavaScript modules under `/webview` and `/.vite` found one assignment that adds `browser_context` to a Chat request body: the `Mqa()` assignment shown above. The other two textual occurrences are cloud-browser-context deletion endpoints in settings, not desktop Chat context initialization.
- We examined 37 desktop log files for October 16, 2026 (approximately 4.4 MB). They do not expose Chat HTTP request bodies. Text matches inside diagnostic-task reasoning summaries were excluded as evidence of network traffic.
- The active session's startup log at `2026-10-16T05:54:16.684Z` reports `allowDebugMenu=false allowDevtools=false allowInspectElement=false buildFlavor=prod packaged=true`. This confirms the production inspection settings, not the contents of an outbound request.

**Interpretation:** the evidence points to context being omitted during client request construction, before serialization, rather than demonstrating that context is lost in transport. This remains an inference about the live request. We have not observed the actual native request body, the backend's context association, or the server-side guard that raises the exception. The cross-chat submission limitation documented above still applies.

A fix in the official client could supply the authorized browser context to the request builder. These findings do **not** establish that a server-side change is mandatory, nor that a local preference can repair the native tool. No supported local setting that initializes this context was identified.

To resolve the remaining uncertainty, a supported native-request capture or an OpenAI-side trace would need to establish whether `browser_context` / `instance_id` are present, alongside the request ID, timestamp, and client surface. Private prompts, cookies, and tokens are not needed in a public report.

#### Scope and integrity
This report concerns only `Browser.list_tabs` failing in normal Chat mode in the native desktop app. Desktop Work is included as a successful comparison test, not as a workaround.

The installed app was inspected read-only. App signature verification outside the diagnostic sandbox passed: `valid on disk` / `satisfies its Designated Requirement`. No app patching or re-signing was performed.

Could a maintainer confirm whether Browser access is intended to work in normal native desktop Chat in this build, and whether native/context initialization or the cross-chat submission path needs to supply the originating extension identity?
