issues.title: ACP: /rename reports success but doesn't rename the session

labels.name: area:sessions
labels.description: Session management, resume, history, session picker, and session state

labels.name: area:non-interactive
labels.description: Non-interactive mode (-p), CI/CD, ACP protocol, and headless automation

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

In ACP mode (`copilot --acp --stdio`), `/rename <name>` reports success but doesn't rename the session. Copilot advertises the command in `available_commands_update`, and sending it as a `session/prompt` ends `end_turn` in about 1 ms, with no model call, with the reply `Session renamed to: <name>`. But nothing is saved: the session's `workspace.yaml` keeps its old `name` and `user_named: false`, and `session/list` keeps returning the old `title`, from the same process and from a new one. `/session rename <name>` behaves the same.

ACP has no client method to set a session's title (titles are agent-owned and reported with `session_info_update`), so `/rename` is the only way for an ACP client to rename a Copilot session.

### Affected version

GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.95

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Start `copilot --acp --stdio` and `initialize`.
2. `session/new` with a `cwd`, and send one ordinary prompt, so the session is saved and listed (its title is the first message).
3. Send a `session/prompt` with the text `/rename My new name`.
4. The reply is `Session renamed to: My new name`, with `stopReason: end_turn`.
5. Call `session/list` with that `cwd`, in the same process or a new one: the session's `title` is still the first message.
6. Open `~/.copilot/session-state/<id>/workspace.yaml`: still the old `name`, and `user_named: false`. No `session_info_update` is sent with the new title.

### Expected behavior

`/rename <name>` over ACP renames the session as it does in the interactive CLI: it saves the name (`name`, `user_named: true`), `session/list` returns it, and Copilot sends a `session_info_update` with the new `title`, so the client can update its view.

### Additional context

- Windows 11, x86_64. Driven from a Node ACP client (`@agentclientprotocol/sdk`).
- Writing `name` and `user_named: true` into `workspace.yaml` by hand does change the title in `session/list`, so the listing side works. Only the command doesn't save.
- In the 1.0.95 bundle, one session implementation's `renameSession()` calls the native `session.name.set`, and another's is an empty stub (`async renameSession(t){}`, next to `getWorkspace(){return null}`). The ACP session seems to get the stub. The success message is printed either way.
- Related: #4244 (`/rename` in VS Code agent sessions), #2622 (a manual name overwritten by an automatic one).

issues.title: ACP: plugin skills aren't available in ACP sessions, though the plugin's agents are
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

In ACP mode (`copilot --acp --stdio`), skills from enabled plugins aren't available in a session. The plugin itself loads, since the `agent` config option offers its agents. But none of its skills:

- are in `available_commands_update`, so an ACP client can't offer them as slash commands;
- show in `/skills list` sent over ACP, which lists only project and personal skills;
- reach the model: asked to list its skills, it names only the personal one.

Outside ACP, with the same `COPILOT_HOME` and folder, the skills are there: `copilot skill list` lists them under "Plugin skills", and in `copilot -p` the model lists them.

### Affected version

GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.104 (also seen on 1.0.92)

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Enable plugins that have skills, and add one personal skill as a control. Here, two plugins from local marketplace directories, which `copilot plugin list` shows under "Live Plugins". Between them they have 12 agents and 36 skills.
2. `copilot skill list` lists the 36 under "Plugin skills".
3. Start `copilot --acp --stdio`, `initialize`, and call `session/new` with a `cwd`.
4. The `agent` config option offers the 12 plugin agents (`<plugin>:<agent>`).
5. `available_commands_update` has 33 commands: the 32 built-in commands and the personal skill. None of the plugin skills are there.
6. Send `/skills list` as a `session/prompt`. It lists only the personal skill ("Found 1 skill").
7. Send `Without using any tools, list the names of all the skills in your available skills list, comma-separated, and nothing else.` The reply names only the personal skill.
8. In the same folder, run `copilot -p` with the same text. The model lists the personal skill and the plugin skills.

### Expected behavior

An ACP session has the same skills as the interactive CLI and prompt mode, plugin skills included:

- they're offered in `available_commands_update`, as 1.0.40 did for skills ("Skills are available as slash commands in ACP clients, matching the CLI experience");
- `/skills list` lists them;
- the model can use them.

### Additional context

- Windows 11, x86_64, driven from a Node ACP client, in a scratch `COPILOT_HOME` with no extensions installed.
- Project and personal skills work over ACP. `/skills reload` picks up new ones and sends `available_commands_update`.
- Related: #2753 (plugin skills missing from `<available_skills>` in interactive sessions). There, a comment ties it to extensions that call `joinSession()`. Here no extension is installed, and prompt mode isn't affected.

issues.title: ACP: /session delete, cleanup and prune fail with "sessionsApi ... is unavailable for this session"
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

In ACP mode (`copilot --acp --stdio`), Copilot advertises `/session` in `available_commands_update`, but its `delete`, `cleanup` and `prune` subcommands fail over ACP. Sent as a `session/prompt`, each ends with `end_turn` in about 1 ms, without a model call, and replies with an error:

| Prompt | Reply |
|---|---|
| `/session delete <id>` | `Failed to run /session: Error: slash command effect sessionsApi.list is unavailable for this session` |
| `/session cleanup` | `Failed to run /session: Error: slash command effect sessionsApi.list is unavailable for this session` |
| `/session prune --older-than 1 --dry-run --include-named` | `Failed to run /session: Error: slash command effect sessionsApi.pruneOld is unavailable for this session` |

Nothing is deleted: the sessions' folders stay in `session-state`.

An ACP client has no other way to delete Copilot sessions. `initialize` offers `sessionCapabilities` `list` and `close` only, without ACP's stable [`session/delete`](https://agentclientprotocol.com/protocol/v1/session-delete).

### Affected version

GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.104

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Start `copilot --acp --stdio` and `initialize`.
2. Call `session/new` twice, for sessions A and B.
3. Send session A a `session/prompt` with the text `/session delete <B's sessionId>`.
4. The reply is the `sessionsApi.list` error above, with `stopReason: end_turn`. Session B's folder is still in `session-state`.
5. Send `/session cleanup`, then `/session prune --older-than 1 --dry-run --include-named`. Each gets its error above.

### Expected behavior

These subcommands work over ACP as they do in the interactive CLI:

- `/session delete <id>` deletes the session.
- `/session cleanup` removes empty or abandoned sessions.
- `/session prune --older-than <days>` deletes old sessions, or lists them with `--dry-run`.

Each replies with what it did.

Better still for ACP clients: advertise `sessionCapabilities.delete` and support `session/delete`. Then a client can delete a session without sending a prompt through another one.

### Additional context

- Windows 11, x86_64, driven from a Node ACP client, in a scratch `COPILOT_HOME`.
- `prune` checks its arguments before it fails. Without `--older-than` it replies with its usage, and `--older-than 0` gets `Invalid number of days: 0`. It fails once it needs the sessions API.
- This is like #5115. There, `/rename` over ACP replies that it renamed the session but saves nothing. In both cases the command is advertised over ACP, but the ACP session lacks what it needs.
- Related: #2555 (advertising every slash command over ACP) and #1451 (`/cleanup`).

issues.title: Regression (1.0.88 → 1.0.89): MCP OAuth authorization page opens on every ACP session instead of the challenge being resolved silently

labels.name: area:non-interactive
labels.description: Non-interactive mode (-p), CI/CD, ACP protocol, and headless automation

labels.name: area:mcp
labels.description: MCP server configuration, discovery, connectivity, OAuth, policy, and registry

issues.body:
## Describe the bug

An OAuth-protected HTTP MCP server that has a **valid, unexpired** access token in
`~/.copilot/mcp-oauth-config` is answered with HTTP 401 on every new `--acp`
session, and the CLI responds by opening the OAuth authorization page again.
Because the browser SSO session is already established, the flow self-approves
and the tab closes — so the user sees an unrequested sign-in page flash open on
*every single session start*, with no way to suppress it.

This is a **regression**: `1.0.88` connects the same server, with the same token,
and resolves the identical OAuth challenge silently — no page, no interaction.

Critically, the stored token has **no refresh token** (the tokens file contains
only `accessToken`, `expiresAt`, `scope`), so there is no silent renewal path —
the CLI appears to fall straight through to the interactive flow rather than
using the access token it already holds.

## Affected version

- **Last known good: `1.0.88`**
- **Broken: `1.0.89`**

A single version bump. Both were tested on the same machine, minutes apart, against
the same MCP server and the same on-disk token.

| Installed | Size | SHA-256 (first 16) | `--no-auto-update --version` | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Aug 14 | 152.1 MB | `4F590F1F60F3F2BD` | 1.0.80 | works — challenge resolved silently |
| Sep 23 | 144.2 MB | `E2160809894BA950` | **1.0.88** | **works** — challenge resolved silently |
| Sep 29 | 144.8 MB | `155778DD92A2171A` | **1.0.89** | **broken** — page opens every session |

**Secondary reporting bug worth fixing on its own:** plain `copilot --version`
reported `1.0.89` for *all three* binaries, including the 1.0.80 one. Only
`copilot --no-auto-update --version` reveals the real built-in versions above.
That made this regression very hard to characterise — it looked like one version
behaving two different ways. If `--version` is reporting a cached/candidate
package rather than the running build, it should say so.

- OS: Windows 11 (10.0.26200)
- Mode: `copilot --acp` (ACP server), 4 × `--plugin-dir`
- MCP protocol negotiated: `2025-11-25`

## Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Configure an OAuth-protected HTTP MCP server in `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json`:
   `https://mcp.internal.example.com/servers/REDACTED-MCP/mcp`
2. Complete its OAuth flow once. Confirm `~/.copilot/mcp-oauth-config` now holds a
   registration with `"isStatic": false` and a paired `*.tokens.json` whose keys are
   exactly `accessToken`, `expiresAt`, `scope` — i.e. **no `refreshToken`**, and
   `expiresAt` comfortably in the future (mine was ~3 days out).
3. Start `copilot --acp` and drive `initialize` → `authenticate` → `session/new`,
   passing that server in `mcpServers`.
4. Observe: the authorization page opens even though the token is still valid.
5. Repeat step 3. It opens again, every time.

## Expected behavior

With a valid unexpired access token on disk, `session/new` should connect the MCP
server using that token and open nothing. If the server genuinely rejects the
token with 401, the CLI should surface an actionable error rather than silently
launching a browser authorization flow on every session — that behaviour is
unusable for headless or unattended ACP clients.

## Actual behavior — CLI log

From `~/.copilot/logs/process-*.log` on the **Sep 29** build (hostnames redacted):

```
[ERROR] [rust:rmcp::transport::worker] worker quit with fatal: Transport channel closed,
        when Client(OAuthChallenge {
          www_authenticate_header: "******\"https://mcp.internal.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/servers/REDACTED-MCP/mcp\"",
          response: McpOAuthHttpResponse { status_code: 401, header_count: 6, has_body: true } })

[INFO]  [rust:acp::mcp_oauth] opened the MCP OAuth authorization page {"server_name":"REDACTED-MCP"}

[WARNING] [rust:copilot_runtime::session::mcp::agent_host] HTTP 401 challenge
        (WWW-Authenticate: ******"https://mcp.internal.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/servers/REDACTED-MCP/mcp")
        {"server":"REDACTED-MCP"}
```

Possibly the same root cause — the new discovery call is rejected for lack of a
bearer token, then falls back:

```
[WARNING] [rust:mcp::client] server/discover failed; retrying with legacy initialize
        {"error":"unexpected server response: HTTP 400 Bad Request: {\"error\":\"Invalid or missing bearer token\"}"}
```

## A/B isolating the build

Same machine, same 3-minute window, **same on-disk token** (issued earlier that day,
`expiresAt` 3 days out), identical client invocation and identical MCP server list.
Only the `copilot.exe` binary was swapped between runs:

| Run | Version | `opened the MCP OAuth authorization page` | `401 challenge` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 15:29 | 1.0.80 (`4F590F1F…`) | **0** | **0** |
| 15:32 | 1.0.89 (`155778DD…`) | **1** | **2** |
| 20:33 | **1.0.88** (`E2160809…`) | **0** | **0** |

Because the token was unchanged and still valid across all three runs, token expiry
is ruled out as the cause; the binary is the only variable. 1.0.88 passing puts the
regression squarely in the 1.0.88 → 1.0.89 change.

On 1.0.88 and 1.0.80 the server issues the **same** OAuth challenge — the log still shows
`worker quit with fatal: Transport channel closed, when Client(OAuthChallenge {…})`
— but it is then resolved without any user interaction:

```
[ERROR] Successfully authenticated with co-design
[INFO]  [rust:rmcp::service] Service initialized as client { … }
[ERROR] Handling tools refresh for co-design
```

So the regression is not "the server started returning 401". It is that 1.0.89 no
longer completes that challenge silently and instead falls back to opening the
interactive authorization page. (Those two lines are also logged at `ERROR` level
on success in 1.0.80, which looks like a separate log-level mistake.)

## Impact

Every new ACP session pops a browser window the operator did not ask for. For any
non-interactive ACP client (our case: a local web UI and scheduled agent runs)
this is disruptive, and on a headless host the flow has nobody to approve it.

issues.title: Org custom models on /chat/completions always fail with 400: CLI sends frequency_penalty/presence_penalty that providers reject (Google AI Studio, OpenAI-compatible)
issues.body:
## Describe the bug

Organization **custom models** (configured in the GitHub Copilot org settings) that are served over `/chat/completions` fail on every request in Copilot CLI with HTTP 400. Custom models served over `/responses` work fine in the same session.

The CLI sends OpenAI-specific sampling fields in every Chat Completions request to a custom model, and GitHub's proxy forwards them unchanged to the third-party provider, which rejects them:

```json
"temperature": 0,
"top_p": 0.95,
"frequency_penalty": 0,
"presence_penalty": 0,
"snippy": { "enabled": false },
"stream": true,
"stream_options": { "include_usage": true }
```

Google AI Studio's response names the field explicitly:

```text
Execution failed: 400 [{
  "error": {
    "code": 400,
    "message": "Invalid JSON payload received. Unknown name \"frequency_penalty\": Cannot find field.",
    "status": "INVALID_ARGUMENT"
  }
}]
```

Xiaomi MiMo (provider type `openaicompatible`) returns a generic `400 Invalid request parameters` (81-byte JSON body), which is very likely the same cause.

This looks like the same sampling-parameter regression reported for local BYOK in #4950 (introduced in 1.0.81), but here it is a hard failure that makes `/chat/completions` org custom models completely unusable from the CLI.

## Results by provider

| Custom model provider (catalog `custom_model.provider`) | `supported_endpoints` | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `azureai` (Azure AI Foundry, gpt-6-luna / gpt-6.1-sol / gpt-6.1-terra) | `/responses` | Works |
| `googleaistudio` (gemini-flash-latest, gemini-4-argon, ...) | `/chat/completions` | 400 `Unknown name "frequency_penalty"` |
| `openaicompatible` (Xiaomi MiMo mimo-v2.6-flash, mimo-v2.6-pro) | `/chat/completions` | 400 `Invalid request parameters` |

All models appear correctly in the `/model` picker and in the CAPI catalog (`capabilities.supports: {streaming: true, tool_calls: true}`, `family: "custom"`).

## Affected version

GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.104 (Windows 11). Copilot Business, org custom models, requests go to `api.business.githubcopilot.com`.

## Steps to reproduce

1. As an org owner, add a custom model from Google AI Studio (or any OpenAI-compatible provider) in the org's Copilot custom models settings.
2. In Copilot CLI, select it via `/model`, or run:
   `copilot -p "say hi" --model "<org>/<key-name>/gemini-flash-latest" --log-level all`
3. Observe the 400. The debug log shows the `Wire request` body containing the fields above, followed by:
   `Upstream model error response shape (body content omitted) {"status":400,...}` and
   `Model provider request failed {"stage":"inference","api_endpoint":"/chat/completions","http_status":400,"failure_kind":"http_error"}`
4. Switch to an Azure Foundry custom model on `/responses` in the same session: it answers normally.

Side note: on the first attempt the CLI also logs `Model HTTP request with a compressed body was rejected; resending it uncompressed {"status":400,"content_encoding":"zstd"}`, and the uncompressed retry fails with the same 400, so compression is not the cause.

## Request IDs (for server-side correlation)

- Gemini (googleaistudio): `04C1:5294A:2E6DEC6:309B2BF:6AE102C3`, `04C1:2DF905:17A52BF:1A3B26D:6AE10A9B`
- MiMo (openaicompatible): `04C0:2A654E:2678A92:28B3279:6AE1026C`, `04C1:2DF905:179D61C:1A326DB:6AE10A7E`, `04C3:2FE0EC:24A422F:26C2232:6AE0FF00` (serviceRequestId `fb5768cd-4895-4282-b3c8-98a8fe123d7e`)

## Expected behavior

For custom models, the CLI (or the CAPI proxy) should not send sampling parameters the provider has not declared support for. Options:

- Omit `temperature` / `top_p` / `frequency_penalty` / `presence_penalty` for `family: "custom"` models (CLI 1.0.80 sent none), or send only non-default values.
- Have the proxy strip non-standard / unsupported fields (`snippy`, penalties) per provider type, e.g. drop penalties for `googleaistudio`.
- Expose a per-model capability flag in the catalog so the client knows which sampling fields are accepted.

## Additional context

- Related: #4950 (same sampling fields forced since 1.0.81, local BYOK), #3448 (control extra request params for BYOK models).
- There is no CLI setting to disable these fields, so there is currently no workaround inside the CLI for `/chat/completions` custom models.

issues.title: Per-agent provider selection for custom agents

labels.name: area:agents
labels.description: Sub-agents, fleet, autopilot, plan mode, background agents, and custom agents

labels.name: area:models
labels.description: Model selection, availability, switching, rate limits, and model-specific behavior

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, improvement, or new functionality

issues.body:
I know about BYOK (`COPILOT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL` plus `COPILOT_MODEL`), `/model`, and the `model` field in custom-agent frontmatter. We use all three. None of them lets two agents in one session talk to two different endpoints, because `COPILOT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL` is process-wide and nothing scopes it to an agent. That is the difference between this and #3624 and copilot-sdk#1545, both closed within hours pointing at the BYOK docs.

## The ask

A `provider` field in custom-agent frontmatter. Or the per-agent `env`/`env_file` scoping that #2879 proposes for secrets, which would do the same job. The main agent keeps the session provider. The subagent gets its own base URL.

## What the runtime already does

I put a recording HTTP server at `COPILOT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL` on 1.0.83-3 and dispatched a custom agent through the `task` tool. Three requests came out of one session:

```
1  model=local-worker-model  tools=24  main agent
2  model=ROUTE-ME-LOCAL      tools=1   subagent; model from its .agent.md frontmatter,
                                       its own instructions in the system prompt
3  model=local-worker-model  tools=24  main agent
```

The `model` override on the `task` tool arrives the same way. The per-agent model id already reaches the provider, and v1.0.62 ("Keep custom agents on their configured model when using BYOK providers") and v1.0.65 for subagents made that deliberate. What it cannot carry is an endpoint to send that id to.

## Use case

A cloud main agent plans and reviews. It hands renames, comment edits, log lines and single-file changes to a subagent running a 27B model on the developer's Mac (MLX, 48 GB). Those tokens cost nothing. I am not claiming the local model matches the cloud one. On our own eight-task benchmark two local models came out indistinguishable from each other, and the only claim I will stand behind is free tokens for mechanical work. Judgement stays in the cloud.

## What we tried

A routing proxy at `COPILOT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL`, keyed on the model id. Known local ids go to the MLX server and the proxy forwards the rest to GitHub. Two problems killed it. It puts the main agent's traffic through GitHub endpoints that are not documented for that use. And the docs say "A declared model or effort that can't be honored falls back to the session's value instead of failing the dispatch", so any proxy error on a local id sends that task to the session model instead. You find out from the bill rather than from an error.

## Related

- #2879 asks for per-agent `env:`/`env_file:` to isolate secrets. Same mechanism, different reason for wanting it.
- #2728 asks for per-agent LSP config, so per-agent configuration beyond `model` is a shape this project already accepts.
- #3709, #3282, #1354, #2554 and #2758 want the model version of this. A commenter on #3709 already asked for subagents to use the other models a provider offers.
- copilot-sdk#1544 named routing subagent tasks to a local endpoint. Its author closed it 14 minutes later while still investigating, and nobody from GitHub replied.

issues.title: Model "auto" always runs with reasoning effort disabled (reasoningEffort: null), and rejects any attempt to configure one

labels.name: area:models
labels.description: Model selection, availability, switching, rate limits, and model-specific behavior

labels.name: area:configuration
labels.description: Config files, instruction files, settings, and environment variables

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

When the model is set to `auto`, every request is sent **without any reasoning effort**:

1. Selecting `auto` sets the session's `reasoningEffort` to `null` (visible in the session's `events.jsonl` as `session.model_change → "reasoningEffort": null`).
2. The auto router (`auto_v2`) picks a model per prompt (`session.auto_mode_resolved`) but **never assigns a reasoning effort** to it — the request goes out with none, confirmed by `reasoning_effort = NULL` and `reasoning_tokens = 0` in `~/.copilot/session-store.db` (`assistant_usage_events`).
3. Trying to set one explicitly is rejected: `copilot --model auto --effort xhigh` fails with `Error: Model "auto" does not support reasoning effort configuration (requested: "xhigh").`

So with `auto` there is **no way at all** to run with reasoning enabled. The degradation is silent — no error, no indication in the UI — and the impact on agentic work is severe: on a large agentic prompt (spec generation with mandatory file reads), the routed model (`gpt-5.3-codex`) ends its turn **without making a single tool call**, replying that it "could not perform the investigation". The exact same prompt, on the exact same routed model, works flawlessly when a reasoning effort is set (see "Same model, only effort differs" below).

### Affected version

GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.80.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

```bash
# 1) auto → no reasoning (silent)
copilot --model auto --allow-all-tools -p "Reply with exactly: ok"

# 2) control: explicit model → reasoning works
copilot --model gpt-5.4 --allow-all-tools -p "Reply with exactly: ok"

# 3) auto + explicit effort → hard error
copilot --model auto --effort xhigh --allow-all-tools -p "Reply with exactly: ok"
```

Then inspect what was actually sent (replace the session ids printed in the `Resume` line):

```bash
sqlite3 -readonly ~/.copilot/session-store.db \
  "SELECT session_id, model, reasoning_effort, reasoning_tokens
   FROM assistant_usage_events ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 5;"
```

Observed results:

| Run | Routed/used model | `reasoning_effort` | `reasoning_tokens` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 — `--model auto` | `gpt-5.4-mini` (via `auto_v2`) | **NULL** | **0** |
| 2 — `--model gpt-5.4` | `gpt-5.4` | `xhigh` | 21 |
| 3 — `--model auto --effort xhigh` | — | — | `Error: Model "auto" does not support reasoning effort configuration (requested: "xhigh").` |

The same happens in interactive mode: switching to `auto` logs
`session.model_change ... "previousReasoningEffort": "xhigh", "reasoningEffort": null`
in `~/.copilot/session-state/<session-id>/events.jsonl`, and every subsequent `session.auto_mode_resolved` runs the chosen model with no effort.

### Same model, only effort differs — night and day

Real-world case that led us here (a large spec-generation prompt, ~19.6k input tokens, requiring file reads and skill loading):

- `auto` → routed to `gpt-5.3-codex`, `reasoning_effort = NULL`: the model ends the turn after **158 output tokens, 0 reasoning tokens, 0 tool calls**, claiming it could not perform the investigation. Reproduced consistently across several sessions.
- Same prompt, same `gpt-5.3-codex`, with `reasoning_effort = xhigh`: normal agentic behavior — tool calls, thousands of reasoning tokens, task completed.

The only variable is the reasoning effort. `auto` mode currently guarantees the degraded path.

### Expected behavior

`auto` should never silently disable reasoning. Either:

- the auto router assigns an appropriate reasoning effort for the routed model on each request (clamping to what that model supports), and/or
- a user-provided effort (`--effort`, settings `effortLevel`, session config) is honored under `auto` and clamped per routed model — instead of being cleared on switch and rejected on the CLI flag.

### Additional context

- This looks like an overcorrection of #2870: there, switching to `auto` **kept** the previous effort and caused loud `400` errors on models that don't support it; the fix apparently clears the effort entirely, trading a loud error for a silent, permanent degradation. #4459 and #4445 show the invalid-combination side of this is still not fully solved either — both symptoms share the same root: the auto router does not manage effort per routed model.
- The ACP server mode (`copilot --acp`) is affected identically, with no workaround at all: `session/set_config_option` with `model=auto` clears the effort and removes the reasoning-effort config option from the session, so ACP clients cannot restore it.

issues.title: Voice server permanent deadlock when pid file is deleted while server process survives (bind-loser exits before writing pid)

labels.name: area:platform-windows
labels.description: Windows-specific: PowerShell, cmd, Git Bash, WSL, Windows Terminal

issues.body:
## Summary
Voice server enters a permanent deadlock ("Failed to connect to or spawn the voice server after 3 attempts: voice server did not write a valid pid file within 8000ms") whenever its pid file is deleted (e.g. by OS temp-directory cleanup) while the server process itself is still alive and holding the named pipe.

## Root cause (traced in shipped 1.0.84-1 win32-x64 build)
Voice IPC uses two independent records of server liveness that can desync:
- A Windows named pipe `\\.\pipe\copilot-voice-<hash>` (kernel object, survives independently)
- A pid file at `%TEMP%\copilot-voice\<hash>.pid` (the client's *only* source of truth)

Both `<hash>` values are derived deterministically: `sha256(cliVersion + "|" + sha256(USERPROFILE).slice(0,8)).slice(0,8)`.

Sequence that produces the deadlock:
1. A server starts, wins the pipe, writes its pid file. It keeps running (idle-shutdown only arms once its connected-client count reaches 0; clients that die without a clean disconnect can keep that count above 0 indefinitely, so a server can persist for days).
2. The pid file is removed independently of the process (observed cause: Windows temp-directory cleanup). The pipe is untouched — it's a kernel object, not a file.
3. `app.js` client logic reads the pid file to decide whether to connect or spawn:
   ```js
   let p = readPid(t.pidFile);
   if (p !== null && isAlive(p)) { connect(t.address) /* ... */ }
   // else: falls straight through to spawning a new server — never attempts connect(t.address) directly
   ```
   A missing pid file skips the connect branch entirely, even though `t.address` is already known deterministically and the pipe is live and accepting connections.
4. The client spawns a new server. The new process computes the same pipe name, tries to bind, and loses to the still-running original.
5. In `voice-server.js`, the losing branch exits **before** ever writing a pid file:
   ```js
   S === "lost" && (log("bind-loser..."), await i.dispose(), process.exit(id)) // id = 10
   // ... pid file write (Lo(t.pidFile, process.pid)) is further down, never reached here
   ```
6. The client waits the full pid-file timeout (`$_n = 8e3`, 8000ms) for a file that can never appear, then retries (`WJe = [0,100,500]`, 3 attempts total), then throws the error above.

Every retry repeats step 4-6 identically — this is a **permanent** deadlock, not a transient failure. It only resolves if something external kills the original server or manually restores the pid file.

## Suggested fixes (either alone fixes it)
1. In the client (`app.js`), when the pid file is missing/stale, attempt `connect(t.address)` directly before spawning — the address is already computed deterministically, so this costs nothing and immediately closes the race.
2. In the server (`voice-server.js`), on `bind-loser`, write the *winning* pid (which is discoverable from the bind failure) to the pid file before exiting, instead of exiting silently with no pid file at all.

Either change means a deleted pid file can never produce an unrecoverable state as long as the real owning process is still alive.

## Environment
- Copilot CLI 1.0.84-1, win32-x64
- Reproduced by manually deleting `%TEMP%\copilot-voice\<hash>.pid` while a previously-started voice server process was still running; the next voice-triggering CLI invocation failed with the exact reported error, deterministically, on every retry.

## Workaround used
Killing the orphaned server process (identified via its named pipe and boot-time server log) releases the pipe, allowing a fresh spawn to bind and write its pid file normally. A local `sessionStart` hook now detects this exact signature (dead/missing pid file + live matching pipe + exactly one candidate `copilot.exe --prefer-version <version>` process) and self-heals by writing the correct pid before the CLI ever attempts to connect.

issues.title: Provide a system-wide Windows installer for enterprise deployment

labels.name: area:enterprise
labels.description: GitHub Enterprise (GHE/GHES) support, org policies, and enterprise settings

labels.name: area:platform-windows
labels.description: Windows-specific: PowerShell, cmd, Git Bash, WSL, Windows Terminal

labels.description: Installing, updating, versioning, PATH setup, and binary distribution

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, improvement, or new functionality

issues.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you'd like to solve

In our environment, GitHub Copilot CLI installs into the user profile and also attempts to execute files from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\copilot`.  This conflicts with our corporate security requirements, which restrict execution from user-writable directories. Installing the main executable centrally is therefore insufficient if the CLI still extracts or runs supporting executables from the user profile.  We need a supported deployment option that works without weakening these restrictions.

### Proposed solution

Provide an official system-wide Windows installer, preferably MSI, with the following capabilities:

- **Machine-wide installation** into an administrator-controlled location such as `%ProgramFiles%\GitHub Copilot CLI`.
- **All bundled executables and runtime dependencies installed centrally**, without extracting or executing them from `%LOCALAPPDATA%`, `%APPDATA%`, or other user-writable locations.
- **Silent installation, upgrade, and uninstallation** for centralized software deployment.
- **Operation without local administrator privileges** after installation.
- **Administrator-controlled updates**, including an option to disable automatic updates and prevent per-user executable downloads.
- **Clear separation between application binaries and user data**. Configuration, authentication information, logs, and session history may remain in the user profile, but application executables should not.
- **Documentation of executable locations and update behavior** so administrators can configure application-control policies appropriately.

## Acceptance criteria

An administrator can deploy GitHub Copilot CLI once for all users. A standard user can then use it without the CLI installing, extracting, updating, or executing its own bundled binaries in user-writable directories.

This should work in an environment where execution from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\copilot` and other user-profile directories is blocked.

## Business value

This would make GitHub Copilot CLI deployable in managed corporate environments without requiring security-policy exceptions or unsupported packaging workarounds.

issues.body:
## Summary
After updating to Copilot CLI 1.0.100 (which also pulled a new voice runtime), voice input no longer works on WSL2. The voice server process segfaults (signal 11) a few seconds after starting, so `/voice` stays on "Fetching voice models" and no model can be downloaded.

## Environment
- Copilot CLI: 1.0.100 (linux-x64), latest at time of report
- OS: Ubuntu (glibc 2.39) on WSL2, kernel 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2
- CPU: x64 with AVX2, 8 cores, 16 GB RAM
- Audio: WSLg PulseAudio available (`/mnt/wslg/PulseServer`)
- Voice worked on earlier versions (e.g. 1.0.98) with the older runtime (`Microsoft.AI.Foundry.Local.Core.so`, ~645 MB)

## Steps to reproduce
1. Update to 1.0.100; the update installs a new voice runtime (`libfoundry_local.so`, ~85 MB).
2. Start `copilot` and run `/voice`, choose Continue.
3. Status shows "Fetching voice models" indefinitely.

## Actual behaviour
Process log:
```
[INFO]  voice server: boot pid=1708 endpoint=/run/user/1000/copilot-voice/<id>.sock
[INFO]  voice server: connected to spawned voice server pid=1708
[WARNING] [VoiceEngine] connection error: read ECONNRESET
[ERROR] [VoiceEngine] fatal: Engine connection closed.
[WARNING] [VoiceEngine] start failed: Engine connection closed.
```
WSL kernel log (repeated on every attempt, ~6-15s after the voice server starts):
```
copilot: MainThread: potentially unexpected fatal signal 11.
WSL (CaptureCrash): Capturing crash for pid: 1708, executable: .../@github/copilot-linux-x64/copilot, signal: 11
```

## Already tried
- Removed stale `/run/user/$UID/copilot-voice/*` socket/pid files
- Deleted `~/.cache/copilot/foundry` and `~/.github-copilot-cli/cache/models`, then re-ran `/voice` to reinstall the runtime. The crash still occurs with the freshly downloaded runtime.
- `ldd` on `libfoundry_local.so` reports no missing libraries.

## Expected behaviour
The voice server stays running, the model list loads, and dictation works.

Possibly related: #4024

issues.title: Input history (command-history-state.json) is last-writer-wins across concurrent copilot processes; prompts typed in one session are erased
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

`~/.copilot/command-history-state.json` is shared by every interactive `copilot` process, and the last process to write it wins. Each process loads the file once at startup and keeps the list in memory. Each time it saves a prompt, it writes the whole list back to the file, without re-reading or merging. When two or more `copilot` processes are open, whichever one writes last erases every entry the others added after it started. Those prompts then disappear from Up arrow and Ctrl+R in every later session.

**Evidence (one machine, 2026-10-27, UTC):** three interactive processes were running at once.

- Process A (1.0.103) had been running since 23:34 the previous day.
- Process C (1.0.103) started at 02:57.
- Process B (1.0.104) started at 03:01, so it loaded the history file at that point.
- The final history file has 50 entries, newest first. B last wrote it at 14:29:54, when B submitted a prompt. It contains:
  - B's prompts from 14:19 to 14:29.
  - C's prompts from 02:58 and 03:00, which were before B started.
  - A's prompts up to 02:43, also before B started.
- **It's missing C's 14:15:13 prompt.** That prompt was submitted normally while the session was idle, with no error, so C's success path should have saved it. B's next write at 14:19:47 erased it.
- A's later prompts (03:00:55, 04:58, 05:00 and 14:12) are also missing. Each came right after a `Submission failed`, so they don't prove this bug either way. If the 04:58, 05:00 and 14:12 messages were late deliveries of "failed" prompts, the CLI never saved them (#5264). If they were retypes, B's later writes would have erased them anyway, because B started at 03:01. The 03:00:55 message came before B started, and #5264 explains why the history file indicates it was most likely never saved.

**Code (shipped `cli-main.js`, 1.0.103 and 1.0.104):** the history manager's `initialize()` loads the file once. `addCommand()` puts the new entry at the front of the in-memory array, then `saveHistory()` writes the whole array through `cliCommandHistoryWrite`. Nothing re-reads or merges the file before writing.

### Affected version

1.0.103 and 1.0.104. The code is the same in both.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

The steps below follow from the code. I haven't run this minimal version yet; the evidence above comes from normal use.

1. Open terminal 1 and run `copilot`. Open terminal 2 and run `copilot`.
2. In terminal 1, submit `alpha`.
3. In terminal 2, submit `beta`.
4. Without exiting the first two, start a third `copilot` and press Up. `beta` is there, but `alpha` is missing.

### Expected behavior

Concurrent sessions shouldn't erase each other's history. Either option would work:

- Under a file lock, re-read the file, merge the new entry by recency, remove duplicates, trim to `commandHistoryMaxSize`, then write.
- Store history as an append-only log and compact it when reading.

### Additional context

- macOS 27.0.1 (26A434), arm64. Ghostty, zsh.
- Several interactive `copilot` processes usually run at the same time on this machine.
- We found this while trying to recover a prompt that the CLI had discarded (#5264). Because of this bug, input history can't be relied on as a safety net for lost prompts.

issues.title: Prompt is discarded after 'Submission failed' (host-ack timeout): composer cleared, not saved to history, delivered late or never
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

When `session.send` fails because the session host stopped acknowledging events (the #5100 state), the CLI clears the prompt the user just submitted and keeps no copy of it. What happens to the prompt afterwards is unpredictable: sometimes it's delivered later anyway, and sometimes it's never delivered. The CLI shows:

```
Submission failed: Error: Request session.send failed with message: session event delivery failed: session host did not acknowledge the assistant.reasoning_delta event within 120s
```

After that, the composer is empty and the text is not put back. Up arrow and Ctrl+R don't find it, and there is no resend option. In the case below:

- **One "failed" prompt was most likely delivered 73 seconds later, after the user had been told it failed.** Input history points to a late delivery rather than a retype (see the timeline).
- **A later multi-paragraph prompt was never delivered.** The user had to rewrite it from memory.

**Why this happens (from reading the shipped `cli-main.js` in 1.0.103 and 1.0.104):** in the interactive submit path, the prompt is added to input history only in the success branch after `session.send` resolves. The error branch only emits `Submission failed`. The pending-submission tracker retires the draft when the send throws, and nothing restores the text to the composer. This means any `session.send` rejection leaves the user with no copy of the prompt, not only the 120s acknowledgement timeout. Whether the prompt still reaches the agent later is decided out of the user's sight.

**How often:** since October 23, this machine's retained session data has **20 `Submission failed` errors across 5 sessions, all with this host-acknowledgement error (the event named varies)**. #5100 notes that the agent's own output keeps being saved to `events.jsonl` after delivery fails. The user's input is the one thing nobody keeps a copy of.

### Affected version

1.0.103 (`copilotVersion` in `session.start`). The same submit and history code is in 1.0.104.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

This isn't deterministic, because it depends on first reaching the #5100 state.

1. Run a long interactive session. Ours was launched through a wrapper that loads several extensions. It used autopilot, many subagents, and a recurring scheduled prompt every 30 minutes. It ran 15 hours with 13 auto-compactions and no resume.
2. Wait until the host stops acknowledging events (#5100). The first visible sign is `Submission failed: ... did not acknowledge ... within 120s`.
3. Keep working. Submit prompts while the agent is busy.
4. Some submissions show `Submission failed`, and each one clears the composer. In our case, after the CLI logged `queue drain abandoned`, the next failed prompt (14:19:03) was never delivered before the user exited 11 minutes later, and no copy of it remained.

Timeline of the affected session (UTC, 2026-10-27):

| Time | What happened |
|---|---|
| 02:59:42 | First `Submission failed ... assistant.reasoning_delta ... within 120s`. The session was about 3.5 hours old. |
| 03:00–13:48 | The session stays partly usable. The agent keeps running turns. Two more `Submission failed` errors appear, at 04:56 and 04:59. Each of the three failures is followed 71–73 seconds later by a typed message arriving as a steering message. The first of these (03:00:55) was most likely the "failed" 02:59:42 prompt delivered late, not a retype. Successful submits write input history, and the history file suggests this one never did (see the explanation below the table). We can't tell whether the 04:58 and 05:00 messages were retypes or late deliveries. All 22 runs of the 30-minute scheduled prompt in this period log a `schedule_delivery_failed` warning ("Scheduled prompt #1 ... failed"), yet each run arrives 3 seconds to 4 minutes later. |
| 14:11:40 | `Submission failed`. A typed steering message arrives 21 seconds later. Like the 04:56 and 04:59 cases, we can't tell whether it was a retype or a late delivery. |
| 14:17:15 | The scheduled run fails again. This time it is not delivered. |
| 14:17:26 | `Scheduled queue processing failed after retry; queue drain abandoned` |
| 14:19:03 | `Submission failed` for a long multi-paragraph prompt. At the same moment the log shows two `Scheduled queue processing failed; retrying once` lines, and no later line reports the retry's outcome. **This prompt was never delivered and no copy of it remains.** |
| 14:29:52 | The user exits. Shutdown also fails with the same cached delivery error. |

Evidence that the 14:19:03 prompt was lost:

- `events.jsonl` has no user-typed `user.message` after 14:12:01. The only later `user.message` is a subagent prompt at 14:14:46.
- The text wasn't restored to the composer.
- It isn't in input history. That file also has a separate overwrite problem (#5265), so the code path above is the stronger evidence here.

Why the 03:00:55 message was most likely a late delivery and not a retype:

1. A second process (call it C) saved two prompts to history at 02:58 and 03:00:13. That process started after this session did, so this session's in-memory history list didn't include those two entries.
2. A third process loaded the history file when it started at 03:01:34, and it wrote the final version of the file at 14:29:54. The final file still contains the 02:58 and 03:00:13 entries.
3. If this session had saved a history entry at 03:00:55, it would have written its own list, which lacked those two entries, over the file before 03:01:34. They survived, so this session saved nothing between 03:00:55 and 03:01:34. Process C didn't write again in that window, because no later C entry from that window appears in the file.
4. In the shipped code, every interactive submit path saves to history when the send call returns. For steering submissions, the submit tracker resolves `true` once the send returns, and history is skipped only if an internal `skipHistory` option is set. No `Submission failed` appeared near 03:00:55, so a retyped prompt's send didn't fail. If it succeeded, it would have saved to history, unless its send took more than 39 seconds to return. The 03:00:55 message was therefore most likely the 02:59:42 prompt, delivered late. Either way, the user was told the 02:59:42 prompt failed and had no copy of it.

### Expected behavior

- Save the draft before sending it (for example, in session state), and clear it only after the session confirms it has the prompt.
- If the send fails, put the text and attachments back in the composer, or keep the prompt visibly marked as failed with a resend option.
- Add the prompt to input history whether or not the send succeeds. History records what the user typed.
- Report delivery honestly. If a "failed" prompt is still queued and will run later, don't say it failed. If it's dropped (for example, after `queue drain abandoned`), say so explicitly.
- If the session is in the permanent failed state from #5100, say so. Carry unsent drafts across `--resume` or `/restart` so they can be resent.

### Additional context

- macOS 27.0.1 (26A434), arm64, 96 GiB RAM
- Ghostty, zsh
- Launched through a wrapper that adds several native extensions. Several other interactive `copilot` processes were running on the same machine.
- `events.jsonl` for the affected session was 444 MB.
- Related: #5100 (the root failure state), #5253, and #5018 (same family). #1780 asks to recover queued prompts after a crash. #4477 covers a prompt lost on stop.

The full logs contain private content and can't be shared publicly. I can provide filtered excerpts on request.

issues.title: Session event delivery permanently fails after one 120s host-ack timeout ("session host did not acknowledge the <event> event within 120s"); session unusable until resume

labels.name: area:sessions
labels.description: Session management, resume, history, session picker, and session state

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

In long-running interactive sessions, prompt submission fails with:

```
Execution failed: Error: Request session.send failed with message: session event delivery failed:
session host did not acknowledge the tool.execution_partial_result event within 120s
```

After the first timeout, every later event delivery to that session host fails immediately with the same message, and the session accepts no more input. The only way to recover is to exit and run `copilot --resume` (or `/restart`).

Related: #5018. It has the same failure that never clears and the same `session.send failed` ending, but on the `permission.requested` 5-second path. This report covers general session event delivery with the 120s deadline, and the trigger appears to be the Node main thread becoming unresponsive.

### Affected version

GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.94 (observed). Also seen on 1.0.90–1.0.92 builds, Oct 1–9. Not yet observed on 1.0.95-3.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

Not deterministic. Conditions present in every occurrence:

1. Start an interactive session (`copilot`) and work in it for many hours: frequent shell tool calls, subagents, several auto-compactions, and at least one `copilot --resume` of the same session.
2. Let the context grow large (model request bodies of ~0.4–2 MB).
3. Eventually a turn stalls. About 120s later, the next prompt submission fails with the error above, and every later prompt fails the same way until exit and `--resume`.

### Expected behavior

- One late acknowledgement shouldn't break event delivery for the rest of the session. Delivery should resume once the host responds, or the session should reconnect automatically without exit and `--resume`.
- The Node main thread shouldn't stall for over 120s in long or large sessions.

### Additional context

**Environment:** macOS 26.7 (25G229), arm64 (Apple Silicon), Ghostty terminal, zsh.

**Log observations (`~/.copilot/logs/process-*.log`, several processes):**

- **The event type in the message varies:** `tool.execution_partial_result`, `session.usage_record`, `prompt_cache_break`, `session.managed_settings_resolved`, `session.background_tasks_changed`. The event named is whichever one was waiting when the deadline passed. `tool.execution_partial_result` shows up most often because one is sent for each chunk of shell output.
- **The failure never clears.** Only the first failure waits the full 120s. After that, every delivery fails within milliseconds with the identical message, which still names the original event. One process logged it 1,645 times.
- **Onset example:**
  ```
  19:28:07 [pending_request_flow] Waiting for detached host delivery flush
  19:28:44 [pending_request_flow] Detached host delivery flush finished {"acknowledged":true}   <- 37s, host already lagging
  19:28:46 [event_sink] Native model usage projection started                                 <- sends prompt_cache_break
  19:30:46 [pending_request_flow] ... session host did not acknowledge the prompt_cache_break event within 120s
  19:30:47 [github_telemetry::node_memory] Node memory snapshot timed out
  ```
  62 more `Node memory snapshot timed out` lines followed in that process, so the Node main thread was unresponsive. This isn't a delivery-transport problem.
- **Affected processes:** long-running (15+ hours, resumed sessions), ~1.7 GB of memory. Between stalls, the main thread was idle in `kevent`, so the stalls come in bursts rather than as a constant spin.

The full logs contain private repository content and can't be shared publicly. I can provide filtered excerpts on request.

issues.title: Copy/Paste broken in Copilot CLI when using SSH inside a tmux session on macOS/Linux → Windows Server 2025

labels.name: area:input-keyboard

labels.name: area:platform-windows
labels.description: Windows-specific: PowerShell, cmd, Git Bash, WSL, Windows Terminal

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

After upgrading to Copilot CLI v1.0.47, copy/paste no longer works when accessing Copilot CLI on a remote Windows Server 2025 machine via SSH **from inside a tmux session**.


### Affected version

v1.0.47

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

| Scenario | Copy/Paste |
|---|---|
| Open Copilot CLI directly on macOS/Linux | ✅ Works |
| SSH into Windows Server, open Copilot CLI | ✅ Works |
| Open tmux session → SSH into Windows Server → open Copilot CLI | ❌ Broken |

Other CLI tools (Codex CLI, Gemini CLI) handle copy/paste correctly in all three scenarios.

## tmux Configuration

```
set -g prefix C-a
unbind C-b

bind C-a send-prefix
bind | split-window -h -c "#{pane_current_path}"
bind - split-window -v -c "#{pane_current_path}"
unbind '"'
unbind %

set -g mouse on
set -g history-limit 50000
set -g allow-passthrough on

set -g default-terminal "tmux-256color"
set -as terminal-features ",xterm*:RGB"

bind r source-file ~/.tmux.conf \; display "Reloaded!"

set -g @plugin 'tmux-plugins/tpm'
set -g @plugin 'tmux-plugins/tmux-sensible'

set -g @plugin 'egel/tmux-gruvbox'
set -g @tmux-gruvbox 'light'
set -g @tmux-gruvbox-statusbar-alpha 'true'

set -g @plugin 'tmux-plugins/tmux-resurrect'
set -g @plugin 'tmux-plugins/tmux-continuum'
set -g @continuum-restore 'on'
set -g @resurrect-capture-pane-contents 'on'

run '~/.tmux/plugins/tpm/tpm'

set -g status-right ''
```

### Expected behavior

Copy/paste should work consistently regardless of whether the terminal is running inside a tmux session.


### Additional context

The `set -g allow-passthrough on` option is already set in the tmux config, which is typically required for OSC52 clipboard passthrough. This suggests Copilot CLI may be using a different clipboard mechanism that does not survive the `tmux → SSH` chain.

issues.title: Add ability to unarchive / restore an archived project session

labels.name: area:sessions
labels.description: Session management, resume, history, session picker, and session state

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, improvement, or new functionality

issues.body:
## Scenario

I accidentally archived a long-running project session that I'd been using as an orchestrator (it had spawned many child sessions via cross-session messages, accumulated significant context across many turns, and had a checkpoint summarizing its state).

When I realized the mistake and tried to resume it, I couldn't find a way to bring the session back. As far as I can tell:

- Archived sessions aren't visible in the normal project session list
- There's no "unarchive" or "restore" action exposed in the UI or via tooling
- The session's state still exists (history, checkpoints, branch, worktree all intact) — it just isn't reachable

The only workaround I found was to create a **new** session and seed its kickoff prompt with a hand-assembled context dump from the previous session's last checkpoint. That works, but:

- It's a clone, not a resume — the new session has a different ID, so any cross-session references from child sessions still point at the dead parent
- It requires me (or an agent) to manually reconstruct context, which is error-prone and loses fidelity
- Any in-flight automations tied to the original session ID are orphaned

## Request

Add a first-class way to **unarchive / restore an archived project session**, ideally:

1. An "Archived" view or filter in the project session list
2. A restore action that brings the session back with the same ID, branch, worktree, and history intact
3. (Optional) Equivalent tooling exposure so agents can recover from accidental archives without the kickoff-prompt workaround

## Why this matters

Archive is a one-click action and easy to hit by mistake. For short-lived sessions the loss is minor, but for long-running orchestrator/parent sessions — the exact ones most valuable to preserve — an accidental archive is currently destructive in practice even though the data is still there.

issues.title: BYOK Azure OpenAI: `429` throttling exhausts all retries in ~0.15s with no effective backoff; retry count/wait not configurable

labels.name: area:networking
labels.description: Proxy, SSL/TLS, certificates, corporate environments, and connectivity issues

labels.name: area:models
labels.description: Model selection, availability, switching, rate limits, and model-specific behavior

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

Using a BYOK **Azure OpenAI** provider (`COPILOT_PROVIDER_TYPE=azure`), transient throttling (`429 Too Many Requests`) causes Copilot CLI to burn all 5 retries near-instantly and abort, instead of backing off. This is especially impactful for self-hosted / air-gapped Azure OpenAI deployments with low quota ceilings (e.g. small TPM/PTU allocations), where brief, fully recoverable throttle windows are common.

I hit this **quickly and often** with an Azure-hosted **GPT 5.4** deployment on a **270K token/min** quota — even routine sessions trip the limit and then fail hard instead of waiting out the short throttle window.

Observed output:

```text
Request failed due to a transient API error. Retrying....
Request failed due to a transient API error. Retrying....
Request failed due to a transient API error. Retrying....
Request failed due to a transient API error. Retrying....
Request failed due to a transient API error. Retrying....

Failed to get response from the AI model; retried 5 times (total retry wait time: 0.15 seconds).
```

All 5 retries are consumed in ~0.15s total (as low as ~0.02s each), so a recoverable throttle is treated as a hard failure.

### Affected version

**Copilot CLI version:** 1.0.51

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Configure a BYOK Azure OpenAI deployment with a low rate-limit ceiling (e.g. GPT 5.4 at 270K token/min).
2. Run Copilot CLI with that provider/model and issue requests that exceed the ceiling.
3. Observe 5 immediate retries and abort with a sub-second total wait time.

### Expected behavior

- On `429`/`503` from a BYOK provider, apply effective backoff:
  - Respect `Retry-After` when present (Azure OpenAI typically returns it) — confirm this path is wired for the `azure`/BYOK provider, not only GitHub-hosted CAPI.
  - When no `Retry-After` is present, fall back to a **default exponential backoff with jitter** (capped at a few minutes) rather than ~0.
- Make retry behavior **user-configurable**, e.g. environment variables such as `COPILOT_RETRY_MAX` and `COPILOT_RETRY_WAIT_MS` for headless/CI use.
- Don't reinterpret a long server-side wait as a transport failure (the ~30–60s client-timeout interaction noted in #2661 

### Additional context

- #2760 (closed, v1.0.32) added `Retry-After`-based bounded exponential backoff, but on BYOK **Azure OpenAI** with 1.0.51 the retries still exhaust in ~0.15s — suggesting the backoff isn't applied on the BYOK/`azure` path, or the throttle response is reaching the client without a usable `Retry-After`.
- Docs confirm no retry settings exist today

issues.title: SessionClient poll loop keeps retrying after session disposal ("Cannot invoke native session after disposal has started"), leaking memory until heap OOM
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

A long-running interactive session gets slower and eventually crashes with `FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory`. On my machine this happens about once a week.

The cause appears to be an orphaned `SessionClient` poll loop. If a session is closed (for example, on `/resume` or when switching sessions) while an MCP server's OAuth flow is still running, the native session gets disposed. The JS-side poll loop does not stop, though. It keeps retrying forever, about once per second for each leaked loop:

```
[ERROR] SessionClient poll loop error (will retry): Error: Cannot invoke native session after disposal has started
```

Each leaked loop adds another stream of these errors, and heap usage climbs until V8 aborts at the ~4 GB limit.

### Affected version

1.0.100 and 1.0.102 (both crashes happened on these builds)

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Configure remote HTTP MCP servers that need OAuth (in my case Confluence and Datadog) and start an interactive session while their tokens are expired or invalid. Both servers return `401`, which triggers the OAuth flow.
2. Close or switch the session (e.g. `/resume` another session) while the OAuth/MCP reload is still in progress.
3. Keep the CLI process running. The log fills with `SessionClient poll loop error` about once per second for each leaked loop, and the process OOMs after a few days.

Here is the log sequence at the moment the loop starts:

```
[INFO] Closing session <id>
[ERROR] [rust:rmcp::transport::worker] worker quit with fatal: Transport channel closed, when Client(OAuthChallenge { ... status_code: 401 ... })
[WARNING] [rust:mcp_engine::agent_host] HTTP 401 challenge (...) {"server":"confluence","error":"MCP authorization was cancelled"}
[WARNING] [rust:mcp_engine::agent_host] HTTP 401 challenge (...) {"server":"datadog","error":"MCP authorization was cancelled"}
[WARNING] [rust:copilot_runtime::session::mcp::session_host] MCP reload lock still held at disposal; draining the graph without it
[ERROR] [rust:copilot_runtime::shared_api::event_log] Failed to retry MCP servers after OAuth listener registration: {"error":"MCP session host is disposed"}
[ERROR] SessionClient poll loop error (will retry): Error: Cannot invoke native session after disposal has started
... (repeats forever)
```

### Expected behavior

Disposing a session should stop its `SessionClient` poll loop, or the loop should exit on this error instead of retrying. Leaked loops should not pile up and exhaust the heap.

### Additional context

- macOS 26.7.1 (Apple Silicon, arm64), iTerm2, zsh; installed via Homebrew cask `copilot-cli`; Node v24.x embedded
- **Crash 1 (Oct 21):** one process OOM'd after the loop had run for about a day.
- **Crash 2 (Oct 27):** two processes launched Oct 21 died within ~10 ms of each other after ~6 days of uptime.
  - One was a V8 OOM (`node::OOMErrorHandler` → `abort`, last GC: `Mark-Compact 3871.5 (4102.0) -> 3851.3 (4086.0) MB`).
  - The other was a SIGABRT raised from `uv_kill`.
  - The OOM'd process had the error loop running continuously for 4+ days.
- **Log volume:**
  - One process rotated through 5 × 10 MB log files containing ~72–75k of these error lines each.
  - Another logged 3 identical errors per second, which suggests 3 leaked loops.
- **Possibly related:** #4699, #4725, #4686 (all OOM reports), but none of them identify this poll loop.
- **Workaround:** restart the CLI periodically.

---
🤖 *This issue was posted on behalf of Caleb Tenberge by GitHub Copilot CLI (Claude Opus 5.5/Anthropic).*

issues.title: GitHub Mobile stays "Queued for Copilot" after remote CLI already responds

labels.name: area:sessions
labels.description: Session management, resume, history, session picker, and session state

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

GitHub Mobile does not refresh a remotely controlled Copilot CLI session after submitting a prompt. The mobile app remains at **"Queued for Copilot"**, even though the local CLI receives the prompt and responds immediately. Opening the same session on GitHub.com shows the response and updates correctly in real time.

This appears isolated to GitHub Mobile session state synchronization rather than prompt delivery, CLI execution, or the remote-control connection.

### Affected version

- GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.80
- GitHub Mobile 1.273.0
- Android 16
- CLI host: Debian 13 x86_64

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Start a repo-less interactive session with `copilot --allow-all --remote`.
2. Open that remote session in GitHub Mobile.
3. Submit `Hi` from the mobile app.
4. Observe that GitHub Mobile displays "Queued for Copilot" and does not show a response.
5. Inspect the local CLI: it received `Hi` immediately and responded `Hi! How can I help?`.
6. Open the same remote session on GitHub.com: the response is present and the browser interface updates correctly.

### Expected behavior

GitHub Mobile should update the remote session in real time, replace the queued state when the prompt is accepted, and display the CLI response just as GitHub.com does.

### Additional context

- The CLI reports remote control connected successfully.
- The Copilot remote service remains active and its GitHub HTTPS connections remain established.
- The CLI log contains no corresponding disconnect or prompt-delivery error.
- Keep-alive is enabled, and the host remains online.
- Related broader report: #2765. This report isolates the failure to GitHub Mobile because the browser works correctly against the same live session.

issues.title: preToolUse hooks silently bypassed under parallel tool calls (timeout->allow fallback + serial dispatch)

labels.name: area:permissions
labels.description: Tool approval, security boundaries, sandbox mode, and directory restrictions

labels.name: area:plugins
labels.description: Plugin system, marketplace, hooks, skills, extensions, and custom agents

issues.body:
## Describe the bug

`preToolUse` hooks are silently bypassed under parallel tool calls because:

1. **`timeoutSec` does not terminate the hook process** — when a hook takes longer than `timeoutSec`, the CLI stops waiting but the hook subprocess keeps running. The CLI then proceeds with an **implicit allow** (fail-open). Any `permissionDecision: deny` that the hook eventually writes to stdout is discarded.
2. **Hook invocations are serialized** — when several tools are invoked in parallel (e.g. from the agent), `preToolUse` hooks are dispatched one-by-one with ~1.5–4 s gaps, even though the tool calls themselves land within a <100 ms window. Combined with (1), the later items in the queue are the ones most likely to exceed `timeoutSec` and get fail-open'd.

The net effect is that a security-oriented hook (e.g. a local guard that blocks dangerous commands) becomes probabilistically unreliable as soon as the agent fires more than a handful of tools concurrently. The reported "hook race condition" turns out not to be a race inside the hook, but a silent allow-fallback on timeout.

## Affected version

```
1.0.35-2 (Windows_NT)
```

Likely affects other recent versions; not tested across matrix.

## Steps to reproduce the behavior

Minimal reproducer using a Python 3 hook. Save as `slow-deny.py`:

```python
import json, sys, time
sys.stdin.read()
time.sleep(15)  # longer than timeoutSec
print(json.dumps({"permissionDecision": "deny", "permissionDecisionReason": "should block"}))
```

And `~/.copilot/hooks/hooks.json`:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "hooks": {
    "preToolUse": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "bash":       "python3 \"$HOME/slow-deny.py\"",
        "powershell": "py -3 \"$HOME\\slow-deny.py\"",
        "timeoutSec": 10
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Start `copilot` and ask the agent to run any shell command (e.g. `echo hi`).

**Expected**: the command is blocked (the hook wrote `deny`, even if late).
**Actual**: the command executes. The hook logs `permissionDecision: deny` after the CLI has already moved on.

A second reproducer shows the serialization behavior: ask the agent to run ~5 shell commands in the same turn. Logging the hook's start time (`datetime.now()`) shows the hooks firing at +0 s, +1.5 s, +4.6 s, +7.1 s, +11.1 s despite the tool calls all starting within ~100 ms.

## Expected behavior

At least one of:

- `timeoutSec` should kill the hook process (so subsequent failure modes are visible), **and** a timed-out hook should fall back to `deny` (fail-closed) — not to an implicit `allow`.
- Provide an explicit configuration knob (e.g. `onTimeout: "deny" | "allow"`) so operators can opt into fail-closed semantics.
- Document the current behavior clearly; right now the docs describe `timeoutSec` without specifying the fallback direction.

Ideally also: dispatch `preToolUse` hooks in parallel rather than serializing them, since each tool call is independent.

## Additional context

- OS: Windows 11, `powershell` invocation path
- Reproduced with minimal `py -3` hook (no `uv`, no third-party dependencies), so the latency is CLI-side scheduling rather than hook startup cost
- Observations:
  - `dur_stdout_written - dur_invoked` for the slow hook is ~15 s (full sleep), confirming the process is not killed at the 10 s timeout
  - For 5 parallel tool invocations, hook start times were spaced 1.5–4 s apart — consistent with a serial queue on the CLI side
  - The bypass probability grows with parallelism, matching community reports of "preToolUse race condition under high concurrency"
- Security impact: any user who relies on `preToolUse` hooks for safety (e.g. blocking writes to sensitive paths, blocking dangerous URLs) silently loses that protection under high concurrency

Happy to share a full minimal repro repo or detailed logs on request.

issues.title: Allow a credential command in providers.json and managed settings so BYOK providers work without a per-invocation launcher

type.description: A request, improvement, or new functionality

issues.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you'd like to solve

Since 1.0.84, `COPILOT_PROVIDER_API_KEY_COMMAND` lets the CLI obtain a BYOK credential by running a command, so short-lived per-user tokens (OIDC/JWT from a gateway, Entra, STS, …) can rotate during a session. 

The gap is that it only exists as an environment variable. The file-based surfaces have no equivalent:

- `providers.json` entries accept only a static `apiKey` / `bearerToken`.
- Enterprise managed settings (MDM / `managed-settings.json`) have no BYOK provider keys at all.

So anything that wants a rotating credential must set the environment before Copilot starts: a wrapper script, a shell alias, or a launcher process. Consequences:

- Plain `copilot` (and anything else that spawns `copilot`, e.g. IDE integrations, scripts, `--acp`) is not routed; only the wrapped invocation is.
- Organizations cannot enforce "route through our gateway with your identity" via policy; the user has to remember to use the wrapper.
- Writing the rotating token into `providers.json` as `apiKey` would put a bearer credential on disk and defeat rotation.

Other coding agents already support this in their config files, which is why the same gateway integration is a static config drop for them but a launcher for Copilot CLI:

- Codex: `model_providers.<id>.auth = { command = "...", args = [...] }` in `config.toml` / managed config.
- Claude Code: `apiKeyHelper` in `settings.json` / managed settings.
- Prior art elsewhere: Git/Docker credential helpers, AWS `credential_process`, kubectl exec credential plugins.

### Proposed solution

Provider registry: accept a command-based credential in `providers.json` provider entries, with the same semantics as `COPILOT_PROVIDER_API_KEY_COMMAND` (run to obtain the credential; cache; re-run near expiry and on 401, then retry once):

```json
{
  "providers": [
    {
      "name": "gateway",
      "type": "openai",
      "baseUrl": "https://gateway.example.com/v1",
      "wireApi": "responses",
      "apiKeyCommand": ["/usr/local/bin/agentdesktop", "credential", "--client-id", "copilot-cli"]
    }
  ],
  "models": [
    { "provider": "gateway", "id": "gpt-4.1", "modelId": "gpt-4.1", "wireModel": "gpt-4.1" }
  ]
}
```

(Field names other than `apiKeyCommand` should follow whatever the current `providers.json` schema uses. A `bearerTokenCommand` twin would mirror the existing `apiKey` / `bearerToken` pair.)

Prefer an argv array executed without a shell; optionally also accept a string executed like the env var does today.

Managed settings: allow the same provider definition (including the command) under enterprise managed settings, so an organization can pin the default provider and its credential source, and users cannot override it with a personal `providers.json` or env var.

Precedence: managed settings win when present; below that, keep env > providers.json > default, consistent with the flag > env > config ordering proposed in #2710. The env var keeps working as an override for ad-hoc use.

Security: never persist the command's output; redact it from logs, `/collect-debug-logs`, session state, and telemetry; run the command with a timeout and a bounded output size; treat non-zero exit as "no credential" rather than sending an empty bearer.

### Example prompts or workflows

```sh
# Dropped once by MDM or a fleet agent, no per-user setup:
#   ~/.copilot/providers.json   the provider entry above
#   ~/.copilot/settings.json    { "model": "gateway/gpt-4.1" }

copilot                            # interactive
copilot -p "summarize this repo"   # non-interactive
copilot --acp                      # spawned by an IDE or ACP client
```

All three route through the gateway with no wrapper or alias, and the token rotates for the life of the session.


### Additional context

Related: #3682 , #3282, https://github.com/github/copilot-cli/issues/2710

issues.title: ⭐  Implement proper HTTP retry logic for 429 responses

labels.name: area:networking
labels.description: Proxy, SSL/TLS, certificates, corporate environments, and connectivity issues

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, improvement, or new functionality

issues.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you'd like to solve

Copilot CLI exhibits aggressive retry behavior when encountering HTTP 429 (Rate Limited) responses. When the CLI receives a 429, it immediately closes the connection and retries without waiting, creating a loop of rapid retries (20+ per minute) even though GitHub requests wait times of 5-10 minutes via the `Retry-After` header.  This behavior causes rapid rate limit quota depletion, unnecessary server load from retry spam, and poor user experience with no feedback about rate limiting.

### Proposed solution

Implement standard HTTP retry patterns:

1. **Exponential Backoff with Jitter**
   ```
   wait_time = min(2^attempt * 60s + random_jitter, 300s)
   ```
   - First 429: Wait 60 seconds (or use Retry-After value)
   - Second 429: Wait 120 seconds
   - Third 429: Wait 240 seconds
   - Subsequent: Wait 5 minutes (capped)

2. **Respect Retry-After Headers**
   - Parse `Retry-After` header from 429 responses
   - Use header value as minimum wait time
   - Apply exponential backoff if subsequent 429s occur

3. **Circuit Breaker Pattern**
   - After 3 consecutive 429s, enter cooldown mode for 10 minutes
   - Display: "Rate limit protection active. Cooling down for 10 minutes..."
   - Reset counter on successful request

4. **User-Facing Progress Indicators**
   - Show clear messages during rate limit waits
   - Display countdown timer for retry
   - Indicate number of attempts made

**Benefits:**
- Prevents rapid rate limit quota depletion
- Reduces server load from retry spam
- Provides clear user feedback
- Follows HTTP best practices

### Example prompts or workflows

**Example 1: Batch file processing**
User processes 50 files with Copilot. Currently, if rate limited mid-batch, Copilot spams retries and burns rate limit quota. With proper backoff, it would gracefully pause and resume.

**Example 2: Long-running sessions**
Developer uses Copilot for 4-hour coding session. Currently hits rate limits in hour 2 and loses remaining time. With backoff, session continues at reduced speed instead of breaking.

**Example 3: Multi-agent workflows**
Copilot delegates to sub-agents for complex tasks. Currently, if sub-agent hits rate limit, parent agent retries immediately causing cascade failure. With backoff, system stabilizes.


### Additional context

### Current Behavior
- Copilot CLI ignores `Retry-After` headers
- No exponential backoff implemented
- Immediate retry on 429 responses
- No user feedback during rate limiting

### Expected Behavior
- Parse and respect `Retry-After` headers
- Implement exponential backoff between retries
- Show user progress during waits
- Circuit breaker after consecutive failures

### Environment
- **Copilot CLI Version:** 1.0.28 (observed, likely affects all versions)
- **Operating System:** Linux, macOS, Windows (all platforms affected)

### Impact
**For Users:**
- Weekly rate limit quota depleted rapidly (sometimes within hours)
- No feedback indicating rate limiting is occurring
- Extended downtime once limits are hit
- Loss of context when forced to restart sessions

**For GitHub Infrastructure:**
- Unnecessary server load from retry spam (20+ requests/minute during rate limiting)
- Wasted compute on requests guaranteed to fail
- Escalating rate limit penalties for affected users (delays increase from 5min → 10min → 15min+)

### Technical Details

**Root Cause:**
The issue stems from two missing features in Copilot CLI's HTTP client:
1. No exponential backoff - retry logic lacks progressive delay increases
2. Retry-After header ignored - client does not parse or respect standard HTTP header

**Client Timeout Behavior:**
Testing reveals Copilot CLI has an internal HTTP client timeout of approximately 30-60 seconds:
- Hold durations under 30 seconds: Client waits successfully
- Hold durations over 60 seconds: Client times out and retries immediately

This suggests the client interprets long response delays as connection failures rather than intentional rate limit handling.
