prs.body:
Related: #185477

## What Problem This Solves

Removes the unreleased personal/corporate security presets, which bundled independent execution, filesystem, sandbox, steering, and conversation-access defaults.

## User Impact

Policy controls return to their pre-preset defaults, including workspace-contained `apply_patch` and opt-in collaborative steering. Automatic quiet requester-owned queue fallback and the explicit `collaborativeSteeringFallback: "reject"` option remain intact.

Configurations containing `security.preset` must remove it before startup; `openclaw doctor --fix` removes the unknown field through its existing backed-up repair flow. Explicit controls are preserved, but preset-derived restrictions are not expanded or retained: configure those controls directly if needed.

## Why This Change Was Made

This is a selective revert, not a revert of #185477 as a whole. It removes preset expansion, schema/help/docs, and the corporate-only fixture; restores initial-creation/Doctor steering defaults; and preserves the preparation/steering regressions and unrelated fixture repairs. Automatic queue/notice behavior and inbound-authority logic are untouched.

Simplification removes the preset policy owner without adding a compatibility shim: production TypeScript is 50 lines added/61 removed; tests are 64 added/612 removed. The existing unknown-key repair owns removal of the unreleased setting.

prs.title: feat: add GitLab connections, publication, issues and comments
prs.body:
Related: #185864

## What Problem This Solves

Teams using GitLab need native session publication and issue/comment workflows with the requesting person's verified account, including self-hosted GitLab.

## User Impact

Adds GitLab under **Profile → Git connections → Add provider**, following GitHub's **Manage connections / Verify**, **My GitLab / System GitLab**, and **For me / For the system** controls. The person enters a server URL and OAuth returns automatically to Profile. Initially, each deployment configures one HTTPS issuer and OAuth application; a different server requires administrator setup. No deployment hostname, configured client ID, authorization link or credential is embedded in the contribution.

The same **My GitLab** connection authorizes `gitlab_publish` and `gitlab_issues`. Session publication supports adopting a clean local checkout into a native managed worktree, an explicit target branch, and an explicitly requested initial empty draft MR. It uses the requesting person's verified commit identity and records the publisher separately from an existing MR's original author. Issues and comments include discovery, mutations, threaded discussions, own-note edits/deletion, metadata, links and time.

Missing, expired, ambiguous or revoked requester authority fails closed. There is no automatic System, agent, colleague or ambient CLI fallback. Explicitly selected managed operations remain a separate native lane. GitLab publication currently supports Gateway-local managed workspaces; simultaneous GitLab instances and cloud repository publication are excluded.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reuses native profile/OAuth custody, admitted requester authority, session/worktree ownership and publication recovery. The bundled GitLab plugin uses public closed protocol contracts and narrow authenticated Gateway methods; tokens remain in the Gateway. It does not introduce a provider framework or copy user OAuth grants into shell commands.

The generic host handoff retains one exact admitted plugin/tool request across turn yield. Scope projection must retain the same opaque requester source and profile; revocation and plugin lifetime remain enforced. Only the call that actually yields is exempt from the yield abort. Workspace adoption checks canonical project identity and live project policy before binding, then publication rechecks before effects. Remote history is preserved while accepted local task changes receive the connected user's verified author/committer credit. Uncertain push/MR outcomes retain the original request and require recovery instead of an automatic replacement.

OAuth uses PKCE and single-use user-bound state. Issue/note mutations retain observed-version, own-note and literal-body protections, and placed workers retain the admitted requesting user.

## Evidence

### Shared GitHub/GitLab connector refactor

Corrective head: `51eb551e1e873d317126a30652be3734cc0abdda`, preserving the contributor’s updated `d95c10d6e50cd9ea0df49a384c3a046b7d1a1402` head. Requested by @steipete in [the original discussion](https://x.com/steipete/status/2115277629641404760).

- Shared owners now handle local commands, Git/config guards, accepted workspace snapshots, commit/trailer helpers and conditional push arguments. GitHub API/credentials, GitLab’s private Git environment, OAuth lifecycles and publication custody/recovery remain distinct.
- One typed managed-identity config writer replaces the duplicate implementations while retaining CAS, agent lifecycle checks, sandbox overrides, inheritance cleanup and GitLab’s live-owner check inside every retry. All affected static, dynamic, namespace and benchmark callers use the new owners.
- Final candidate: **157 tests passed across 11 files** (77 native OAuth/GitLab/handoff/filter checks in 77.62s wall; 80 shared-identity/workspace, real-Git and GitHub publication checks in 85.32s wall). Core and affected-test/script typechecks, scoped lint (49 source/test + 2 script files), formatting (53 files), mock ratchet and diff checks passed in a secretless AWS Crabbox. The 21-test baseline passed; the pending-merge guidance regression failed on the original implementation and passed with the shared owner. Earlier unchanged-consumer proof covered additional workspace, cron and tooling paths. New/shared contract test time: identity config 32ms, workspace 467ms, GitLab private-Git/push 111ms. The retained 56.9s GitHub consumer suite exercises real Git/SQLite revocation and uncertain-write recovery; helper-only proof would miss those boundaries. No live provider write is claimed.
- Independent local autoreview (Codex, P0–P2), `d95c10d6…51eb551e`: no actionable findings. An earlier missed dynamic import was corrected and re-reviewed. This covers the corrective range, not the entire pre-existing feature or its scanner holds.
- Relative to `d95c10d6`, this correction removes 44 production TypeScript lines net and adds 107 test lines. The measured test ceiling is 6,303,664; the increase retains distinct cross-provider CAS/sandbox/retry, pending-merge and real conditional-push checks. Three obsolete mock allowances were regenerated away. Hosted CI timing is pending.

The PR remains draft with its existing protected review/scanner gates intact. Main has since advanced: the generated `docs/.generated/config-baseline.sha256` conflict also reproduces on the unmodified contributor head `d95c10d6` against `14526249956c67b`; it is not introduced by this refactor. No generated digest was hand-edited, and no deployment or live GitLab write is claimed.

### Earlier GitLab feature evidence

The following contributor evidence predates this corrective refactor; prior-head CI does not qualify the corrective head.

Candidate: `d95c10d6e50cd9ea0df49a384c3a046b7d1a1402`, preserving published history and normally merged with upstream `228596060e33dfcddbb6740416f381daac6f84fe`. This PR remains **draft** while exact-head CI, scanner qualification and deployment acceptance are pending.

- Native publication RPC/integration/executor checks: **28 passed**, covering two independently connected users, exact commit credit, empty draft creation, lost-response recovery, selected base, local commits, canonical mismatch and OAuth/project-policy revocation before binding/effects. These use real local Git and simulated provider responses; they do not prove a live GitLab write.
- Native host handoff and GitHub regressions: **10 passed**, including actual turn yield, same-conversation result delivery, service revocation and sibling-call cancellation. Registered-tool/prefix/optional-plugin regressions: **91 passed**.
- Core/extension types, affected Gateway/agent-tool test types, scoped type-aware lint, core-to-extension boundary, generated plugin inventory and formatting passed before the upstream merge; merged core and Profile UI types and all 16 requester/handoff regressions passed again. The native PR-selected extension package boundary also passes (3 compiles and its canary). Protocol registry/generated/native determinism checks passed for the added methods.
- Exact-head full native build passed on `d95c10d`, including protocol/packages, plugin declarations/assets and production UI. The latest normal merge resolved only the test-count baseline; the contribution patch excluding that scalar is byte-identical to the audited preceding candidate. Core types and all 16 requester/handoff regressions passed again on this head. Local, fork and PR heads match; GitHub reports the PR mergeable and maintainer edits are enabled.
- Complete outgoing 266-file patch scanned offline with official TruffleHog 3.99.4, provider verification disabled: 208 unverified syntactic records / 55 distinct candidates. Private deployment/client/key marker checks found zero matches. Independent review classified the four new candidates as source identifiers; the three invalid-URL rejection fixtures are unchanged. All fingerprints from the 11 corrective commits are also present in the reviewed final patch. Scanner clearance is not claimed.

The test-line ceiling is explicitly raised from 6,295,000 at the updated comparison base to the measured 6,303,557. The preceding corrective batch added 1,769 lines above its previous published ceiling to retain distinct requester isolation, actual yield/cancellation, canonical project, pre-binding policy revocation, attribution and recovery regressions. No unrelated tests were deleted to conceal feature cost. The correction since the preceding public revision is 1,066 production/config additions and 66 removals, 1,798 test additions and 11 removals, and 64 documentation additions and 6 removals. The protocol contract and common publication-session authorization replace parallel caller parsing/retention; the existing native workspace and publication owners remain authoritative. The generic handoff is a separate descendant commit series for focused review; the complete GitLab consumer is required for the requested workflow.

### Open review gates

ClawSweeper's input-safety hold remains. The latest protected run reports 32 findings but exposes only one reserved-domain URI rejection fixture. The other findings cannot be individually qualified from the exposed diagnostics. [The existing audit comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/185928#issuecomment-6456014323) requests maintainer inspection and exact safe-fixture qualification. No scanner bypass, fixture obfuscation or policy suppression was applied. prs.title: fix: keep active workspaces usable after personal Hide or Show
prs.body:
Fixes #186472

## What Problem This Solves

Personal **Hide from Involving me** and **Show in Involving me** actions can interrupt an active guest's workspace operations with `Local sandbox workspace authority changed`, even though the session, workspace and permissions remain the same. A fresh native reproduction reaches the registered involvement handler and then fails at the retained workspace predicate guard. The failure also appeared during an ordinary shared Studio task before its active runs ended.

## User Impact

Personal list choices should leave ongoing authorized workspace work usable. This repair preserves saved files and existing workspace authority while still publishing the actual private involvement change to readers that depend on it. Resets, archives, worktree replacement and permission revocation retain their existing guards. There is no new configuration, storage schema, public field or access grant.

## Why This Change Was Made

The involvement writer already produces exact session metadata, but the collaboration receipt discarded that postimage and retained only an `unchanged` sharing marker. The generic retained-entry publisher could not reconstruct a truthful entry from that marker and made the workspace predicate unknown.

The collaboration receipt now carries the existing private metadata receipt from the native writer. Pending and committed readers use the writer's entry and available snapshot postimages; superseded commits preserve observed mismatches without overwriting newer state. Public session notifications retain their existing marker and omit the private payload. This reuses the current metadata owner and optional-snapshot size budget without adding SQL reads or teaching generic predicates that every sharing marker means the entire entry stayed unchanged.

## Evidence

On b61ab6deb40cc640aec077b6e6a7b93a44b5422c, the new native regression failed immediately after successful personal Hide at `local-workspace-projection.ts:518`; the focused case took 2.295 seconds. It holds one real managed-workspace owner across Hide and Show, synchronizes newly saved files after each action, and checks that a later reset revokes that owner.

The existing lost-reply test also checks stable, involvement-sensitive and complete-entry predicates while retaining its single-dispatch and private-event assertions. Changed-file formatting and lint, all selected production/test type graphs, and 202 related test cases passed. The 16 optional PostgreSQL conformance cases were not run in this SQLite setup. The separate single-worker timing run passed all 11 cases in the two changed test files: the workspace regression took 1.774 seconds and the lost-reply case took 0.517 seconds. File wall times were 41.69 seconds (including cold worker transformation) and 6.47 seconds; hosted CI timing is pending. The docs link audit also passed.

Exact-head natural Studio proof and visual evidence, independent engineering review, hosted CI and the automated PR review remain pending. This PR is not ready to land until those obligations are complete.

prs.title: fix(embedded-agent-runner): use monotonic clock for stuck-recovery settle deadline
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a stuck embedded agent session is recovered, the recovery routine waits up to `settleMs` for the captured session's owner to settle. The wait window is computed from `Date.now()` (wall clock), but the actual wait is driven by monotonic timers — so if the host clock is adjusted (NTP sync / manual change) between computing the window and starting the wait, the settle window is stretched or shrunk, leaving stuck-recovery arbitrarily hung or prematurely timed out.

- Problem: `abortAndDrainCapturedEmbeddedAgentRun` seeds `settleDeadline = Date.now() + settleMs` and reads `remainingMs = settleDeadline - Date.now()`, then feeds `remainingMs` to monotonic consumers (`waitForCapturedSessionNativeAttemptEnd` and `waitForReplyOperationOwnerSettlement` → `setTimeout`). A wall-clock rollback after the seed inflates the remaining budget; a forward jump shrinks it.
- Solution: derive both the seed and the remaining-budget read from `performance.now()` so the deadline stays in the same monotonic clock domain as its consumers. A clock adjustment then no longer distorts the settle window.
- What changed: two lines in `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/runs.ts` (`abortAndDrainCapturedEmbeddedAgentRun`), plus a regression test folded into `runs.force-clear-terminal.test.ts`.
- What did NOT change: no public API, no persisted state, no steady-clock behavior change.

## Why This Change Was Made

The settle deadline is a per-process, in-memory budget consumed only by monotonic timers; it is never serialized, never compared against wall-clock epochs, and never crosses a process boundary. The monotonic clock is therefore the correct domain for both the seed and the read. Both consumer chains go through canonical timer helpers (`resolveTimerTimeoutMs`) that already `Math.floor` internally, so the float values from `performance.now()` are safe with no extra `Math.floor`.

- Best fix: yes — a two-line monotonic-clock alignment, with no new guard branch or helper.
- Alternative considered: keeping `Date.now()` and clamping the budget with `Math.min` — rejected because it only caps the inflation direction and does not remove the cross-clock-domain mismatch.
- Risk: steady-clock behavior is identical; the deadline never leaves the process.

## User Impact

Stuck embedded-agent recovery now settles on schedule regardless of host clock adjustments. Users no longer see recovery sessions hang far past their configured `settleMs` after an NTP sync or manual clock change, and healthy recoveries are not prematurely timed out by a forward jump. With a steady clock (the common case), behavior is unchanged.

## Evidence

### Isolated Gateway recovery under a -60 s wall-clock step

An isolated Gateway (OpenClaw 2026.10.7) with a real agent and a real provider model (OpenAI-compatible endpoint, redacted) ran a cron agent turn that was still in its model call when the job timeout fired; the Gateway's own `cleanupTimedOutAgentRun` then performed the recovery. The fix is applied to the build exactly as in the diff; the pre-fix run uses the same build with only the two clock reads reverted to `Date.now()`. A proof-only loader shifts `Date.now()` by -60 s the moment the settle deadline is seeded (monotonic clocks untouched), landing the rewind exactly in the window the fix targets.

```console
# pre-fix (Date.now) — same Gateway, same recovery
[proof-clock] settle deadline seeded from Date.now
[proof-clock] wall clock stepped -60000ms after the settle-deadline seed
[proof-clock] settlement wait armed on a monotonic timer: budget=74997ms
[proof-clock] settlement wait armed on a monotonic timer: budget=74997ms
lane task error: ... error="cron: job execution timed out (last phase: model-call-started)" durationMs=-54881
cron: cleaned up timed-out agent run {"aborted":false,"drained":true,"forceCleared":false}
```

```console
# post-fix (performance.now) — same Gateway, same recovery
[proof-clock] settle deadline seeded from performance.now
[proof-clock] wall clock stepped -60000ms after the settle-deadline seed
[proof-clock] settlement wait armed on a monotonic timer: budget=14997ms
[proof-clock] settlement wait armed on a monotonic timer: budget=14997ms
lane task error: ... error="cron: job execution timed out (last phase: model-call-started)" durationMs=-54749
cron: cleaned up timed-out agent run {"aborted":false,"drained":true,"forceCleared":false}
```

The negative `durationMs` is the Gateway's own measurement across the -60 s step: the rewind was live while the recovery ran. Recovery still completed (`drained:true`), and the bound handed to the real monotonic settlement timers was 14997 ms after the fix versus 74997 ms before it. In this run the aborted run's owners settle promptly, so the drain returns instead of consuming the deadline; the deadline is the worst-case bound the recovery may wait, and the rewind inflated that bound.

| clock state | before fix (`Date.now()`) | after fix (`performance.now()`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| -60 s step at the settle-deadline seed | settlement bound **74997 ms** (15 s + 60 s rewind) | settlement bound **14997 ms** |

### Focused test — pre-fix RED / post-fix GREEN

The regression test (`runs.force-clear-terminal.test.ts`) runs the real owner, rolls the wall clock back 60 s after the deadline is seeded, and observes that recovery returns `drained:false` within the bounded budget.

- Pre-fix (source reverted to `Date.now()`): **fails** — recovery is still pending after 1 s of fake timers (the budget inflated to ~60 s by the rewind), so the await never resolves.
- Post-fix: **7 passed** in `runs.force-clear-terminal.test.ts` (the new case settles in ~10 ms).

### What was not tested

- A real wall-clock jump on a production host: the rewind is injected in-process by a proof-only loader scoped to this run.
- A recovery whose captured owners outlive the settle budget — the bound was measured here, not consumed.
- Open PR collision: no open PR touches `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/runs.ts`; #184116 touches `run/attempt-timeout-prepare.ts` (a different function).

prs.title: fix(gateway): keep node host-stats checkpoint deadline on the monotonic clock
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a node reports host telemetry (CPU/memory) to the Gateway, `NodeHostStatsCheckpoints` throttles disk persistence to one write every 5 minutes per node. That deadline lived on the wall clock: the timer delay was `Math.max(0, deadline - Date.now())` and the callback re-read `Date.now()` to decide whether the budget had elapsed. A clock correction therefore moved the budget: a backward jump slipped the checkpoint by the jump size, and a forward jump fired it early.

- **Problem**: system-clock corrections slip or pre-fire host-telemetry checkpoint persistence, with no error surfaced.
- **Solution**: pair every received sample's persisted wall-clock receipt with the monotonic clock while the two are still in sync (`record`), snapshot that deadline with the sample being written, and promote it once the write succeeds. Both the `setTimeout` delay and the fire-time check then run on `performance.now()`, and later schedules reuse the stored deadline instead of re-reading the wall clock.
- **What changed**: `src/gateway/node-registry.host-stats.ts` (`NodeHostStatsCheckpoints` and its private checkpoint type) plus three cases folded into the existing `host stats checkpoints` suite in `src/gateway/node-registry-pairing.test.ts`.
- **What did NOT change**: `updatedAtMs` remains a persisted wall-clock epoch (compared across restarts/processes), and the public API (`record` / `forget` / `close`) is untouched.

## Why This Change Was Made

`updatedAtMs` is a persisted epoch written by `updateHostStats` (`params.observedAtMs ?? Date.now()`) and stored through `persistHostStats`, so its seed cannot become `performance.now()` without breaking the cross-restart contract. The fix keeps the epoch as the source of truth and derives a parallel monotonic deadline (`savedAtMonotonicMs`) at the receipt boundary, like `src/infra/update-doctor-deadline.ts`.

Deriving it once is what makes the budget stable. A live node publishes telemetry every 60s, so deriving on each `schedule()` would re-read the corrected wall clock on the next report and move an armed deadline again; a `setTimeout` firing a millisecond early would do the same through the re-arm path. The timer also writes a *buffered* sample, so converting at write time would fold a clock step since that sample's receipt into the following budget — hence the receipt-time capture and the per-write snapshot. `NodeHostStatsCheckpoints` is the only owner that arms the timer, so the fix lives there: no new parser, policy branch, configuration surface, or persisted state.

## User Impact

Gateway operators get reliable node host-telemetry persistence: after a clock correction in either direction, CPU/memory stats still land in the store inside the 5-minute window anchored to the saved receipt instead of slipping or firing early.

## Evidence

Runtime capture through the shipped entry points: `startGatewayServer()`, a node-role `GatewayClient` over loopback, the `node.event` / `node.host.stats` frame, and `device.pair.list` for the persisted node surface. Each row below is the same script with the checkpoint owner's wall clock stepped once while telemetry keeps arriving; the step is owner-scoped because this capture runs the Gateway and its clients in one process.

| Signal | `origin/main` (before) | head `f1cdec` (after) |
|---|---|---|
| Backward step (-30 s): timer delay after the later report | 329761 ms (budget + 30 s) | 299889 ms (same deadline) |
| Backward step: durable sample when the deadline passes | still `512` (slipped) | `300` (latest, on time) |
| Forward step (+30 s): delay after the later report | 269921 ms (budget - 30 s) | 299809 ms (same deadline) |
| Forward step: 30 s before the deadline | `300` (fired early) | `512` (still waiting) |
| Forward step: at the deadline | `300` | `300` (on time) |

### Raw terminal output (backward step, current head / origin/main)

```console
[proof] first sample persisted: memoryFreeBytes=512 updatedAtMs=1793031594197
[timer] checkpoint setTimeout delay=299898ms
[clock] checkpoint owner wall clock stepped by -30000ms
[timer] checkpoint setTimeout delay=299889ms
[proof] at the deadline: memoryFreeBytes=300 updatedAtMs=1793031594307 (first saved updatedAtMs=1793031594197)
PASS: checkpoint persisted on the armed monotonic deadline despite the wall-clock step
```

```console
[timer] checkpoint setTimeout delay=299767ms
[clock] checkpoint owner wall clock stepped by -30000ms
[timer] checkpoint setTimeout delay=329761ms
[proof] at the deadline: memoryFreeBytes=512 updatedAtMs=1793027633985 (first saved updatedAtMs=1793027633985)
[proof] after the grace window: memoryFreeBytes=300 updatedAtMs=1793027634223
FAIL: checkpoint slipped past the deadline by the wall-clock step (persisted late)
```

### Raw terminal output (forward step, current head / origin/main)

```console
[clock] checkpoint owner wall clock stepped by 30000ms
[timer] checkpoint setTimeout delay=299809ms
[proof] 30000ms before the deadline: memoryFreeBytes=512 updatedAtMs=1793032821880
[proof] at the deadline: memoryFreeBytes=300 updatedAtMs=1793032822070
PASS: checkpoint waited for the armed monotonic deadline despite the forward clock step
```

```console
[clock] checkpoint owner wall clock stepped by 30000ms
[timer] checkpoint setTimeout delay=269921ms
[proof] 30000ms before the deadline: memoryFreeBytes=300 updatedAtMs=1793033214990
FAIL: checkpoint fired early after the forward clock step
```

### Regression (folded into the existing `host stats checkpoints` suite)

| Tree | Quiet | Keeps reporting | Buffered write | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `origin/main` | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | 3 failed |
| `f5085d8` (earlier revision) | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | failed |
| `663e15c` (earlier revision) | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | failed |
| head | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | 112 passed |

All three assert that nothing persists before the armed deadline and that the next checkpoint stays anchored to its receipt.

**Scope**: all five node-registry test files pass (112 tests); `oxfmt`/`oxlint` clean; no lockfile changes; no open PR touches this file.

prs.title: fix(subagents): keep the subagent spawn reconcile budget on the monotonic clock
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The subagent spawn reconciliation deadline was measured on the wall clock (`Date.now()`), so a host clock jump (NTP correction, VM pause/resume, manual time change) corrupted the retry budget and could wrongly kill a healthy reconciliation, or silently stretch the Gateway timeout for an unhealthy one.

- Problem: `reconcileSubagentAgentDispatch` in `src/agents/subagents/spawn/subagent-spawn-gateway.ts` seeded `deadline = Date.now() + SUBAGENT_AGENT_RECONCILE_TIMEOUT_MS` (6_400ms) and recomputed the remaining budget with `Date.now()`. That value feeds two monotonic consumers: the Gateway RPC timeout (`callGateway` `timeoutMs`) and the inter-iteration `delay` (`node:timers/promises` `setTimeout`). A forward wall-clock jump between two iterations drives `remainingMs = deadline - Date.now()` below zero and the loop rethrows the original unavailable error, killing a reconciliation that would otherwise recover; a backward jump stretches the timeout and the delay past the intended budget.
- Solution: measure the budget on `performance.now()`, the clock both consumers already run on. A difference of two monotonic reads is immune to wall-clock drift.
- What changed: the three reads inside `reconcileSubagentAgentDispatch` — deadline seed, `remainingMs`, and the `delay` upper bound — switched from `Date.now()` to `performance.now()`. The constants (`800` / `6_400`), the retry/throw policy, the dispatched request shape, and transport-error handling are unchanged; no wire behavior changed. `deadline` stays a pure in-process closure value (never serialized or reported across processes), so nothing observes it as an epoch.

## User Impact

A subagent spawn no longer fails spuriously when the host clock is corrected or a VM is resumed during the 6.4s reconciliation window, and the Gateway RPC retries and inter-iteration delays reflect real elapsed time only.

## Evidence

**Regression (RED → GREEN)** — the existing `reconciles ambiguous dispatch (terminal=…)` case in `src/agents/subagents/spawn/subagent-spawn.test.ts` now steps `Date.now()` forward 10s on the pending replay, and still requires the admitted run plus the 800ms per-call Gateway RPC cap. It reuses that case's single 800ms interval wait, so no new sleep is added, and the suite's test-line total stays flat (`net delta: 0`; the ratchet reports "Tree is over the ceiling; this change does not add test lines").

```console
$ OPENCLAW_VITEST_RUNTIME=node node scripts/test-projects.mts --maxWorkers=1 \
    src/agents/subagents/spawn/subagent-spawn.test.ts                  # fixed source
 Tests  33 passed (33)

# same file, subagent-spawn-gateway.ts restored to the base revision
 × |infra| src/agents/subagents/spawn/subagent-spawn.test.ts > spawnSubagentDirect seam flow > reconciles ambiguous dispatch (terminal=false)
   → AssertionError: expected { status: 'error', …(3) } to match object { status: 'accepted', …(2) }
 Tests  1 failed | 32 passed (33)
```

**Real Gateway transport trace** — isolated Gateway (`startGatewayServer`: token auth, loopback, fake OpenAI-compatible provider) driven by the production `callNativeSubagentGateway` over a real WebSocket. The first `agent` RPC gets a 60ms client timeout, so the run is created but the reply arrives after the client gives up; `Date.now()` is then stepped forward 10s while that same call is reconciling. Base revision:

```console
[proof] trial ambiguous dispatch timeoutMs=60
[proof] +139ms wall clock stepped +10000ms
[proof] +221ms rejected gateway timeout after 60ms
```

Same harness on the fixed source:

```console
[proof] trial ambiguous dispatch timeoutMs=60
[proof] +137ms wall clock stepped +10000ms
[proof] +1148ms reconciled status=in_flight runId=reconcile-proof-target-60-441174-1-3
```

| Gateway run after the step | healthy run abandoned | `status=in_flight`, `runId=reconcile-proof-target-60-441174-1-3` |
| Inter-iteration delay | collapsed to zero by the step | full 800ms interval |
| Remaining budget at the next read | negative, so the loop aborted | about 5.4s left, so the replay ran |
| Unit regression (`reconciles ambiguous dispatch`) | 1 failed, 32 passed | 33 passed |

The step is the only difference between the runs: on the base revision it zeroes the delay and then drives `remainingMs` negative, so the loop rethrows the original timeout and abandons a healthy run; on the fixed revision the interval and the budget come from `performance.now()`, so the replay of the same idempotency key returns the already-admitted run (single run — a second launch would have produced another run id).

prs.title: fix(media-understanding): keep provider operation deadline on the monotonic clock
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Provider video-generation deadlines were computed on the wall clock (`Date.now()`), so a host clock jump (NTP correction, VM pause/resume, manual time change) corrupted the remaining-time budget and could abort perfectly healthy provider requests before their timeout, or silently stretch the timeout for unhealthy ones. This is the canonical owner of the provider-operation deadline, so the fix lands once and heals 30+ providers (byteplus, fal, google, minimax, openai, openrouter, pixverse, runway, together, xai, zai, ...).

- Problem: `deadlineAtMs` was seeded with a wall-clock timestamp and the remaining budget was recomputed with `Date.now()`. When the wall clock jumps forward, `remaining = deadlineAtMs - Date.now()` goes negative and a healthy request is aborted immediately; when it jumps backward, `remaining` is inflated and real timeouts are stretched.
- Solution: seed `deadlineAtMs` with `performance.now() + resolvedTimeoutMs` and compute the remaining budget with `performance.now()`, keeping the whole deadline on the monotonic clock.
- What changed: in `src/media-understanding/shared.ts`, `createProviderOperationDeadline` now seeds the deadline on the monotonic clock, and both consumers of the deadline (`resolveProviderOperationTimeoutMs` and `waitProviderOperationPollInterval`) read the remaining budget from the same monotonic clock. The `resolveDateTimestampMs` / `resolveExpiresAtMsFromDurationMs` wall-clock imports are no longer used there and were dropped.
- What did NOT change: the deadline payload shape (`deadlineAtMs`, `label`, `timeoutMs`), the timeout-resolution policy (`resolveTimerTimeoutMs`, `Math.max(1, Math.min(defaultTimeoutMs, remaining))`), the thrown timeout error, and every downstream provider request helper that consumes the resolved `timeoutMs`. No provider signature or wire behavior changed.

## Why This Change Was Made

The canonical `ProviderOperationDeadline` mixed two clock domains: it was seeded on the wall clock but consumed downstream by `buildTimeoutAbortSignal`'s `setTimeout`, which runs on the monotonic clock. Crossing clock domains makes the deadline non-monotonic under wall-clock jumps. The minimal, complete fix is to express both the seed and every remaining-budget read on the monotonic clock, which is the same clock the abort signal actually uses. A pure arithmetic difference of two monotonic reads is inherently immune to wall-clock drift.

- Best fix: yes. Fixing the canonical owner means every provider shares the corrected behavior without per-provider changes.
- Alternative: switch the deadline to a resolved absolute monotonic deadline per provider — rejected as it multiplies call sites and leaves the same underlying non-monotonic seed in the shared path.
- Risk: `deadlineAtMs` values are no longer wall-clock timestamps. Nothing in the repo serializes or diagnoses them as such; all call sites only subtract to derive a remaining budget. A temporary debug log that prints the raw value would now show a small monotonic counter instead of an epoch, which is expected.

## User Impact

Users running media-understanding providers no longer see healthy generation/download requests fail early (or hang too long) whenever the host clock is corrected or a VM is paused and resumed. Deadlines now behave identically regardless of wall-clock jumps, so provider timeouts reflect real elapsed time only.

## Evidence

**Live runtime proof** (drives the shipped production function under a simulated wall-clock jump; pre-fix model uses the wall clock, post-fix uses the monotonic clock, same 60s budget):

```console
$ node --import tsx .../BUG-104-...-evidence/proof.mjs
deadline seed  pre-fix (wall-clock epoch): 1793119296061
deadline seed  post-fix (monotonic):       61910.856693
remaining @now pre-fix : 59998
remaining @now post-fix: 59998.316386

wall-clock jump +120s (NTP correction / VM pause):
  pre-fix  remaining = -60002 => ABORTS a healthy request (bug)
  post-fix remaining = 59998.103593 (immune: monotonic clock ignores the wall-clock jump)
```

**Regression test (RED → GREEN)** — a new case "keeps the deadline on the monotonic clock across wall-clock jumps" drives a wall-clock jump forward/backward and asserts the remaining budget is unaffected. Against the pre-fix source it fails, against the fixed source it passes:

```console
$ npx vitest run src/media-understanding/shared.test.ts -t "across wall-clock jumps"   # pre-fix
 × provider operation deadlines > keeps the deadline on the monotonic clock across wall-clock jumps
   → expected 120000 to be 60000
 Test Files  1 failed (1)

$ npx vitest run src/media-understanding/shared.test.ts   # post-fix
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  29 passed (29)
```

The pre-fix failure (`expected 120000 to be 60000`) is the bug: after the forward wall-clock jump the remaining budget goes negative and the resolver returns the default timeout instead of the healthy remaining 60000ms.

Open PR collision check: searched open PR topics for this deadline/clock pattern and scanned changed-file lists of open PRs touching `src/media-understanding/`; no open PR modifies this file or the same fix region. (Related, distinct wall-clock fixes already merged: #169908, #165889.)

prs.title: fix(browser): keep withTimeout pause accounting on the monotonic clock
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A browser gateway request that briefly shares a startup budget while the wall clock jumps forward loses almost its entire remaining deadline and can be killed immediately after resume. The pause accounting inside `withTimeout` measured the paused span with `Date.now()` but subtracted it from a monotonic `setTimeout` budget, so a clock jump corrupted the remaining time. Switched the pause bookkeeping to the monotonic clock.

- Problem: pause time was measured on the wall clock (`Date.now()`), but it was deducted from the remaining budget that is armed as a monotonic `setTimeout`. A wall-clock jump (clock moving forward while a request is paused in shared startup) collapsed the remaining budget to the 1ms floor, so a healthy request that resumed and still needed to finish would be killed as a false timeout. A backward clock jump inflated the budget instead.
- Solution: keep the pause start and the pause-duration subtraction on the monotonic clock, so the remaining budget is unaffected by wall-clock adjustments.
- What changed: `extensions/browser/src/sdk-node-runtime.ts` — the `withTimeout` pause accounting uses `performance.now()` for the arm seed, the per-arm reset, and the pause-duration subtraction. Added a fake-clock test that moves only `Date` (not `performance.now()`) while paused and asserts the resume re-arm keeps the original budget.
- What did NOT change: the deadline's overall semantics, the parent/child nested pause accounting, cancellation behavior, or the timeout floor of 1ms. No serialization or cross-process state is involved, so the full swap to the monotonic clock is safe.

## Why This Change Was Made

`withTimeout` shares a request budget across nested Gateway/local layers and pauses the clock while work is parked in shared browser startup (`waitForBrowserStartup`). The paused span is measured with the wall clock but charged against a budget that is enforced with a monotonic `setTimeout`. The two clock domains disagree whenever the system clock is adjusted (NTP step, manual change, VM suspend/resume), which makes a healthy request look like it overran its deadline. The pause fields are plain closure-local values that are never serialized, persisted, or compared across processes, so the whole accounting can move to `performance.now()` without needing a dual-clock domain. This aligns the fix with the rest of the monotonic-deadline family already shipped for the browser node-host proxy deadline.

## User Impact

Browser gateway requests that pause in shared startup keep their full remaining deadline even when the wall clock jumps while they wait, so a legitimate request is no longer killed as a false timeout (or granted an inflated budget) due to a clock adjustment. Requests that do not exercise shared startup are unaffected.

## Evidence

A real runtime proof drives the production path through the shipped browser node-command entry point: a real node-host (`openclaw node run` with a real Chrome browser) served by the real Gateway, invoking the shipped `browser.proxy` node-command `POST /tabs/open`. That request pauses in `waitForBrowserStartup` (shared startup), then resumes and opens a real tab. A `--import` preload injects a persistent wall-clock-only jump (`Date.now()` stepped, `performance.now()` untouched) armed exactly at the pause-entry subtraction. It records the `setTimeout` delay re-armed on resume — that delay is the remaining budget. The same proof runs against both the pre-fix (`Date.now`) and post-fix (`performance.now`) source. Four-quadrant matrix (real `nodes invoke` output):

| wall-clock step | pre-fix (Date.now) | post-fix (performance.now) |
|---|---|---|
| **forward +30000ms** | **FAILED** `browser proxy timed out for POST /tabs/open after 20000ms`; resume re-arm `delay=1` | **SUCCESS** durable tab, url `about:blank`; resume re-arm `delay=19982.391377000007` |
| **backward -30000ms** | SUCCESS but budget inflated: resume re-arm `delay=49986` (~50s, 2.5x intended) | **SUCCESS** durable tab; resume re-arm `delay=19986.168682999996` (bounded ~20s) |

Raw proof log lines (inline, current head `98b59aa2925`):

```
forward pre-fix   STEP 30000ms on pause-entry Date.now ... at Object.pause (sdk-node-runtime.ts:62:55)
forward pre-fix   withTimeout-arm delay=1            <- resume re-arm collapsed to 1ms
forward post-fix  withTimeout-arm delay=19982.391377000007   <- budget kept ~20s
backward pre-fix  STEP -30000ms on pause-entry Date.now ... at Object.pause (sdk-node-runtime.ts:62:55)
backward pre-fix  withTimeout-arm delay=49986        <- resume re-arm inflated to ~50s
backward post-fix withTimeout-arm delay=19986.168682999996   <- budget bounded ~20s
```

Forward step: pre-fix collapses the budget to 1ms, timing out a healthy `/tabs/open`; post-fix completes. Backward step: pre-fix inflates the budget to ~50s; post-fix keeps it bounded at ~20s.

Regression test folded into the existing `describe("withTimeout")` suite in `extensions/browser/src/sdk-node-runtime.test.ts` (no timer-spy scaffolding): it parks the request in shared startup, moves only the wall clock (`vi.setSystemTime`) while paused, then resumes and asserts the budget survives. It is RED on pre-fix and GREEN on post-fix:

```
$ npx vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-browser.config.ts sdk-node-runtime   (pre-fix)
 FAIL  keeps a paused budget monotonic across a wall-clock step
AssertionError: expected Error: browser request timed out to be 'ok'
 Test Files  1 failed (1)      Tests  1 failed | 2 passed (3)

$ npx vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-browser.config.ts sdk-node-runtime   (post-fix)
 Test Files  1 passed (1)      Tests  3 passed (3)
```

The test fold keeps the test-line ratchet green: `net delta: -1` (no test lines added).

Open PR collision check: searched open PR topics and scanned changed-file lists for `extensions/browser/src/sdk-node-runtime.ts`; no open PR touched this file. The related browser node-host proxy deadline PR (#185753) changes only `invoke-browser.ts` and its test, and does not touch `withTimeout`, so it is complementary.

prs.title: feat: enable native plugin UI without a Labs opt-in
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Installed native plugin interfaces still require a separate Labs opt-in even though the same infrastructure already serves bundled plugins.

## User Impact

Enabled user-installed plugins can show native UI by default, without a Labs detour. Existing explicit `gateway.controlUi.experimental.customPlugins: false` values remain off; there is no new configuration key or migration.

**Upgrade behavior:** when the key is omitted, already-enabled plugins may begin loading their native browser UI after upgrading. Native UI is trusted, unsandboxed code running with each signed-in viewer's Gateway permissions. Existing authentication, scope, provenance, asset grants, and lifecycle checks remain unchanged.

Install surfaces explain that plugins may include browser code; installed details and existing enable reviews identify native UI from the inspected manifest. No extra modal, checkbox, or permission gate is added. All plugin APIs retain their existing experimental API-stability policy.

## Why This Change Was Made

Move browser-execution disclosure to ordinary plugin installation and enablement instead of hiding the whole capability behind Labs. Keep the existing advanced opt-out for compatibility, and share the effective default between admission and browser refresh notifications. prs.title: fix(subagents): stop requester wakes retrying changed owners
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes requester subagent completions retrying forever when cleanup or recovery changes the child's completion owner between wake admission and settlement.

## User Impact

An already delivered result can finish its bookkeeping after child cleanup. A wake refused before dispatch records failed delivery and attempts one deduplicated notice in the requester transcript. Distinct ordinary failed waves receive distinct notices; retries and batched delivery retain their shared notice identity. Retained wakes converge on their next evaluation without manual database edits or a migration.

If the requester transcript is unavailable, the notice failure is logged and settlement still finishes. Notice append and settlement are deliberately separate: a crash between them may leave a failure notice followed by a later successful delivery.

## Why This Change Was Made

Dispatch and terminal bookkeeping previously shared the child's strict execution-custody check. After custody changed, both the original write and its failure settlement rejected the same captured row; retained callbacks and the durable wake kept the loop alive.

Terminal bookkeeping now resolves the current row while preserving the run, requester, cancellation ownership, delivery generation, wake generation, frozen cohort, pause notice, and delivery policy. Dispatch keeps strict authority checks. Quiet completion also checks observed progress, and stale quiet decisions release their pending receipt instead of consuming newer work. Permanent owner rejection no longer retains a dispatch replay. If settlement commits but publication fails, its retained receipt reconciles through the existing transaction owner against acknowledged postimages, instead of comparing against the obsolete pre-turnover child snapshot.

The change reuses the existing settlement, cancellation comparison, transcript idempotency, and persisted wake owners. There is no new state store, schema, configuration, or retry mechanism. Production code grows by 95 lines for the explicit settlement boundary and failure notice; test lines stay flat, replacing obsolete custody-rejection assertions with behavior proof. The lifecycle owner remains at its existing 700-line cap.

## Evidence

- Two lifecycle-turnover regressions failed against base `7c0f75ece787e7be7248ea712b9c1df3aacfa814`, reproducing both the wake failure and the repeated failure-settlement rejection. They pass with the fix, including database reopen, a second sweep, and no duplicate dispatch.
- The two-wave notice regression failed on the previous published head: two distinct rejected waves produced only one notice. It passes with the corrected notice identity, checking one notice per wave across reopen/sweep.
- Final suites after receipt reconciliation: **40 requester admission, 13 expiry-receipt, 231 lifecycle, and 39 isolated requester-wake product-flow tests passed**. The three-shard command took **329.90 s**, including a **191 s** isolated runtime build; Vitest phases took **36.23 s** for admission/expiry, **16.19 s** for lifecycle, and **63.56 s** for product flow. Product-flow tests use synthetic model/delivery fixtures; no production Gateway or external model was used.
- Core and agents/session test typechecks, targeted lint/format, changed-source line-cap ratchet, one-page MDX validation, and `git diff --check` passed.
- A further hosted finding reproduced in both existing committed-publication cases after adding child lifecycle turnover: **2 failed, 38 skipped** on the preceding head, then **2 passed, 38 skipped** after repair. The four-line test enhancement keeps net test-line growth at zero.
- Independent Codex autoreview of the final staged candidate, including committed-receipt reconciliation, against the base above: P1 scope, complete, no actionable findings. An earlier quiet-progress finding was fixed and covered before this review.

The [first CI run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40619642675) caught two expiry-receipt regressions: accepting an old receipt after cancellation or a delivery-generation change. Both reproduced locally and were fixed by retaining the existing cancellation/generation checks; the six focused lifecycle/progress/expiry cases passed afterward. No CI rerun or baseline exception was used to hide these failures. Subsequent CI runs [40621198053](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40621198053) and [40624609743](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40624609743) passed for their respective preceding heads; the [final-head CI run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40626506749) passed for `5d554f966a9ae857921e8df2b180820bb22e8296` (41 successful jobs, 28 skipped). Both required `openclaw/ci-gate` contexts passed, and the exact-head native watcher returned GREEN.

The supplied incident logs establish the repeated rejection but do not identify the exact production field that changed. The regression proves the lifecycle-turnover mechanism; deployment verification remains separate.

prs.title: fix(channels): an inbound message is lost when ingress retention pruning hits a locked database
prs.body:
Closes #186428

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a Discord message is lost for good when the state database is busy as it arrives. The retention prune that runs before the durable append throws `database is locked`, so the event is never written to the ingress queue.

## User Impact

User impact: a busy state database no longer drops inbound messages at admission. A failed retention prune is reported through the monitor's `onError`, and the next admission prunes again. Discord's log line changes from `discord handler failed: …` (message lost) to `discord ingress drain failed: database is locked` (message kept).

This applies to every channel that prunes on admission (`retention.pruneIntervalMs: 0`): Discord, LINE, Microsoft Teams, SMS, Signal and webhook hooks. Webhook channels used to fail the HTTP request and rely on provider redelivery. Discord has no redelivery, so it was the one losing messages.

No config or migration changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

`createChannelIngressAdmission` awaits `pruneBeforeAdmission()` in the same `try` as the append. A prune error rejected `monitor.admit()` before the append was even tried. The drain's retry and dead-letter handling only apply to events that are already in the queue, so nothing ever retried this one.

The monitor owns retention, so the fix is in the monitor's prune callback: `pruneIfDue("admission").catch(reportError)`. Pump-owned pruning already reports failures the same way and does not affect queued events. `lastPrunedAt` is not advanced on failure.

Accepted edge case, not changed here: if the append itself fails on every attempt, admission still fails closed and Discord still loses that message (Discord sets `appendRetryDelaysMs: [0]`). That needs an in-memory retry or a redelivery source, which is a larger design change. This PR removes the failure that does not need to block the append.

Production +3/-1, tests +7 (folded into the existing append-failure cases to stay within the test-lines ratchet).

## Evidence

- **Regression test, red before the fix:** `src/channels/message/ingress-monitor.admission.test.ts` › "settles %s append failure after a failed prune without duplicate acknowledgment". Both cases now run with prune-on-admission and prune rejecting once with `database is locked`. Before the fix, both cases failed because `admit()` rejected with the lock error. After the fix, both pass with their original append-failure outcomes, and `onError` receives the lock error first.
- **Focused tests:** `src/channels/message/ingress-monitor*.test.ts` and `extensions/discord/src/monitor/ingress.test.ts` pass, except `ingress-monitor.restart-drain.test.ts` › "reaches ingress idle after the Gateway commits restart drain". That one times out (30 s fixture limit) on my loaded local host on the base commit as well, so it is environmental and left to CI.
- **Checks:** `pnpm tsgo:core` and `pnpm tsgo:core:test` pass. oxlint (`OPENCLAW_OXLINT_SKIP_PREPARE=1`) and oxfmt on the changed files pass. `git diff --check` is clean.
- **Field observation (2026.10.6, Linux):** on our Discord Gateway, `channelIngress.prune` runs on every admission and holds the state DB writer for 1.0–2.2 s (mostly commit). `channelIngress.enqueue` has waited 1.09 s on host admission behind it. Messages were lost with `discord handler failed: Error: database is locked` during this contention. Log excerpts are in #186428.
- **Gap:** no live Discord run under real lock contention. The test injects the lock error at the queue's `prune`, which is the same boundary admission calls.

prs.body:
Related: #165312 (P1), specifically the [headless background-tab reproduction](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/165312#issuecomment-6014153598).

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a missing activation step that can stall background-tab screenshots after a headless browser switches from raw CDP capture to Playwright.

## User Impact

User impact: headless background tabs receive the same pre-capture activation in both screenshot backends, including element and labeled captures. Known headed browsers keep their existing focus behavior. This draft does not establish a fix for the original intermittent headed/Xvfb hang or recover a capture that is already stuck.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared Playwright capture path now follows the existing raw-CDP rule using the running browser's observed launch mode. Screenshot media helpers move intact into a sibling module to keep the route within its line budget. Existing capture deadlines, emulation restoration, and queue ownership remain in place.

The focus-sensitive risk is activating a headed browser by mistake; added mode coverage checks that an observed headed launch overrides a conflicting profile configuration for both backends.

## Evidence

Source inspection against `bfcaa1b2cd1cf2f0e7d617b773e4743218eb219c` found activation in `captureScreenshot` but none in the shared Playwright screenshot owner. Both screenshot routes and snapshot-label capture now carry the same launch-mode fact. The pinned [Playwright Chromium implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/v1.64.1/packages/playwright-core/src/server/chromium/crPage.ts) implements `bringToFront` with `Page.bringToFront`; its screenshot path does not perform that activation.

Added regression coverage for true/false/unknown launch modes, launch-mode propagation to both backends, and a real Chromium route sequence that backgrounds an already captured tab and requests ordinary, labeled, and snapshot-label images. Existing interruption tests continue to target capture/restoration ownership.

Validation actually completed: `git diff --cached --check` passed; an independent read-only source review found and corrected the new regression's `path` versus `imagePath` handling. No additional concrete P0–P2 finding remained in that review. Production delta is +18 lines after accounting for the helper move; tests/test support are +51 lines.

[Remote Chromium regression](https://github.com/ZengWen-DT/openclaw/actions/runs/40626440967) passed the background-tab route test on a temporary child of head `160ab685fbad35d3e60612d469d85a98c65f4619` (1 passed, 15 skipped; test body 1.085 s). This uses real headless Chromium and production route handlers with a test route context.

[Remote base comparison](https://github.com/ZengWen-DT/openclaw/actions/runs/40627216743) ran the same candidate test with the two production screenshot paths restored to the PR parent. The test passed both before and after, so it did not reproduce the reported stall or establish a behavioral before/after fix.

**Not yet verified:** a shipped browser-server path and headed focus preservation. Full CI and the standard autoreview helper have not been run. This remains a draft; the remote test is not a before/after reproduction.

prs.title: fix(signal): stop typing when reply turns end
prs.body:
Closes #127565

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes Signal typing indicators remaining active until provider expiry after an OpenClaw reply ends, including silent replies and failed turns.

## User Impact

Signal receives an explicit typing stop for the same conversation and account when the reply lifecycle closes. No configuration changes are required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Signal reply adapter supplied only a typing-start callback even though the provider already supports terminal stop. This wires both callbacks into the existing shared lifecycle, retaining its late-start ordering and deduplication. Stop errors are logged without failing or repeating the reply.

The small Signal-local adapter extraction keeps the existing oversized event handler within its line-cap ratchet; shared lifecycle code is unchanged.

## Evidence

- Conflict refresh onto main `4420648c404`; current head `c097ca5eaf8cadc61eb69fb5ee1c96fd27be816c` retains the existing reply-typing change and adapts the test-worker routing. The prior refresh failed a focused remote test because its harness API had changed; this head adapts that test and a new remote run is pending. Prior results below refer to earlier heads. Real Signal start/stop proof remains outstanding.

Candidate `65196c9a6b23cb7a3f0a1965ea08bfe4501841ac`, tree `1ea994699ab1740f219c927a4f756e9d0295a8a3`, retains the tested base `d0194c3401f9c225dfd24d232715011e7dbf3f5d`. The exact patch applies cleanly to main `77cecb5449650c8efd3c261fecb4be08f82e7eed`; the newer SDK wrappers preserve typing callbacks. This is source-composition verification, not a runtime rerun on the newer main.

- Eight new monitor-boundary cases fail against the unmodified production handler and pass with this change. They cover final and silent replies, reply/delivery failures, producer AbortError, delayed-start ordering with two-recipient isolation, stop-error logging, and never-mode no-start behavior.
- Focused verification passed 124 tests across six files in 153.269 seconds. The monitor proof exercises real ingress, event handling, dispatch, shared typing lifecycle, and provider request encoding; the reply producer and external transport are mocked.
- Focused production and test type checks, changed-file syntax lint and formatting, Signal MDX validation, and diff checks passed. Canonical autoreview found no actionable P0–P2 findings.
- Test cost: `pnpm test extensions/signal/src/monitor.typing.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` passed 8 tests in 135.296 seconds wall time, including 89.752 seconds of compiled-worker preparation and 31.322 seconds of test time on a contended host. This reuses the existing monitor harness to verify that actual inbound-turn wiring reaches provider cleanup, which shared-helper tests alone cannot prove. CI timing is pending.

Validation limits: no live Signal daemon/account or client UI was tested. Cancellation proof is a reply producer throwing AbortError, not monitor-shutdown cancellation. Never mode is supplied to the real signaler rather than resolved end-to-end from configuration. The changed-check aggregate passed 20 stages before the extension-wide type check exited 137 without diagnostics. One serial retry using the native throttled policy repeated those 20 passes and stopped at the same typecheck, again exit 137 without diagnostics (365.726 seconds total; 163.87 seconds in that stage). The exit is consistent with resource pressure but its exact cause was not independently established; later aggregate stages were not reached. The broader Signal extension run was interrupted after observing 501 passing tests and 20 UNIX-socket bind failures (EPERM under the host policy). Full build, full tests, and complete repository/doc gates have not passed; this is a draft.

prs.body:
Related: #153976.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes provider fallback attempts and failure attribution when a local session transcript projection is rebuilding.

## User Impact

The original storage error stops the turn without consuming another configured provider candidate. There is no configuration or stored-data change. This does not wait for rebuilding, retry the user's message, or improve rebuild speed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add the existing projection exception to the existing runtime-coordination classification. That owner already stops fallback for local failures, including errors preserved through provider-looking wrappers. The change leaves failure wording, visibility and recovery ownership in place.

The hydration recovery proposed in #164843 addresses a separate wait/retry boundary. This change only prevents a storage error that reaches fallback from being treated as a provider failure.

## Evidence

A direct Node 26.5.0 probe calls the real `runWithModelFallback` owner with two synthetic candidates and the actual storage exception, in isolated state with no provider transport. On both unpatched main `38c85c2fe23` and the real published OpenClaw 2026.10.5 package, the direct exception and a provider-looking `503` wrapper execute two candidates and report a provider failure. With this fix, each executes once, reports no provider failure or fallback step, and preserves the identical original error. The wrapper previously lost that error in aggregate fallback failure.

The two regression cases extend the existing fallback-owner table; they add no test-only production seam. The full touched suite passes 51/51 with the official agents-core Vitest config on Node 26.5.0 (296.16 seconds wall on the local Mac; CI duration is not yet available). A focused run of the two new cases also passes (2/2; 92.70 seconds wall). The owner boundary is needed to verify that neither another candidate nor provider-failure callbacks run; a classification-only test would miss that behavior.

Targeted formatting, typed lint, the owning `agents-other` test typecheck and `git diff --check` pass. The canonical independent review of the exact committed candidate against the pinned base completed as `scoped-clean`, with no P0-P2 findings.

No live provider request or production transcript is used or claimed. No new state, policy, configuration, retry owner or recovery path was added; the production delta is one error-classification entry. No Gateway or channel E2E acceptance is claimed.

prs.body:
Closes #103846.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes Anthropic OAuth refreshes silently returning the unchanged credential while it is inside the manager's pre-expiry refresh window.

## User Impact

Anthropic OAuth credentials now rotate when the auth manager has already admitted a refresh, instead of waiting until the stored raw expiry and repeatedly treating a no-op as success.

## Why This Change Was Made

The manager deliberately enters the refresh path within its five-minute margin, but the built-in fallback delegated to `getOAuthApiKey`, whose default contract refreshes only raw-expired credentials. The explicit refresh adapter now calls the same helper with `forceRefresh: true`. The default helper behavior, plugin precedence, provider lookup, error wrapping, and the manager's existing persistence path remain unchanged.

## Evidence

- The existing Anthropic OAuth owner test now calls the real `getOAuthApiKey` helper with four minutes remaining and `forceRefresh: true`, observes the real provider's captured token request, and verifies rotated credentials.
- The existing auth-profile manager test asserts that the built-in fallback passes `{ forceRefresh: true }` to that helper. Its hosted suite also proves the manager persists a forced plugin refresh and preserves the established failure behavior.
- The earlier standalone adapter test was removed because the real plugin runtime correctly handled Anthropic before the built-in fallback; moving the assertions to the two owning boundaries avoids that false premise and reduces test code by 32 lines overall.
- Prior hosted run `40601445065`: 19 CI jobs passed; all CodeQL, OpenGrep, Workflow Sanity, and dead-code workflows passed. The two direct failures were the superseded standalone test and the test-line ratchet. The current revision removes 45 standalone test lines and adds 13 focused lines, changing the PR's test delta from +45 to -32.
- `node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check src/llm/utils/oauth/index.ts src/agents/auth-profiles/oauth-provider-operations.ts src/llm/utils/oauth/anthropic.test.ts src/agents/auth-profiles/oauth.fallback-to-main-agent.test.ts` — passed.
- `git diff --check` — passed.
- Local targeted Vitest could not load the existing configuration because this dependency snapshot lacks `@solidjs/vite-plugin` and `@openclaw/proc-safe/windows-job`; it failed before collecting tests.
- Required scoped oxlint could not load the existing configuration because the same snapshot lacks `eslint-plugin-solid`; `tsgo` is absent from the snapshot. No dependency files or `node_modules` contents were changed.

Current-head hosted run `40626102042` completed successfully: all 30 CI jobs finished with 21 successes and 9 conditional skips, including `checks-node-changed-2` and `checks-fast-baseline-ratchets`. Workflow Sanity, OpenGrep, CodeQL Critical Quality, CodeQL, and macOS dead-code reporting also passed.

prs.title: fix(inworld): redact reflected credentials in HTTP errors
prs.body:
Closes #146804

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Inworld speech and voice-list errors include the full Basic credential when a failed upstream response reflects the request's Authorization header.

## User Impact

Error messages mask recognized credentials while keeping the HTTP status and surrounding diagnostic text. This addresses the thrown provider error; persistence in downstream logs or transcripts is a separate question.

## Why This Change Was Made

The two endpoints already share a bounded error reader. Apply the public SDK redactor in tools mode before truncating its diagnostic, with a lazy import to preserve the cold capability-catalog import contract. The existing byte cap, read timeout, Unicode-safe character cap, request authorization, and successful response handling retain their owners.

This follows the report and prior repair by @wangmiao0668000666 in #146742. I read the issue's complete discussion and all discussion/review comments on #146742 and #141319, and checked their current states: both closed unmerged. The author closed #146742 after 31 days in the stale queue without progress after assignment; #141319 was closed by the active-PR limit. Neither was closed for rejecting the proposed behavior. A fresh issue-number and semantic PR search found no open equivalent repair.

## Evidence

On base `6c890b1fc7d99fdb47647f3da62ad5ad4f24cdc5`, an isolated manual probe executed the complete production Inworld module against a local HTTP server that reflected a synthetic Authorization header. Both TTS and voices failures contained the full synthetic credential before the change and masked it afterward. The production response reader and redactor dependency graph were pinned to that same base.

Seven additional checks passed: redaction before the 400-character cutoff, ordinary diagnostic whitespace, the 8 KiB overflow marker, Unicode-safe truncation, body-read failure, successful audio decoding, and successful voice listing. All nine requests released their resources, and importing the provider alone did not import the security runtime. Repository-configured formatting and diff whitespace checks passed.

These are manual source-module probes: the SSRF admission adapter and logging-config lookup were substituted; no Gateway, real Inworld service, or packaged plugin/SDK resolution was exercised. No test files were added or changed, and no build, full test suite, or project typecheck was run. Keeping this as a draft with those validation gaps explicit.

prs.title: fix(gateway): retain metadata errors after late startup refreshes
prs.body:
Related #177455 — draft proposal; production reachability is unproven.

## What Problem This Solves
The focused in-process tests demonstrate that a late attachment refresh can overwrite a newer publication failure, allowing a subsequent auth or skills change to clear the original error. Whether this overlap occurs through a shipped Gateway entry point remains unproven.

## Proposed Behavior
For the tested overlap, the original publication error stays visible without extra metadata refreshes or change broadcasts. A later successful publication can still restore metadata normally. This is not yet a demonstrated production user impact.

### Maintainer decision requested

[The merged lifecycle simplification #173092](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/173092) explicitly accepted completion-order or temporarily cached optional metadata diagnostics. This proposal narrows that tradeoff for a newer publication failure using the existing state field, without restoring event-version machinery. **Should a terminal publication error remain authoritative until a successful publication?** No maintainer decision on this distinction is recorded yet.

Focused tests establish metadata-runtime failure retention and recovery; a running Gateway trace of this startup ordering and its client-visible effect is still outstanding, as noted in [the review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/177771#issuecomment-6278513882). This is a draft proposal, not an owner-approved change.

### Production ordering counterevidence
Further source tracing found that normal HTTP startup [awaits request-runtime readiness before post-attach model publication](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/2977d820ffffb3e7591c2e41aa96638b288784f8/src/gateway/server-startup-finish.ts#L194). Request-runtime initialization awaits the initial lifetime sidecars, which await metadata attachment; the config reloader starts later. Normal hot reload does not reattach this context. No naturally overlapping generic replacement caller was identified in a bounded investigation. The current tests deliberately delay attachment refresh across that unproven boundary; they must not be presented as a running-Gateway reproduction. An alternative embedded/reentrant path has not been ruled out. Keeping this draft until both reachability and the maintainer decision are resolved.

## Why This Change Was Made
Let attachment catch-up initialize availability only while no publication state has been observed. Publication events retain authority; existing catch-up warnings and recovery behavior remain unchanged.

## Evidence
- Both new resolve/reject regressions fail on the base: subsequent skills/auth changes cause three refresh calls instead of one.
- Frozen final source: three related test files, 48/48 passed with runner exit 0. Tests use the real metadata runtime and cover original-error identity, no extra broadcasts, successful recovery, reverse ordering and shutdown.
- Core production and selected Gateway test typechecks, focused lint/format, line-cap, state-schema and three Gateway boundary checks pass.
- Canonical autoreview was attempted on the same cloud host but its Codex connection was rejected with HTTP 403; no valid automated review was produced. A separate parent-thread code/lifecycle review was performed. Full repository tests were not run.

AI-assisted implementation and tests, all executed in a managed cloud environment.

prs.title: fix(anthropic): preserve newlines in seeded tool input
prs.body:
Related: #109478

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes multiline file content gaining a literal backslash-n when an Anthropic response seeds complete tool input at the start of a content block.

## User Impact

Newlines in valid seeded tool arguments reach the write tool unchanged, while intentionally literal backslash-n text stays literal. No configuration change or migration is needed. This covers the direct Anthropic raw-SSE boundary identified in the issue, not every provider symptom or a complete Gateway session.

## Why This Change Was Made

Parse valid outer SSE JSON strictly before using the existing malformed-JSON recovery. Repair heuristics can otherwise mistake the end of a line such as `as f:` for a Windows-path prefix. Shared repair defaults and malformed-frame error redaction stay unchanged.

## Evidence

- Conflict refresh onto main `f76e79be6a8`; current head `2419556fa289054a248fc96448ab894e9410d882` retains the current loopback listener and adapts the existing regression cases. The previous head failed the repository test-lines ratchet; [refreshed-head CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40625651235) passed. Earlier evidence below refers to the revisions identified there; live Anthropic model proof remains outstanding.

- **Red on base:** with the regression added to upstream `f1689ee0c6b402ed7ea812a863afba40b0739329`, real loopback HTTP → Anthropic SDK raw SSE → provider/reducer → default write-tool execution saves bytes `92,110` instead of newline byte `10` after `as f:`. The malformed outer-JSON escape control passes.
- **Green with the fix:** the four focused files below pass **89 tests**. The new regression compares actual saved bytes against independent expected content containing both a newline and intentional literal backslash-n. Malformed escape recovery, shared Windows-path recovery, error redaction, ping handling, and managed transport coverage remain passing.
- Published head `8f7b147718832f05e644ab5d3e1cee80e5f34e8f` has exactly the tested/reviewed tree `c2e475f738edb4b4615738e136484abb12582534` and tested parent above. Publication changed commit metadata only from local `35071c9347fbc0069732a8a94d9cd2862cadd5b3`.
- P0–P3 independent autoreview: no actionable findings. Final assertion-safety and formatting checks pass. The changed-check run also passed targeted lint, production typecheck, and all 29 core-test type graphs.
- **Broad local checks are not green:** `node scripts/check-changed.mjs --timed` exits 1. The unchanged baseline index reproduces three UI max-lines suppression failures and the SQLite worker inventory's `SuppressedError` during disposal. Core-test root budgets exceed 720 (agents-tools 721, gateway-root 721, infra 724, plugins-platform 727); membership/configuration is unchanged by this patch. Knip reports four unused exports in untouched files. Full baseline Knip and the complete root-budget check were not separately rerun; unchanged inputs support attribution but are not a clean full-baseline run. No unrelated guard or source was modified.
- Linux, Node 24.19.0, pnpm 12.12.1, repository-pinned Bun fork and frozen dependencies. This is deterministic local transport/write-boundary proof, not a live Anthropic request. Exact-head [CI run 39433440293](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/39433440293) completed successfully: 49 jobs passed, 29 were scope-skipped, and the meaningful `openclaw/ci-gate` passed. Earlier draft-scoped skips are not validation.

Focused command:

```sh
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/ai/src/providers/anthropic.test.ts packages/ai/src/providers/anthropic.sse-parse-error.test.ts packages/ai/src/utils/json-parse.test.ts packages/ai/src/transports/transport-stream-shared.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```


### Standalone public-package runtime evidence (October 20)

The [documented published package entry](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/8f7b147718832f05e644ab5d3e1cee80e5f34e8f/docs/reference/openclaw-ai.md#quick-start) is `createLlmRuntime` from `@openclaw/ai`, followed by `registerBuiltInApiProviders` from `@openclaw/ai/providers` and `runtime.streamSimple`. I built the actual `packages/ai/dist/index.mjs` and `providers.mjs` exports with the normal package build configuration and executed a standalone Node driver outside Vitest.

The driver connects those built public exports to the unchanged production `Agent` loop and default `createWriteTool` (loaded from source through the repository TypeScript loader). A deterministic local HTTP server supplies complete seeded tool input, then a final response after receiving the real tool result. There is no mocked SDK, reducer, agent loop, write operation, or filesystem. The expected file is an independently specified 45-byte numeric buffer. A third request checks malformed outer-JSON escape recovery.

Build command (both revisions; 2 GiB heap and one build worker):

```sh
OPENCLAW_TSDOWN_MAX_OLD_SPACE_MB=2048 node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/tsdown-build.mts --config tsdown.ai.config.ts --concurrency 1
```

  requests=3; advertisedWrite=true; toolResultReturned=true

  saved bytes at header boundary: 102,58,92,110,32

prs.title: fix(ci): bound artifact verification GitHub API requests
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Artifact verification waits indefinitely when `gh api` accepts a connection but never returns. The existing retry loop only runs after the request exits.

Fixes #130570. This follows the withdrawn, unmerged #123037, whose author explicitly welcomed continuation. I read the issue discussion and the full discussions on #123037, #108986, and the existing retry repair #120654; current main still contains the unbounded call.

## Why This Change Was Made

Give each GET in the existing shared helper a fixed 30-second deadline and a 10-second SIGKILL grace. Deadline exits 124 and 137 receive a diagnostic and follow the existing three-attempt retry policy. The current workflow callers of `verify-upload` run on Ubuntu, where GNU `timeout` is available; the command is checked with the other verification prerequisites.

Authentication rejection, fresh-artifact-only 404 retries, output isolation, and immutable artifact/producer validation retain their existing owner. The portable Bash entrypoint is unchanged.

## Evidence

Executed the complete before/after `verify-upload` CLI locally with real Bash, GNU timeout, and jq, using a controlled executable in place of gh. The deployed 30s/10s values and normal retry delays were used:

- Baseline: still on the first stalled request after 42.02s; terminated by the external probe.
- First request stalls, second succeeds: success at 32.11s.
- First request survives SIGTERM (delivery recorded), then SIGKILL permits retry: success at 42.10s.
- All three requests stall: failure after 96.04s with three calls and the deadline diagnostic.
- Normal success, an i/o timeout followed by recovery, fresh-artifact 404 recovery, immediate authentication rejection, immediate producer-attempt 404 rejection, and digest mismatch all behaved as expected.
- No partial response escaped to stdout; completed cases cleaned up their temporary request files.
- `bash -n` passed; the diff has no whitespace errors. One production file changes. No repository tests were written or changed, and no build was run.

Draft pending hosted CI and maintainer review. These are local CLI/process probes with a substituted gh executable; they do not establish real GitHub transport or release-workflow execution.
