prs.body:
### Summary

On Node 24.16.0 through 24.18.0 (fixed in 24.18.1), calling `next()` on a `node:sqlite` `StatementSync` iterator that already returned `done` restarts the statement and leaves it stepped. The connection then holds a WAL read snapshot while `isTransaction` is `false`, so every WAL checkpoint stays blocked and the `-wal` file grows until the Gateway restarts. The upstream fix is nodejs/node@af9ff0490c (CVE-2026-58041, "sqlite: invalidate tag store iterators on statement reset"), which also marks the iterator done on `SQLITE_DONE`. Root cause, bisect and production before/after: #143524.

This PR:

1. **Guard (code).** Once the observed iterator wrapper has seen `done` (from `next()` or from an earlier `return()`), later `next()` and `return()` calls are answered by the wrapper with a fresh copy of the terminal result and never reach the native iterator. The native iterator is not stepped after `done` and is not finalized twice. On main the engines field already excludes the affected releases; the guard removes the dependency on the probe and on the Node version.
2. **Docs.** A "Known Node 24 issues" table on `/install/node-compatibility` (the Fixed-in cell names nodejs/node@af9ff0490c and CVE-2026-58041) and a "SQLite WAL grows and checkpoints stay blocked" runbook on `/gateway/troubleshooting/gateway-service-and-process`, linked from the troubleshooting index.

### Why main's existing iterator check does not cover 24.18.0

Line numbers are on main `c96f35d5d60`.

- **Where and when it runs.** `assertSafeSqliteRuntime()` (`src/infra/sqlite-native-runtime.ts:124-184`) runs from `openNodeSqliteDatabase()` (`src/infra/node-sqlite.ts:112`), once per process: the result is cached at `sqlite-native-runtime.ts:127-129`, and worker isolates reuse the parent's result through environment data (`:130-140`). It calls `probeSqliteIteratorBehavior()` (`src/infra/sqlite-native-observer.ts:25-45`) on a one-row `:memory:` statement (`sqlite-native-runtime.ts:149-154`).
- **What it decides.** The probe steps the iterator past `done` once more and records `nextAfterDoneIsTerminal = previous.next().done === true` (`sqlite-native-observer.ts:29`). On 24.18.0 that extra `next()` restarts the statement and returns the row again, so the probe correctly reports `false`. The probe does not reject the runtime: the only hard gate in that function is the SQLite WAL-reset version check (`assertSqliteWalResetSafeVersion`, `sqlite-native-runtime.ts:26-36`, called at `:135` and `:157`), and SQLite 3.53.1 on 24.18.0 passes it. The probe result is stored as `iteratorBehavior` and handed to the observer (`node-sqlite.ts:107-115`, `sqlite-native-runtime.ts:168-183`).
- **Why a post-done `next()` still reaches the native iterator.** The only consumer is the observed iterator wrapper. When native `next()` returns `done`, it sets `done = native.iteratorBehavior.nextAfterDoneIsTerminal` (`sqlite-native-observer.ts:346-347`). On 24.18.0 that is `false`, so the wrapper only calls `lifetime.stopObservation(true)` (`:351`) and leaves `done` false. The next call passes the early-out at `:336` (`done` is false), re-activates the lifetime (`:339-342`) and calls `nativeNext.apply(this, args)` (`:345`), which is exactly the restart. In other words the check makes the observer *account for* a restartable cursor (custody tracking); it does not *prevent* the restart, and nothing later steps the restarted statement to `done` or resets it, so the snapshot stays held. On runtimes where the probe returns `true`, the post-done call is still forwarded (`:336`, `done || ...`), it is just harmless there. `return()` after `done` is forwarded to native as well (`:360-366`).
- **Released builds.** The probe is on main only. The `v2026.10.5`, `v2026.10.6` and `v2026.10.7` tags do not contain `nextAfterDoneIsTerminal`; their wrapper re-arms a finished lifetime and forwards post-done `next()` unconditionally. 2026.10.5's engines field (`>=24.16.0 <25 || >=26.1.0`) admits 24.16.0 through 24.18.0; 2026.10.6 and 2026.10.7 require `>=24.22.1 <25 || >=26.12.1`.

With this PR the wrapper answers from `terminal` before any of that (`sqlite-native-observer.ts:340-342` and `:363-365` on this branch), so the outcome no longer depends on the probe or on the Node version.

### Scope

- The guard covers iterators created by `statement.iterate()` on databases opened through `openNodeSqliteDatabase()`, where `trackSqliteSchema()` installs the observer (`sqlite-schema-facts.ts:223`). That is every OpenClaw state and agent database.
- Grep for direct `node:sqlite` use outside it (non-test code under `src`, `extensions`, `packages`): `new DatabaseSync(` appears in `src/gateway/worker-environments/bootstrap.ts` (`:memory:`), the workspace-quiescence worker scripts, `src/infra/update-managed-service-handoff-sqlite-source.ts`, `src/infra/bun-sqlite-close-probe.worker.ts`, `src/infra/sqlite-native-runtime.ts` (the probe itself, `:memory:`) and the knowledge-source-ingest skill scripts. Of these, two call `iterate()`: the close-capability probe worker (`bun-sqlite-close-probe.worker.ts:28`, one `next()` on a temp database that it then closes, never past `done`) and the knowledge-source-ingest skill scripts (`extensions/knowledge/skills/knowledge-source-ingest/scripts/source-manifest.mjs`, `discrawl-normalize.mjs`), which use `for...of` loops in short-lived CLI processes on their own files. A `for...of` loop stops at `done` and never calls `next()` again. So neither is exposed, and no Gateway state or agent database iterates outside the observer.
- `iteratorBehavior.nextAfterDoneIsTerminal` and `iteratorBehavior.returnAfterDoneIsInert` lose their only consumer in this diff. Grep finds no other reader: the remaining references are the probe (`sqlite-native-observer.ts:16-45`), admission parsing/transport (`sqlite-native-runtime.ts:59-96`) and one test (`node-sqlite.test.ts:266-268`). I left them in place to keep this PR small and can remove the probe and the transport field in a follow-up if you want.

### Tests

Run on a temporary Linux VM (Debian 12, n2-standard-16), not on the reporting Windows host. Branch head `4ddc356d618` on base `c96f35d5d60`.

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/infra/sqlite-native-observer.test.ts src/infra/node-sqlite.test.ts` on Node 24.22.1: 2 files, 80 tests passed.
- The extended test (`sqlite-native-observer.test.ts:79`) spies on the native iterator prototype's `next` and `return`, finishes an iterator once by exhaustion and once by `return()`, then calls `next()`, `return()`, `next()`, `return()`. It asserts all four results equal the terminal result, native `next` is not called again, native `return` is called 0 times (exhausted) or exactly once (returned), and no native execution stays pending.
- Negative proofs on the same VM:
  - return guard removed: fails with `expected "return" to be called +0 times, but got 2 times`.
  - next guard removed (post-done `next()` forwarded as on main): fails with `expected "next" to be called 3 times, but got 5 times`.
  - main's `sqlite-native-observer.ts` with the new test: fails.
  - Guards restored: 12/12 pass.
- Same test file on Node 24.16.0, 24.18.0, 24.18.1, 24.22.1, 26.4.0 and 26.5.1: 12/12 on each.
- Standalone repro (no OpenClaw; finish an iterator, call `next()` once more, then `wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)` from a second connection): restarts and holds the snapshot on 24.16.0, 24.17.0, 24.18.0 and 26.4.0; returns `done` and checkpoints fully on 24.18.1, 24.22.1 and 26.5.1. 26.5.1 carries the same CVE fix (nodejs/node@d08fde8a16).
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:test:src`, `pnpm tsgo:all`: all exit 0.
- oxlint on the two touched TS files: 0 warnings, 0 errors (293 rules). oxfmt check on all five touched files: clean. `pnpm format:docs:check`: clean (1400 files). markdownlint (`lint:docs` config): 0 issues.
- `pnpm docs:check-links`: 16006 internal links, 0 broken. `pnpm docs:check-mdx`: passed. `pnpm docs:check-links:anchors` reports 7 findings, none from this diff (all present on main, e.g. `docs/gateway/troubleshooting.md:87`, an unchanged line). The new links resolve: `/install/node-compatibility#supported-versions` (`## Supported versions`), `#known-node-24-issues`, `/gateway/troubleshooting/gateway-service-and-process#sqlite-wal-grows-and-checkpoints-stay-blocked`, and `/cli/doctor/sqlite-maintenance` (`docs/cli/doctor/sqlite-maintenance.md`). `openclaw logs --follow` is documented in `docs/cli/logs.md` and listed by `openclaw logs --help`.

Tested Node range for the bug: leaks on 24.16.0, 24.17.0 and 24.18.0, fixed in 24.18.1 (also clean on 24.19.0 through 24.22.1 in the Gateway bisect on #143524). Gateway-level reproduction and bisect were on Windows; the standalone repro and this test run were on Linux, so the bug is not OS-specific.

Related: #143524 (root cause), #164294 (same fingerprint, most reports list Node 24.18.0).

prs.body:
## Purpose

Prepare the Requesty provider cutover from bundled core code to the separately maintained `openclaw/requesty` plugin ([source package PR, merged](https://github.com/openclaw/requesty/pull/2)), while preserving `requesty/*` model references and catalog-backed onboarding.

## Change

Remove the bundled runtime and its bundled-only tests and workspace importer. Register the `requesty` provider as an official external package with an exact npm version and integrity pin; retain the existing provider icon and config-overlay identifier. Regenerate plugin inventory and configuration baselines, and update provider installation guidance.

## Validation

Local targeted external-provider catalog and bundled-artifact contracts pass. Generated configuration and plugin-inventory checks, docs links, and changed-file formatting pass. The replacement package candidate was installed via OpenClaw's CLI in isolated state, with synthetic-key onboarding and a separately imported provider-policy artifact. A second full pinned local ClawSweeper review on the current-main merge candidate also found no actionable correctness or security defect; it marked end-to-end publication proof incomplete. The local tarball hash is only a proposed pin; it must be compared with the actual published registry artifact before this PR is ready to merge.

## Gate before merging

The published OpenClaw 2026.10.7 npm archive does not contain Requesty; its release tag predates the provider merge. Requesty is present on current main but not in that published release. This cutover still requires a real replacement package before it can reach users. Do not merge this removal until `@openclaw/requesty-provider@2026.10.7` is genuinely published, the catalog integrity matches npm, and an official catalog-backed installation proves onboarding and cold policy behavior. GitHub refused this account's attempt to make `openclaw/requesty` public; an org owner must change visibility. Package publication and repository visibility remain separate authorization and permission gates. This PR is intentionally draft until those gates and current-head CI pass.

prs.title: fix: reject oversized daily memory-flush payloads
prs.body:
Related: #90354. Focused replacement for #96291, following [Peter's request for a fresh smaller PR](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/96291#issuecomment-6378881568).

## What Problem This Solves

Pre-compaction memory flushes can append an oversized payload to a daily note even though the write is append-only; the reported roughly 1,200-character line reaches the file before downstream validation rejects it.

## User Impact

This **draft candidate** rejects a daily-note `content` payload above **800 JavaScript UTF-16 code units** before provenance recording or file mutation, with a model-facing request for a shorter pointer. Accepted content stays byte-for-byte intact. The existing separator can add a newline outside the payload. The limit applies to each new payload, not the total stored note.

**Maintainer policy decision remains open:** the candidate currently applies 800 unconditionally to canonical `memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md` targets. Default-on, explicit opt-in, or declining this policy remain @steipete's decision. No opt-in configuration contract has been invented. Runtime validation does not resolve this policy question or establish merge readiness.

## Why This Change Was Made

Five changed files, +242/−4 at `24d26272c852c59a66348a2baff6d64ea48bfc39`; production remains +17/−3. The old 58-file branch is not revived. Target admission, containment, authority, duplicate checks, append operations, provenance, and plugin-owned persistence keep their existing owners. No service guard, QA framework, SDK, configuration contract, validation threshold, or baseline is changed.

The original patch is `3f1dee65`; `9f93ebce` adds a legacy-byte fixture and one QA scenario; `d782f1ec` merges main `1b6eb7bf` to preserve upstream test cleanup. The latest fixture-only correction correlates actual Responses tool IDs by exact arguments and waits for the actual foreground reply after any queue acknowledgement.

## Evidence

Executed on 26 October 2026.

Environment: Ubuntu under WSL2, working systemd user bus, pinned Node 24.22.1 and pnpm 12.15.0. All checks used normal repository wrappers and guards. Isolated HOME/state/workspace/profile and allocated loopback ports kept these tests separate from operator state. No operator service was stopped, restarted, reconfigured, or disabled.

### Real Gateway automatic memory flush

**PASS at `24d26272c852c59a66348a2baff6d64ea48bfc39`**, using the repository QA runner, a real isolated Gateway child, real automatic pre-compaction flush, real tools, and real filesystem. AIMock supplies fixed model replies; this is not live-provider proof.

| Operation | Observed result | Stored bytes | SHA-256 |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| Read pre-existing 1,239-unit Unicode/CRLF note | Full legacy content and tail read; original bytes unchanged | 3,039 | `88f42d43822630c7c4877b8ca755a090fc1ce77fc9dc6c175325046a58094b4e` |
| Append exact 800-unit whitespace/CRLF payload | Accepted verbatim, with existing append separator | 3,840 | `ec55b7ae244714582a33fb564e41e61195f51be582ab50506a8325df40b4438f` |
| Attempt 801 units | Deterministic max-800 tool rejection; bytes unchanged | 3,840 | same |
| Attempt 1,200 ASCII characters | Deterministic max-800 tool rejection; bytes unchanged | 3,840 | same |

The scenario compares raw Buffers after each operation, correlates actual tool-result IDs with the AIMock request journal, requires successful flush/session completion, and verifies the foreground model reply. Result: 1 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped. The QA suite recorded 90.804 s; the outer CLI invocation took 685.22 s, including its normal 509.4 s rebuild after the Git head changed.

### Stored-note compatibility across a source-runtime upgrade

**PASS: release `v2026.10.7` / `157d8c2bc3ea2fa183afdc11088e69690bf8e64e` → candidate `24d26272c852c59a66348a2baff6d64ea48bfc39`.** Both source runtimes used the same isolated state, configuration, workspace, daily note, token and loopback port.

1. The stable foreground Gateway returned `health.ok=true`; authenticated HTTP `/tools/invoke` → `memory_get` returned the complete Unicode/CRLF daily note, with no truncation.
2. Only the proof Gateway was stopped. The candidate ran `doctor --fix --non-interactive` (exit 0, including normal UI asset preparation) and `config validate` (passed), retaining the state and note.
3. The candidate foreground Gateway returned `health.ok=true`; the same authenticated `memory_get` returned the identical full text. Raw stored bytes matched the pre-upgrade expected Buffer: **1,239 UTF-16 units / 3,039 bytes**, SHA-256 `88f42d43822630c7c4877b8ca755a090fc1ce77fc9dc6c175325046a58094b4e` before and after. Candidate stage completed at 11:31:01 UTC.

Doctor's exit 0 is not a clean-environment/security audit: it also reported the disposable local token field, absent provider credentials/automation authority, and optional environment capabilities. Those warnings were retained; no provider credentials or broader authority were added.

This demonstrates stored daily-note compatibility across a **source-runtime upgrade** using the supported Doctor lifecycle. It does not exercise the package updater, embedding/search rebuilds, or a live model. The automatic-flush boundary is the separate Gateway scenario above.

### Focused regressions and static checks

- **78 tests passed across six files at `d782f1ec`**, 375.92 s wrapper wall time (378 s outer wall), using the repository-selected test runtime. The final commit changes only the YAML scenario; these six test files and production code are unchanged. Includes host and host-backed sandbox wrapper coverage for boundary acceptance, oversized rejection, missing-file preservation, authority/path restrictions, and legacy raw-byte preservation. This is not a container sandbox test.
- Candidate Gateway preparation and stable runtime build passed with pinned dependencies and normal supply-chain/runtime-publication checks.
- Scoped type-aware lint (0 warnings/errors), production core and agents-root test typechecks, five-file formatting including pinned Bun parity, docs MDX, diff whitespace, line-growth/max-lines/environment/assertion-safety ratchets all passed on the exact final content. Lint initially lacked the `eslint-plugin-solid` development dependency omitted by the Gateway install profile; the supported unfiltered frozen install succeeded and the identical lint retry passed. No lockfile/configuration edits or skipped lifecycle checks.
- Native AutoReview of the final YAML-only correction: exit 0, `scoped-clean`, no actionable P0–P2 findings. The helper used its documented GPT-6 Sol fallback after the default GPT-6.1 Sol was unavailable to the account. The review included unchanged transport/AIMock context and verified frozen inputs; it is a source review, not runtime proof.

The focused regression invocation was:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run \
  src/agents/agent-tools.memory-flush-append-write.test.ts \
  src/agents/agent-tools.memory-flush-writer.test.ts \
  src/agents/agent-tools.read.workspace-mutations.test.ts \
  src/agents/agent-tools.workspace-outside.test.ts \
  src/agents/agent-tools.prefix-stability.test.ts \
  src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-memory.tools.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```

## Evidence provenance and limitations

The earlier systemd-user-bus failure occurred before any Gateway scenario ran. The first new runtime attempts exposed fixture assumptions about normalized Responses tool IDs and queued foreground acknowledgements; they were failures, not runtime passes. After correction, attempt 5 passed on `d782f1ec` plus the uncommitted YAML delta. The result above is a fresh run of the published final commit.

Historical 81-test results at `3f1dee65` remain valid for that original revision only; they are not the current 78-test run. The original base-red check had 6 expected failures / 22 passes. No live-provider, package-updater, embedding/search, native Windows, or full monorepo/CI pass is claimed. The QA YAML is classified as an unknown surface by the broad lane classifier; that all-lanes run was not executed. The observed GitHub check snapshot had 8 successes / 73 skipped, with no failures; skipped checks are not passes. The stable health snapshot reported CPU event-loop degradation while its health RPC and full memory read passed; this is not performance validation.

The implementation remains a per-payload policy proposal. Cumulative logical-flush limits, line-count/line-length policy, existing-file read ceilings, and the old branch's stricter daily symlink policy are outside this PR.

## Reproduction

The fresh-checkout procedures below were source-reviewed and Bash-syntax-checked. The recorded runtime invocations ran against already prepared pinned checkouts; these copyable clone/build blocks were not rerun end-to-end. They use the supported CLI and keep service inspection and authentication intact. A guard failure is a blocked run, never a reason to bypass the guard.

<details>
<summary>Real Gateway boundary — fresh isolated checkout</summary>

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Reproduction of the real Gateway/AIMock check. See RUNTIME-EVIDENCE.json for executed results.
# This fresh-checkout procedure was source-reviewed and syntax-checked, not run end-to-end.
# The recorded runtime command ran against the same pinned, already prepared checkout.
# Prerequisites: Linux user bus, Node 24.22.1, pnpm 12.15.0, Git, and free build space.
set -euo pipefail
for key in OPENCLAW_SYSTEMD_UNIT OPENCLAW_LAUNCHD_LABEL OPENCLAW_WINDOWS_TASK_NAME \
  OPENCLAW_SERVICE_MARKER OPENCLAW_SERVICE_KIND OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_SERVICE_PID VITEST; do
  if [[ -n "${!key-}" ]]; then
    printf 'Refusing inherited %s; start an ordinary clean shell.\n' "$key" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
done
proof=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/openclaw-184049-qa.XXXXXX")
mkdir -p "$proof/home" "$proof/state"
chmod 700 "$proof" "$proof/home" "$proof/state"
exec env -i PATH="$PATH" USER="$(id -un)" LOGNAME="$(id -un)" SHELL=/bin/bash LANG=C.UTF-8 \
  HOME="$proof/home" PROOF_ROOT="$proof" \
  XDG_RUNTIME_DIR="${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-/run/user/$(id -u)}" \
  DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS="${DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS:-unix:path=/run/user/$(id -u)/bus}" \
  npm_config_userconfig=/dev/null CI=1 bash -s <<'PROOF'
set -euo pipefail
proof="$PROOF_ROOT"
node --version
pnpm --version
busctl --user list --no-pager >/dev/null
git clone --depth 1 --branch codex/memory-flush-payload-bound \
  https://github.com/AdrianIp0204/openclaw.git "$proof/source"
git -C "$proof/source" fetch --depth 2 origin 24d26272c852c59a66348a2baff6d64ea48bfc39
git -C "$proof/source" checkout --detach 24d26272c852c59a66348a2baff6d64ea48bfc39
export HOME="$proof/home" OPENCLAW_HOME="$proof/home"
export XDG_CONFIG_HOME="$proof/home/.config"
export OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR="$proof/state"
export OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH="$proof/state/openclaw.json"
export OPENCLAW_OAUTH_DIR="$proof/state/credentials"
export OPENCLAW_PROFILE="pr184049-qa-${proof##*.}"
unset OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PASSWORD OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_URL OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT
node --input-type=module - "$proof/port" <<'JS'
import fs from 'node:fs';
import net from 'node:net';
const server = net.createServer();
server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', () => {
  fs.writeFileSync(process.argv[2], String(server.address().port), { flag: 'wx', mode: 0o600 });
  server.close();
});
JS
export OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT="$(cat "$proof/port")"
cd "$proof/source"
OPENCLAW_BUILD_PRIVATE_QA=1 node scripts/worktree-setup.mjs gateway --plan
OPENCLAW_BUILD_PRIVATE_QA=1 node scripts/worktree-setup.mjs gateway
OPENCLAW_ENABLE_PRIVATE_QA_CLI=1 OPENCLAW_BUILD_PRIVATE_QA=1 \
pnpm openclaw --profile "$OPENCLAW_PROFILE" qa suite \
  --provider-mode aimock \
  --scenario memory-flush-daily-payload-bound \
  --concurrency 1 --fail-fast \
  --output-dir .artifacts/qa-e2e/memory-flush-daily-payload-bound
PROOF
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Stable-to-candidate stored-note compatibility — two terminals</summary>

# Latest-stable daily-note compatibility reproduction

**Runtime sequence executed successfully on 26 October 2026.** This procedure checks a real source-runtime upgrade from release
`v2026.10.7` (`157d8c2bc3ea2fa183afdc11088e69690bf8e64e`) to PR commit
`24d26272c852c59a66348a2baff6d64ea48bfc39`, retaining the same isolated state and
workspace. Both actual Gateways returned the full 1,239-unit / 3,039-byte legacy note
through authenticated `memory_get`; its SHA-256 remained
`88f42d43822630c7c4877b8ca755a090fc1ce77fc9dc6c175325046a58094b4e`.
Candidate Doctor exited 0 and configuration validation passed. See
`RUNTIME-EVIDENCE.json` for the recorded results and health limitations.
The fresh-checkout blocks below were source-reviewed and syntax-checked, but were
not executed as one complete script; actual runtime commands used prepared pinned
checkouts. This does not test the package
updater, automatic flush, embeddings/search, or the unresolved new-write policy.
Run the separate AIMock scenario for the automatic-flush boundary.

Prerequisites: Linux with a working systemd user bus, sufficient free disk space,
Node `24.22.1` (or a compatible `>=26.12.1` release), pinned pnpm `12.15.0`, Git,
and two Bash terminals. Use source you have reviewed and trust. Do not alter or
disable any service-inspection check. A service guard failure is a blocked run.

In terminal A, prepare isolated sources and state:

```bash
set -euo pipefail
assert_proof_shell() {
  local key
  for key in OPENCLAW_SYSTEMD_UNIT OPENCLAW_LAUNCHD_LABEL OPENCLAW_WINDOWS_TASK_NAME \
    OPENCLAW_SERVICE_MARKER OPENCLAW_SERVICE_KIND OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_SERVICE_PID VITEST; do
    if [[ -n "${!key-}" ]]; then
      printf 'Refusing inherited %s; start an ordinary clean shell.\n' "$key" >&2
      return 1
    fi
  done
}
assert_proof_shell
unset OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_URL OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT
busctl --user list --no-pager >/dev/null
proof=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/openclaw-184049-upgrade.XXXXXX")
mkdir -p "$proof/home" "$proof/state" "$proof/workspace/memory" "$proof/evidence"
chmod 700 "$proof" "$proof/home" "$proof/state"
printf 'export PROOF_ROOT=%q\n' "$proof" > "$proof/env.sh"
printf 'export PROOF_PROFILE=%q\n' "pr184049-${proof##*.}" >> "$proof/env.sh"
declare -f assert_proof_shell >> "$proof/env.sh"
cat >> "$proof/env.sh" <<'SH'
assert_proof_shell || return 1
unset OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_URL OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT
proof_env() {
  env -i PATH="$PATH" USER="$(id -un)" LOGNAME="$(id -un)" SHELL=/bin/bash LANG=C.UTF-8 \
    HOME="$PROOF_ROOT/home" PROOF_ROOT="$PROOF_ROOT" PROOF_PROFILE="$PROOF_PROFILE" \
    XDG_RUNTIME_DIR="${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR:-/run/user/$(id -u)}" \
    DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS="${DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS:-unix:path=/run/user/$(id -u)/bus}" \
    npm_config_userconfig=/dev/null CI=1 "$@"
}
oc() {
  local checkout="$1"; shift
  assert_proof_shell || return 1
  proof_env env \
    HOME="$PROOF_ROOT/home" OPENCLAW_HOME="$PROOF_ROOT/home" \
    XDG_CONFIG_HOME="$PROOF_ROOT/home/.config" \
    OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR="$PROOF_ROOT/state" \
    OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH="$PROOF_ROOT/state/openclaw.json" \
    OPENCLAW_OAUTH_DIR="$PROOF_ROOT/state/credentials" \
    OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT="$(cat "$PROOF_ROOT/port")" \
    OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN="$(cat "$PROOF_ROOT/token")" \
    pnpm --dir "$checkout" openclaw --profile "$PROOF_PROFILE" "$@"
}
SH
source "$proof/env.sh"
proof_env node --version
proof_env pnpm --version
proof_env node -e "process.stdout.write(require('node:crypto').randomBytes(32).toString('hex'))" > "$proof/token"
chmod 600 "$proof/token" "$proof/env.sh"
proof_env node --input-type=module <<'JS'
import fs from 'node:fs/promises';
import net from 'node:net';
const root = process.env.PROOF_ROOT;
const bytes = Buffer.from('# Existing daily notes\r\n\r\n' + '歷史🐈'.repeat(300) + '\r\nLEGACY_TAIL');
await fs.writeFile(root + '/legacy.expected', bytes);
await fs.writeFile(root + '/workspace/memory/2026-10-25.md', bytes);
const server = net.createServer();
server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', async () => {
  await fs.writeFile(root + '/port', String(server.address().port));
  server.close();
});
JS
proof_env git clone --depth 1 --branch v2026.10.7 https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw.git "$proof/stable"
proof_env git -C "$proof/stable" checkout --detach 157d8c2bc3ea2fa183afdc11088e69690bf8e64e
proof_env git clone --depth 1 --branch codex/memory-flush-payload-bound https://github.com/AdrianIp0204/openclaw.git "$proof/candidate"
proof_env git -C "$proof/candidate" fetch --depth 2 origin 24d26272c852c59a66348a2baff6d64ea48bfc39
proof_env git -C "$proof/candidate" checkout --detach 24d26272c852c59a66348a2baff6d64ea48bfc39
for name in stable candidate; do
  (
    cd "$proof/$name"
    # Build preparation must not initialize the state used for the upgrade proof.
    mkdir -p "$proof/build-$name/home"
    build_env() {
      proof_env env HOME="$proof/build-$name/home" OPENCLAW_HOME="$proof/build-$name/home" \
        OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR="$proof/build-$name/state" \
        OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH="$proof/build-$name/state/openclaw.json" \
        OPENCLAW_OAUTH_DIR="$proof/build-$name/state/credentials" \
        XDG_CONFIG_HOME="$proof/build-$name/home/.config" \
        OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT="$(cat "$PROOF_ROOT/port")" \
        OPENCLAW_PROFILE="pr184049-build-$name-${proof##*.}" "$@"
    }
    build_env pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
    build_env env OPENCLAW_RUN_NODE_SKIP_DTS_BUILD=1 pnpm build
    proof_env git rev-parse HEAD > "$proof/evidence/$name-sha.txt"
  )
done
oc "$proof/stable" setup --baseline --workspace "$proof/workspace"
oc "$proof/stable" config set gateway.mode '"local"' --strict-json
oc "$proof/stable" config set gateway.port "$(cat "$proof/port")" --strict-json
oc "$proof/stable" config set gateway.auth.mode '"token"' --strict-json
oc "$proof/stable" config set gateway.auth.token "\"$(cat "$proof/token")\"" --strict-json
oc "$proof/stable" config validate
printf 'Terminal B: source %q\n' "$proof/env.sh"
oc "$proof/stable" gateway run --bind loopback --port "$(cat "$proof/port")" --auth token
```

The commands preserve the real `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` and `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS`.
Source preparation, builds, runtime commands and probes use a clean environment,
so inherited provider credentials and source/plugin overrides do not enter them.
They reject inherited service selectors, service markers, and `VITEST`, and clear
Gateway URL/port environment overrides in both terminals and every `oc` call.
Each `oc` call then sets the proof-owned port, including before configuration exists.
Both pinned revisions support skipping TypeScript declarations for this runtime
build; the Gateway compatibility check does not require declarations.
They do not install a service, stop the operator Gateway, use `--force`, or bypass
the configured-mode check. If the selected port becomes occupied, stop and choose
another free port; do not kill its listener.

In terminal B, run the printed `source .../env.sh` command. After the Gateway is
ready, run this block with `stage=stable`:

```bash
set -euo pipefail
stage=stable
oc "$PROOF_ROOT/$stage" health --json | tee "$PROOF_ROOT/evidence/$stage-health.json"
proof_env env PROOF_STAGE="$stage" node --input-type=module <<'JS'
import fs from 'node:fs/promises';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';
const root = process.env.PROOF_ROOT;
const healthOutput = await fs.readFile(root + '/evidence/' + process.env.PROOF_STAGE + '-health.json', 'utf8');
const health = JSON.parse(healthOutput.slice(healthOutput.indexOf('{')));
assert.equal(health.ok, true);
assert.notEqual(health.status, 'starting');
const expected = await fs.readFile(root + '/legacy.expected');
const port = await fs.readFile(root + '/port', 'utf8');
const token = await fs.readFile(root + '/token', 'utf8');
const response = await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:' + port + '/tools/invoke', {
  method: 'POST', signal: AbortSignal.timeout(60000),
  headers: { authorization: 'Bearer ' + token, 'content-type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ tool: 'memory_get', agentId: 'main',
    args: { path: 'memory/2026-10-25.md', from: 1, lines: 120 } }),
});
assert.equal(response.status, 200);
const result = await response.json();
assert.equal(result.ok, true);
assert.equal(result.result.details.status, 'ok');
assert.equal(result.result.details.truncated, undefined);
assert.equal(result.result.details.text, expected.toString('utf8'));
const actual = await fs.readFile(root + '/workspace/memory/2026-10-25.md');
assert.deepEqual(actual, expected);
const evidence = { stage: process.env.PROOF_STAGE, tool: 'memory_get', read: 'ok',
  units: expected.toString('utf8').length, bytes: actual.length,
  sha256: createHash('sha256').update(actual).digest('hex'), unchanged: true };
await fs.writeFile(root + '/evidence/' + process.env.PROOF_STAGE + '-read.json', JSON.stringify(evidence, null, 2));
console.log(evidence);
JS
```

`health` reporting `status: starting` is not a pass. Both the real tool-result
assertions and raw-byte assertions must pass. A missing/disabled tool or a failed
read is a failed or blocked compatibility check, never an empty successful read.

Stop **only the foreground test Gateway** with Ctrl+C in terminal A and wait for
its shutdown and the shell prompt. Keep the state, configuration, and notes.
Then in terminal A:

```bash
oc "$PROOF_ROOT/candidate" doctor --fix --non-interactive 2>&1 | tee "$PROOF_ROOT/evidence/candidate-doctor.log"
oc "$PROOF_ROOT/candidate" config validate
oc "$PROOF_ROOT/candidate" gateway run --bind loopback --port "$(cat "$PROOF_ROOT/port")" --auth token
```

In terminal B, repeat the probe block with `stage=candidate`. Retain both evidence
JSON files, health reports, exact source SHAs, and Doctor's exit status/output.
Afterward stop the test Gateway with Ctrl+C and retain the isolated directory for
review. A reproduction result is evidence only after its commands actually run;
the recorded results above apply only to the stated revisions and environment.

and [the memory reader](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/24d26272c852c59a66348a2baff6d64ea48bfc39/extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts#L554).

prs.title: fix: streamed replies that quote an empty command output no longer re-scan the whole reply per delta
prs.body:
Closes #184522

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes quadratic processing when a streamed final answer quotes an empty-command transcript, including indented code and lazy blockquote continuations.

## User Impact

Long quoted command output streams without repeatedly reparsing the entire reply. Placeholder removal, Markdown code protection, reply directives, and block-delivery whitespace retain their existing behavior. No configuration or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Builds on @JasonBuildAI's original placeholder activation/checkpoint fix and preserves the contributor's commits. The remaining cases had two causes: the shared Markdown checkpoint retained whole open containers, and block delivery rebuilt full canonical snapshots whenever the display projection preserved indentation or removed a placeholder.

The canonical Markdown owner now provides bounded continuation context for proven indented blocks and simple blockquote paragraphs. Unresolved syntax retains the conservative path. The existing placeholder probe also bounds rejected-line work and preserves split CRLF/replacement tails. Block delivery consumes the same canonical incremental pipeline in its existing trailing-whitespace-preserving mode after snapshot equality establishes alignment; corrections and scope changes still reconcile canonically. No second grammar or parser is introduced.

## Evidence

- 685 differential cases / 42,138 checks, including every two-chunk split and 1-/4-character schedules: zero mismatches. Three reference-title variants add 1,350 passing direct/full-path checks. Additional subscriber fixtures compare live and delivered output and exercise reply directives and a forced pre-tool flush.
- Explicit character-work bounds fail on both main and the original PR for the remaining indented/lazy cases and pass after this change. Subscriber regressions separately reduce full-snapshot calls at 4 KiB from 2,048/2,040 to below the fixed bound of 32.
- 98/98 affected subscriber tests passed (58.65 s wall). Shared streaming suite: 95/95 passed (24.04 s); focused owner/sibling suites also passed. Core typecheck, scoped type-aware lint, formatting, and applicable baseline ratchets passed. Test lines decrease by one; the ceiling is unchanged.

Counted String/RegExp method spans at four-character deltas (16/32/64 KiB), comparing main `e5206cbd`, original PR `916b43c5`, and repaired runtime `479c137e`:

| Shape | Main | Original PR | Repaired owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Indented | 402,176,344 / 1,608,627,030 / 6,434,350,150 | 671,171,837 / 2,644,547,008 / 10,493,893,514 | 2,932,031 / 5,869,937 / 11,745,881 |
| Lazy blockquote | 300,226,883 / 1,201,132,948 / 4,804,983,224 | 447,509,480 / 1,746,533,304 / 6,896,174,075 | 3,136,013 / 6,274,795 / 12,554,529 |

The unchanged bound is 256 counted characters per input character. Instrumentation counts searched, compared, and sliced spans; it does not claim VM instruction or allocation counts. Repaired work grows approximately 2× per doubling, versus approximately 4× before.

Real isolated Gateway `chat.send` on macOS, with a deterministic provider emitting phased Responses events in four-character deltas:

| Shape | 16 KiB | 32 KiB | 64 KiB |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Indented, main | 15,653 ms | 71,489 ms | Transport reset/retry; aborted at 155,314 ms |
| Indented, repaired | 635 ms | 1,371 ms | 3,737 ms |
| Lazy blockquote, main | 3,337 ms | 6,051 ms | Not run |
| Lazy blockquote, repaired | 345 ms | 467 ms | 781 ms |

Every completed repaired row returned the exact expected bytes. Fenced 16 KiB control: 244 ms. Native Ollama `qwen3:8b` through the same Gateway returned the expected 35-character fenced empty-command transcript in 3,542 ms, without fallback. These are single warm whole-turn observations on a shared host, separate from the deterministic work counts above.

Production: +201/−22 lines, net +179. Tests: +291/−292 lines, net −1. The production growth retains one canonical grammar while adding bounded continuation/probe state and the block consumer's distinct whitespace contract; test boilerplate was consolidated without dropping coverage.

Independent Codex review on final head `6bf89f01`: no actionable P0–P2 findings. CI caught an optional-field inference error in the generated test table; the final follow-up adds its explicit scenario type and passes the exact failing type graph. Production files are byte-identical to the Gateway-tested `479c137e` runtime. The full build passed in 3 min 55 s.

Limits: proof is local macOS, with deterministic provider replay plus a real local-model control. The performance claim covers the measured append workloads; genuine corrections and unresolved Markdown syntax retain canonical fallback. `/v1/responses` cannot represent shrinking lazy-placeholder corrections; the real Gateway `chat.send` entry point supplies that proof. This PR does not change that separate Responses limitation.

prs.title: fix(agents): keep sandbox CDP probe deadline on the monotonic clock
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Starting a sandbox browser can hang past its configured startup deadline, or fail early on a healthy browser. `waitForSandboxCdp` seeded its `deadline` and read its remaining-time checks from `Date.now()` (wall clock), while the fetch-abort timer and the poll `sleep` consumed those values through libuv monotonic timers. When the wall clock steps back (NTP correction, manual time change), the `while (Date.now() < deadline)` guard can never become true, so the probe spins until the hung container is force-removed; when the wall clock steps forward, a healthy request is aborted early and the browser startup is reported as timed out.

- **Problem**: the deadline and remaining budget are computed on the wall clock but consumed by monotonic timers, so a wall-clock jump distorts the startup budget in both directions.
- **Solution**: seed and read the deadline from `performance.now()`, so the guard, the abort timer, and the poll sleep share one monotonic domain.
- **What changed**: `src/agents/sandbox/browser.ts` — `waitForSandboxCdp` now uses `performance.now()` for the deadline, the loop guard, and the two remaining-time reads. The helper stays private; the regression drives it through the real browser-startup path (`onEnsureAttachTarget`) against a real `node:http` peer. The existing "stalled CDP request" test's fake-timer config also fakes `performance`, so `advanceTimersByTimeAsync` moves the deadline on the same clock.
- **What did NOT change**: the deadline is a process-local closure variable; nothing serializes, persists, or compares it across processes. The browser-registry `createdAtMs`/`lastUsedAtMs` timestamps stay wall-clock on purpose; `ensureSandboxBrowser` and the container lifecycle are untouched.

## Why This Change Was Made

The deadline is a purely process-local budget: it is not serialized, persisted, or compared across processes by any `Date.now()` consumer, so switching to the monotonic clock is the correct, minimal fix (the same pattern already merged for the wall-clock family, e.g. #169908, #155863). Keeping the helper private avoids a test-only production seam: the existing lifecycle fixture already invokes the probe through `onEnsureAttachTarget`, so the regression extends that path instead of importing the helper.

- **Best fix**: yes — the owner function reads one clock end-to-end; no new parser, policy branch, or config surface. A parallel monotonic deadline alongside a wall-clock epoch was not needed; nothing outside the closure consumes the value across a process/DB boundary.
- **Risk**: none identified — `performance.now()` exists on Node 16+, and `setTimeout`/`sleep` accept the float it returns.

## User Impact

Sandbox browser startup now honors its configured timeout regardless of wall-clock adjustments: a step-back no longer makes the CDP probe spin past the deadline, and a step-forward no longer aborts a healthy probe early. Users see either a timely "browser not reachable" failure or a successful attach, instead of a hung startup or a false timeout.

## Evidence

**Shipped entry point, real Docker sandbox, real clock step.**

`openclaw gateway` (this checkout, isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`) plus the shipped `openclaw agent --agent main -m "hi"` turn, with `sandbox.mode: "all"`, `backend: "docker"`, and browser `autoStartTimeoutMs: 8000`. The scripted model requests the `browser` tool (`open about:blank`); the browser plugin attaches to the sandbox bridge, and the bridge's `onEnsureAttachTarget` calls `waitForSandboxCdp` against the container's mapped CDP port. The image is the contract-labelled sandbox-browser image (`org.openclaw.sandbox-browser.contract=2026-05-12-cdp-relay-auth`).

The container's CDP peer answers `500` and logs every request with a `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` timestamp — that is the peer the probe really polls (each probe request carries the sandbox `Authorization` header; the plugin's reachability check does not). While the probe waits, the host `CLOCK_REALTIME` is stepped with `sudo date -s` by ±60 s, a real NTP-style jump; `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`/`performance.now()` is untouched. The step is applied on the first **authenticated** probe request, i.e. after the budget was seeded on the pre-step clock. The peer is a stub rather than Chromium because this environment has no outbound network to build a real browser image; the probe transport, container lifecycle, and clock are real.

| source | wall-clock step | probe wait (container log, monotonic) | outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| this PR | +60 s | **8.3 s** | deadline expires at the 8 s budget |
| this PR | −60 s | **8.3 s** | step-back does not extend the budget |
| base | +60 s | **0.2 s** | premature "not reachable" abort |
| base | −60 s | **68.6 s** | budget stretched by the jump |

Raw container log (first authenticated probe request → last), base −60 s vs this PR −60 s:

```console
# base (Date.now), -60s step
[fixture] GET GET /json/version HTTP/1 -> 500 (elapsed=47452ms first=47452ms auth=1)
[fixture] GET GET /json/version HTTP/1 -> 500 (elapsed=116103ms first=47452ms auth=1)   # 68.6s
# this PR (performance.now), -60s step
[fixture] GET GET /json/version HTTP/1 -> 500 (elapsed=54812ms first=54812ms auth=1)
[fixture] GET GET /json/version HTTP/1 -> 500 (elapsed=63084ms first=54812ms auth=1)   # 8.3s
```

Every run ends in the same production failure — `Sandbox browser CDP did not become reachable on 127.0.0.1:<port> within 8000ms. The hung container has been forcefully removed.` — the difference is only when it appears. In the base −60 s run the client surfaced a bridge-level error first while the container log shows the probe still waiting 68.6 s: the probe outlived the request.

**Regression tests (RED on the base commit, GREEN with the fix).**

```console
$ git show HEAD~1:src/agents/sandbox/browser.ts > src/agents/sandbox/browser.ts   # base
$ npx vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.agents.config.ts src/agents/sandbox/browser.create.test.ts
× keeps sandbox browser attach inside the monotonic deadline across a 60000 ms wall-clock step
  AssertionError: expected 'Sandbox browser CDP did not become re…' to be 'attach target reached before bridge c…'
× keeps sandbox browser attach inside the monotonic deadline across a -60000 ms wall-clock step
 Tests  2 failed | 26 passed (28)

$ git checkout -- src/agents/sandbox/browser.ts                                   # fix
$ npx vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.agents.config.ts src/agents/sandbox/browser.create.test.ts
 Tests  28 passed (28)
```

The negative row asserts the deadline still expires after a step-back (no budget stretch); the positive row asserts attach still happens when the browser turns healthy inside the monotonic budget (no premature abort). The sign of the delta is preserved, so the two rows no longer exercise the same rewind.

`oxfmt --check` and `oxlint` are clean; the diff has no config, persistence, or new public surface.

prs.title: fix(update-repair): use monotonic clock for deadline budget
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When the update repair agent runs an embedded agent turn, the per-turn deadline is derived from `Date.now()` (wall clock) but the remaining budget is consumed by a monotonic timer (undici `headersTimeout`/`bodyTimeout`). A wall-clock forward jump (e.g. NTP sync) collapses the remaining budget toward 1ms — `Math.max(1, deadline - Date.now())` — and prematurely aborts healthy repair turns. A rewind inflates the remaining budget and lets stalled HTTP calls run far past the configured timeout.

`src/infra/update-repair-agent.runtime.ts` seeds the deadline with `Date.now()` and hands `Math.max(1, deadline - Date.now())` to `runEmbeddedAgent`, which eventually reaches `ensureGlobalUndiciDispatcherStreamTimeouts`. Fix: seed and remaining-budget read both now use `performance.now()` so the deadline stays in the same clock domain as the downstream monotonic timer.

- **Problem**: deadline computed with `Date.now()` (wall clock) is consumed by a monotonic undici stream timeout, so system time adjustments distort the repair turn timeout.
- **Solution**: use the monotonic clock (`performance.now()`) for both the deadline seed and the remaining-budget handed to the embedded agent.
- **What changed**: `src/infra/update-repair-agent.runtime.ts` (two clock-domain alignments) and one regression test in the existing suite.
- **What did NOT change**: the outer `setTimeout(() => controller.abort(...), params.timeoutMs)` — it uses a fixed constant, not a remaining budget, and Node `setTimeout` is already monotonic.

## Why This Change Was Made

`runScopedUpdateRepairTurn` is the canonical owner of its per-turn deadline: it seeds `deadline` at the top of the function and derives `timeoutMs` from it before passing it to `runEmbeddedAgent` → `runEmbeddedAgentEntry` → `attempt-setup.ts` → `ensureGlobalUndiciDispatcherStreamTimeouts` (undici, monotonic). Mixing a wall-clock seed with monotonic consumption is the defect; aligning both operations to `performance.now()` keeps the deadline entirely monotonic. The deadline is process-local (a closure variable, never serialized or compared across processes), so the monotonic clock is the only correct choice.

- **Best fix**: yes — two equivalent one-line changes put the whole deadline pipeline in the monotonic domain; no new structure or configuration surface.
- **Risk**: none identified. `timeoutMs` is an in-process argument to the embedded agent runner; the outer abort timer is a fixed constant and unchanged.

## User Impact

Repair turns complete within their configured timeout regardless of wall-clock adjustments. Under a clock rewind, a stalled HTTP call no longer hangs beyond the turn budget; under a forward jump, healthy repair turns are no longer prematurely aborted with a 1ms timeout.

## Evidence

**Shipped CLI entry point proof (`openclaw triage --run` + real provider, head `4db0649`).** The shipped `openclaw triage --run` command triggers embedded repair via `runUpdateRepairLoop` → `runLocalUpdateRepairTurn` → `runScopedUpdateRepairTurn` — the exact function where the deadline seed (line 339) and remaining-budget read (line 431) were changed from `Date.now()` to `performance.now()`. A `--import` preload injects an NTP-style +310s forward jump into `Date.now()` at the budget-read site (stack-line matched), leaving `performance.now()` monotonic. The same preload, config, provider (Qwen3-235B), and budget apply in both builds.

**Shipped `openclaw triage --run`, clock jumps +310s between deadline seed and remaining-budget read:**

| build | clock domain | shipped entry behavior | repair turn outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| pre-fix (`Date.now`) | wall → wall (+310s) | port 1 starts; `[PROBE] Date.now seed seen` → `[PROBE] Date.now budget read seen, injecting +310s`; `remaining = max(1, 300000 − 310000) = 1ms` | turn aborts ~43s after start (1ms budget starves the HTTP call) |
| post-fix (`performance.now`) | monotonic → monotonic | port 1 starts; `Date.now` injection never fires (line-matched calls use `performance.now`); full budget consumed | turn completes normally — 6 real model requests issued |

```
PRE-FIX : [PROBE] Date.now seed seen / budget read seen → injecting +310s
           Starting repair turn 1 with zte/Qwen3-235B-A22B → embedded repair aborted (~43s)
POST-FIX: [PROBE] (no Date.now interception — monotonic clock unaffected by the jump)
           Starting repair turn 1 with zte/Qwen3-235B-A22B → 6 model requests; turn completes full budget
```

**In-process proof (round 1, still valid):** A line-matched `Date.now` shim in the in-process proof (budget 50s, real Qwen3-235B) collapses `timeoutMs` to 1ms on pre-fix, while post-fix delivers ~28–32s and returns `status: ok`.

prs.title: fix(agents): keep exec approval followup observation deadline on the monotonic clock
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an async `exec_approval_followup` run completes on the gateway, OpenClaw keeps observing it for a bounded 6-minute window before deciding whether to resume the originating session. That observation window is budgeted on the wall clock (`Date.now()`) but consumed by the monotonic timer that backs the gateway `agent.wait` RPC. When the system wall clock is adjusted (NTP step, VM clock sync, or a laptop waking from hibernation), the two clocks diverge and the observation window is distorted.

- **Problem**: `waitForAgentFollowupRun` seeds `observationDeadline = Date.now() + timeout` and reads `remainingMs = deadline - Date.now()`, passing that budget into a gateway wait consumed on the monotonic clock (`performance.now()` / `setTimeout`). Budget computed in one clock domain, spent in another.
- **Solution**: align the whole observation budget to the monotonic clock — seed `observationDeadline` and read `remainingMs` / `retryDelayMs` with `performance.now()`, matching the monotonic consumer.
- **What changed**: `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-approval-followup.ts` (3 deadline reads `Date.now()`→`performance.now()`; per-wait budget rounded up with `Math.ceil` for the gateway `agent.wait` integer `timeoutMs` schema); the deadline regression test now controls the monotonic clock.
- **What did NOT change**: the transport retry/backoff policy and the observation lifecycle (reason `"deadline"`, `transportErrors` accounting) are untouched.

## Why This Change Was Made

The observation deadline is a pure process-local closure (never serialized/persisted/cross-process), so a monotonic clock is the only correct source. The gateway consumer already computes its own monotonic `DispatchDeadline`; passing it a wall-clock-derived remaining budget is a cross-clock-domain mismatch. Switching the three reads keeps the seed and every remaining-budget read on the same (monotonic) domain, zero external contract change.

- **Best fix**: yes — one canonical owner, no new parser/policy branch.
- **Alternative**: keep `Date.now()` and rely on the per-wait `Math.min` cap; rejected because the cap only bounds a single wait, not the total observation window, nor the `retryDelayMs <= 0` exit from a forward wall jump.
- **Risk**: low — `Math.ceil` on the remaining budget never shrinks the observation window and always yields an integer accepted by the gateway validator.

## User Impact

Exec approval follow-ups for async commands now complete on a stable, clock-skew-proof observation window. Under NTP/hibernation clock steps, a healthy agent run is no longer prematurely declared complete (dropping slow terminal output), and a finished run is no longer observed far beyond its deadline.

## Evidence

**1. Shipped exec-host public-entry clock-skew proof, both directions.** Driven through the exec-host **public shipped entry** `sendExecApprovalFollowupResult` (`bash-tools.exec-host-shared.ts`) — the exact function `exec-host-node.ts` / `exec-host-gateway.ts` call after an approved async exec. It registers the handoff, then `sendExecApprovalFollowup` runs through the **production** `GatewayRecoveryRuntime` the Gateway registers at startup — **no** `registerGatewayRecoveryRuntime` override, **no** internal-function call. Both the `agent` dispatch (production `recovery.dispatchAgent` → real in-process `agent.run`, accepted against a synthetic-provider run that stays pending) and the wait (production `recovery.waitForAgent` → shipped wait transport) are unmodified shipped code. A 30 s wall step (−30 s / +30 s) is injected inside `waitForAgentFollowupRun` via a `Date.now` proxy; a pass-through probe on `recovery.waitForAgent` records the round-1 budget handed to the wait transport. (Observation budget shortened 6 m→20 s as a disclosed control; the per-wait cap cannot mask it.)

```console
# BACKWARD (−30s rewind)
[proof] production recovery runtime present = true (Gateway auto-registered)
[proof] recovery.waitForAgent budget timeoutMs=20000 -> shipped wait transport   # post-fix: BOUNDED
[proof] recovery.waitForAgent budget timeoutMs=49999 -> shipped wait transport   # pre-fix: INFLATED +30s
# FORWARD (+30s jump)
[proof] recovery.waitForAgent budget timeoutMs=20000 -> shipped wait transport   # post-fix: BOUNDED, observation proceeds
[proof] outcome=undefined elapsed=2652ms / NO agent.wait dispatched             # pre-fix: observation ENDED IMMEDIATELY (drops slow output)
```

| leg | skew | production-recovery budget (round 1) | window |
|---|---|---|---|
| post-fix | −30 s | 20000 | bounded |
| pre-fix | −30 s | 49999 | inflated +30 s |
| post-fix | +30 s | 20000 (proceeds) | bounded |
| pre-fix | +30 s | none (ends immediately) | drops slow output |

Keeping the budget on the monotonic clock makes the shipped wait budget immune to wall-clock steps in both directions. The accepted run stays the sole delivery owner (`direct_deliveries=0`; no competing direct delivery), and the integer `timeoutMs` passes the shipped `validateAgentWaitParams`.

**2. Integer-boundary proof (P2).** `performance.now()` is fractional; the `agent.wait` schema requires an integer `timeoutMs`. `sendExecApprovalFollowup` was driven through a recovery runtime whose `waitForAgent` re-runs the shipped validator on the exact params. Same fractional remaining budget (59999.75 ms), before vs after the one-line `Math.ceil`:

```console
before: [waitForAgent] timeoutMs=59999.75 -> shipped validator: REJECT
after : [waitForAgent] timeoutMs=60000   -> shipped validator: ACCEPT
```

`Math.ceil(59999.75) === 60000` never shrinks the budget; `Math.max(1, ...)` keeps the positive minimum.

**3. Regression.** Pre-fix the new test fails (`Number.isInteger(59999.75)` false); post-fix it passes, full suite green (18/18).

**What was not tested**: the divergence itself (NTP/hibernation) is injected by the proof; direct-delivery and session-resume paths are unchanged and covered by existing suites.

**Collision check**: `origin/main` still has the wall-clock reads (bug live); sibling PR #181942 touches the same three reads for the same defect; both open.

prs.title: fix(sessions): escape terminal controls in cleanup store headers
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes terminal actions and forged header lines when a session store path (or agent id) passed to `openclaw sessions cleanup` contains control characters. The human-readable `Session store:` and `Agent:` headers were interpolated raw, so an ANSI escape or bell byte in the store selector could reach the terminal.

## User Impact

`openclaw sessions cleanup` human output now safely renders the store path and agent id in `Agent:` / `Session store:` headers. JSON output and store selection are unchanged; the underlying path is not modified.

## Why This Change Was Made

The file already imports the canonical terminal sanitizer and applies it to the `Session label:` header in the same renderer. This change applies that same policy to the `Agent:` and `Session store:` headers at their existing output owners, so both the gateway-delegated apply result and the local dry-run preview follow one consistent rule.

## Evidence

**Real CLI proof — both changed renderers (shipped binary, current head `81e5197`).** The dry-run preview and the apply result each render the `Session store:` header through a changed output owner; both are proven through the shipped CLI with the same control-char store path (saved as `sess` + `ESC[31m` ANSI red + `ions` + `BEL` + `.sqlite`), A/B: sanitizer wired (post-fix) vs unwrapped at the same owner (pre-fix). Both captures were recorded on the current head (`81e5197`); the production patch is byte-identical across `9d2c650` → `81e5197` (later commits only harden the regression test), so the post-fix output is the current head's behavior.

**Dry-run preview** (`openclaw sessions cleanup --dry-run`, control-char `session.store` config path that does not exist on disk, so it resolves as an in-memory preview):

| lane | `Session store:` header (raw terminal) |
|------|----------------------------------------|
| pre-fix | `/tmp/oc-proof-184747/agents/main/agent/sess^[[31mions^G.sqlite` |
| post-fix | `/tmp/oc-proof-184747/agents/main/agent/sessions.sqlite` |

**Apply result** (`openclaw sessions cleanup --store <real-init-store-with-control-chars> --enforce`, stays local and renders `renderAppliedResult`):

| lane | `Session store:` header (raw terminal) |
|------|----------------------------------------|
| pre-fix | `/tmp/oc-proof-184747/agents/main/agent/sess^[[31mions^G.sqlite` |
| post-fix | `/tmp/oc-proof-184747/agents/main/agent/sessions.sqlite` |

Both runs reach completion (dry-run: `Maintenance mode: enforce` / `Entries: 0 -> 0`; apply: `Applied maintenance. Current entries: 0`, exit 0). Pre-fix passes `^[[31m` / `^G` through verbatim; post-fix strips the control bytes and renders clean `sessions.sqlite` (cat -v confirms no `^[` / `^G`). The `Agent:` header is the same expression shape (`Agent: ${sanitizeTerminalText(summary.agentId)}`) at the same output owners; a multi-store dry-run proves a control-bearing agent id is also sanitized in that header.

**Regression (P3 + Agent-header coverage).** Two stale/missing assertions were hardened. (1) The dry-run store assertion previously used `vi.clearAllMocks()` then a whole-array `find` — but `clearAllMocks()` does not clear the plain `logs` array, so the assertion could read the apply lane's own sanitized line. It now records `appliedLength = logs.length` before the dry-run invocation and searches only `logs.slice(appliedLength)`. (2) The `Agent:` header was not asserted at all; a multi-store dry-run (previewResults.length > 1) now feeds a control-bearing agent id and asserts the rendered header is clean. Both verified bidirectional: with the respective dry-run sanitizer removed, the store-path assertion fails (`expected "Session store: sessions-café\noperator-forged\tend\rrow" not to match /\p{Cc}/u`) and the Agent-header assertion fails (`expected 'Agent: worker\u001b[31m\u0007main' not to match /\p{Cc}/u`); restored, all 14 tests pass.

- Targeted oxlint, oxfmt, and `git diff --check` pass. Production change is net-zero LOC: four existing output expressions are wrapped in the already-imported sanitizer.
- Open PR collision check: no open PR touches `src/commands/sessions-cleanup.ts`. The upstream family PR #184139 (merged) modified `sessions.ts` and `secrets-store-cli.ts`, not this file.

prs.title: docs(browser): distinguish explicit dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork false from unset
prs.body:
Fixes #184790

## What Problem This Solves

The browser configuration docs said `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` "is off by default", which reads as if an explicit `false` and leaving the key unset were the same. They are not. An explicit `false` turns on strict mode, so ordinary public hostnames such as `https://example.com/` fail with `strict browser SSRF policy requires an IP-literal URL`, while the unset default opens them.

## User Impact

Operators who wrote `dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork: false` to be explicit about the safe default now learn from the docs that it changes navigation behavior, and that leaving it unset is how to keep private destinations blocked. Docs only; no runtime change.

## Why This Change Was Made

`docs/tools/browser/configuration.md` now lists the three states:

- **Unset (default):** private and internal destinations are blocked, and public hostnames open. Leave it unset to keep private destinations blocked.
- **`false`:** strict mode. Navigation also accepts only IP-literal URLs, because Chromium resolves hostnames itself and OpenClaw cannot pin the address that passed the check. Hosts in `allowedHostnames` still open by name.
- **`true`:** private-network destinations are allowed; use only when that is intentionally trusted.

This matches `assertBrowserNavigationAllowed` in `extensions/browser/src/browser/navigation-guard.ts`, which applies the IP-literal rule only when `dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork === false` and the hostname is not in `allowedHostnames`. The surrounding local-preview bullet, which says any explicit policy disables the loopback exception, is unchanged.

## Evidence

### Live run (Windows 11, Node 26.12.1, Chrome)

Each configuration ran a real `openclaw gateway run` with an OpenClaw-managed headless Chrome and isolated state. The run calls `openclaw browser open` for a public hostname, a public IP literal (`http://223.5.5.5/`, which does not redirect to a hostname) and a private address.

This machine sits behind a fake-IP proxy that maps public names into `198.18.0.0/15`, so every policy also sets `allowRfc2544BenchmarkRange: true`, the option the docs already give for this setup. The Gateway process also gets a Node preload that asks DNS for IPv4 only, because the proxy's AAAA answers fall in `2001:2::/48`. Neither touches the policy keys under test.

![live run](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wr-web/openclaw/proof-assets/184790/proof-184790.png)

| `dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` | `https://example.com/` | `http://223.5.5.5/` | `http://192.168.1.1/` |
|---|---|---|---|
| unset | opened | opened | blocked by policy |
| `false` | **blocked: "strict browser SSRF policy requires an IP-literal URL"** | opened | blocked by policy |
| `false` + `allowedHostnames: ["example.com"]` | opened | opened | blocked by policy |

Each documented statement matches the observed behavior.

### Checks

- `pnpm lint:docs`, `pnpm docs:check-mdx` and `pnpm docs:check-links` pass.
- `oxfmt --check docs/tools/browser/configuration.md` passes. The repository-wide `pnpm format:docs:check` wrapper fails on this Windows machine with or without this change.
- `git diff --check` is clean.

prs.title: chore(codex): test warm claim settlement and scope revocation
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

**Tests-only regression coverage; no runtime source change or production fix in this PR.** The proof target here is that a failed owner leaves no orphan native-thread claim and a later attempt can reuse that thread.

A Codex-backed conversation can reject the next turn as “claimed by active work” after failed ownership settlement, even though the failed attempt is no longer running. The existing cleanup lacks targeted coverage at the warm-claim cleanup and monitor-setup revocation seams.

Related: karmaterminal/openclaw#1431 (the queue-behind-*genuinely active* work request is separate and remains open).

## User Impact

No production behavior changes. These tests protect the existing claim-release behavior against regressions that could strand subsequent Codex attempts.

## Why This Change Was Made

Inject a lease-settlement failure after proving warm claim transfer (without a cold resume), and separately revoke session binding authority during monitor setup. Assert cleanup clears each claim and the same native thread can be claimed by a follow-up attempt. The latter is **scope revocation, not a simulated binding-store lease expiry**. The tests complement the existing lifecycle cleanup; they do not implement queueing behind active work.

## Evidence

- Based on upstream `main` `6ba6ad224ae` (2026-10-25); two Codex app-server test files only.
- Focused Codex app-server suites: 2 files, 21/21 tests passed on upstream base.
- Exact PR head 14bf56f9ea33: [GitHub Actions changed-extensions-config](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40253224772/job/121349722824) ran both changed test files, 21/21 passed. Its log includes the warm lifecycle injected-failure test and the monitor-failure binding-scope revocation test; the latter asserts a completed follow-up turn on the same native thread with the claim cleared. [CI gate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40253224772/job/121351049271) passed. These are fixture-driven in-repo assertions, **not** a shipped Gateway/CLI lease-loss trace.
- Extension test typecheck, targeted format and lint pass; line-cap ratchet passes against `upstream/main` for the two changed files. (The default local ratchet base is `origin/main`, a divergent fork, and falsely flags unrelated upstream files.)
- No live service change or end-to-end field reproduction claimed.

**Follow-up proof correction (2026-10-27):** A Claude source review found the monitor case calls `releaseBindingAuthority()` (binding scope, not simulated lease expiry); the warm case now asserts ownership is held at the injected settlement fault and no cold `thread/resume` occurs before it. Updated head `71d416664521dc5f51bf3e6ac2a435786f91f07c`: focused Vitest 21/21, extension-test tsgo, targeted oxfmt/oxlint and diff check passed locally. Hosted CI is pending; no live lease-expiry or production fix is claimed.

prs.title: fix(plugins): scheduled command turns ignore the requester's tool policy
prs.body:
Closes #186281

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: occurrences of requester-scheduled plugin commands resolve tool policy like a live turn with no sender, so the guest `toolsBySender["*"]` entry applies to them (with a subagent deny there, every occurrence fails), and the requester account's current tool policy and the removed-account refusal are skipped.

## User Impact

User impact: scheduled command turns resolve tool policy the way capped automations do. Guest wildcard sender entries no longer apply to them, each occurrence uses the requester account's current group/channel tool policy, and an occurrence whose requester account its channel no longer lists is refused before it runs, naming the account. As for capped automations, sender-specific `toolsBySender` entries, including `"*"`, no longer apply to occurrences, and a later change to the requester's own entry does not reach existing schedules. Plugin schedules now share the capped-automation account check, so open reports of false refusals there (#156895, #186008) would affect them too until that check is fixed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Each occurrence now resolves the job's stored scheduled tool policy once, as capped automations do, and passes it to both admission and native tool preparation (before, preparation never received it). Command schedules record no creator origin, so the schedule's own channel (captured from the live command and checked against the stored job on every occurrence) stands in for it; schedules created from a direct chat on a named account keep working, where a capped automation without a recorded origin would refuse them. The account check runs right after the source check, before the occurrence accepts any input. The background-work docs now say how scheduled command turns resolve tool policy.

## Evidence

- Real Gateway (built `dist`, isolated state, WebChat operator over `chat.send`, local stub provider, a plugin with requester-command scheduled turns, `tools.toolsBySender["*"]` denying `sessions_spawn` / `agents_wait`), schedule created then the occurrence forced with `cron.run`:

  | build | runs | occurrence | command ran | model requests |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | `main` `eb78444932f` | 3/3 | `error`: Scheduled command requires current native subagent eligibility. | no | 0 |
  | this fix | 3/3 | `ok` | yes, with native subagents | 0 |

- Existing `test/plugin-command-scheduled-restart.e2e.test.ts` passes on the fix.
- `commands-plugin.scheduled-turns.test.ts` (repo fixture: real plugin loader, cron service, channel ingress): on `main` the wildcard case and the account case fail at their assertions (the child loses `read`; a later deny for the requester's account is not applied), the direct-chat case passes; with the fix all three pass, together with the existing scheduled-turns, scheduled-turns-restart, `plugin-command-scheduled-run` and `operator-authority` tests (114/114 on the final code). The new cases take 2.3-2.5 s each; the whole file runs in 92 s alone (`--maxWorkers=1`, 31 tests), so they add about 8% to an existing fixture-heavy suite. The fixture now loads a minimal Discord channel that lists the configured accounts and resolves conversation tool policy like the Discord plugin; without a loaded channel, any configured-account check refuses every fixture occurrence.
- `tsgo:core`, core test shards, oxlint, oxfmt, `git diff --check`, line-cap and max-lines ratchets: clean.
- Test-line ratchet: `main` at `b0961419e46` is already 343 lines over its ceiling (6291661 vs 6291318); the new tests add 125 net test lines, so the last commit raises `config/test-lines-baseline.txt` to the tree total, 6291786.
- Named account, real Gateway (built `dist`, isolated state, fake Telegram Bot API, named account `team`, supergroup requester whose sender is linked to an admin profile with `users.linkChannelIdentity`, local stub provider, the same plugin), occurrences forced with `cron.run`. Phase A: an allowed child reads a sentinel file. Phase B: two children with `tools.swarm.maxConcurrent: 1`, the first held at the provider so the second is queued, then the change. Phase C: the first occurrence after the change. Two runs per build and change:

  | build | change (`config.patch` on account `team`) | runs | A: allowed child | B: queued child | C: first occurrence after the change |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | `main` `198b761c325` | account removed | 2/2 | reads the file | runs before the change applies, reads the file | `ok`; its child has `read` and reads the file |
  | this branch | account removed | 2/2 | reads the file | same | `error`: Scheduled account "team" is unavailable. Re-add it to the channel configuration, or recreate this automation from the intended account. No command ran, no child |
  | `main` `198b761c325` | `groups["*"].tools.deny: ["read"]` | 2/2 | reads the file | same | `ok`; its child has `read` and reads the file |
  | this branch | `groups["*"].tools.deny: ["read"]` | 2/2 | reads the file | same | `ok`; its child has no `read` |

  Both changes need a Telegram channel reload, which waits for running work (`deferring until ... complete`), so the queued child runs under the old configuration on both builds; only phase C differs. (This branch was measured at `3aea9294fac`; the later merge with `main` changes none of this PR's files.)

- Registry used by the account check: the occurrence's source check compares the Gateway's current plugin registry with the one it captured on entry, and the account check runs right after it with no `await` in between, so the process-root registry it reads is that captured registry. Instrumented builds of `main` and this branch on the named-account setup above (reload or config change while the occurrence waits for its parent session's turn) recorded the same object for the scheduled runner's scoped registry, the published registry and the process root at every point read: the account check, child tool policy, command runtime and execution admission. A registry published during the wait, including by a plugin that declares `reload.turnHandover` and is replaced mid-turn, makes the occurrence refuse at its next check with `Scheduled plugin command source changed or expired.` before any input, on `main` and on this branch alike; channel configuration changes wait for the running occurrence. On this setup the job carries no cron-level operator source, so its launch does not wait for the parent session; a wait at launch was not exercised.

prs.title: fix: Windows installer setup does not start after the npm shim is installed
prs.body:
Related: #183680

## What Problem This Solves

Windows setup can fail to start after installation, leaving users without clear recovery instructions. This change also fixes an earlier PR regression that rejected valid launcher paths.

## User Impact

Batch launchers in paths containing spaces, `&`, `!`, and literal `%PATH%` can receive the onboarding command. A process-creation failure prints a manual setup command; child failures preserve their exit status.

The original reported silent handoff failure remains unexplained. The original report's cause is not established; this evidence stops before provider authentication and does not establish Codex activation.

## Why This Change Was Made

Windows batch shims launch through System32 `cmd.exe` using the existing attached `Start-Process` owner. A temporary environment value preserves the literal launcher path and is restored after success or failure. Behavioral fixtures exercise the handoff and recovery rather than only checking a constructed command string.

The branch incorporates main at `bb9b2fd4fcbb732371de08a71da8bf317f3965c1`, resolving the test-file conflict while keeping both the upstream conflicted-pull regression and the handoff tests.

## Evidence

- **Fresh installer and interactive input, native Windows:** On Windows 10 / Windows PowerShell 5.1.19041.6456, the unmodified installer from `f1bf6180b2d646fbd41bec93585d921d3daf1fce` (SHA256 `bb1834fe5f16ef64f5d47c4f7a0338e007536ccfa772a1c283595eecf6a91d9d`) installed OpenClaw 2026.10.8 into a new isolated npm prefix in a real SSH ConPTY. Both console input and output reported `IsRedirected=False`. Without manually running `openclaw onboard`, the installer printed `Starting setup...` and opened the wizard. A down-arrow keystroke moved the selection from `Quick start (recommended)` to `Custom setup`; Ctrl+C then cancelled before authentication. The resulting exit code 1 is expected for cancellation. User PATH remained unchanged.
  <details>
  <summary>Sanitized terminal excerpt</summary>

  ```text
  PROOF mode=Fresh PS=5.1.19041.6456 inputRedirected=False outputRedirected=False
  OpenClaw installed successfully (OpenClaw 2026.10.8 (dc2523e))!
  Starting setup...
  * How would you like to start?
  | > Quick start (recommended)
  |   Custom setup
  [Down arrow sent]
  |   Quick start (recommended)
  | > Custom setup (Walk through every setup option.)
  [Ctrl+C sent]
  Setup cancelled.
  USER_PATH_UNCHANGED=True
  openclaw onboard failed with exit code 1.
  ```
  </details>
- **Isolated upgrade and preservation:** The same candidate installer detected the isolated 2026.10.8 installation, installed the published newer **2026.10.10-beta.4** package, ran Doctor migration, and reported `Upgrade complete`. Independently seeded synthetic gateway mode, port and workspace settings still matched; a synthetic workspace data file retained its SHA256, and the upgraded CLI read the preserved gateway mode and port. The test profile had no service before or after, and user PATH stayed unchanged. This is a stable-to-beta upgrade, not proof of an upgrade to a newer stable release; 2026.10.8 was the latest stable version observed.
  <details>
  <summary>Sanitized upgrade output</summary>

  ```text
  UPGRADE_SOURCE=OpenClaw 2026.10.8 (dc2523e)
  [*] Existing OpenClaw installation detected
  [OK] Migration complete
  Upgrade complete.
  UPGRADE_TARGET=OpenClaw 2026.10.10-beta.4 (5a94eab)
  USER_PATH_UNCHANGED=True
  SYNTHETIC_SETTINGS_PRESERVED=True
  SYNTHETIC_DATA_PRESERVED=True
  TASK_PROFILE_SERVICE_ABSENT=True
  UPGRADED_CLI_READS_PRESERVED_GATEWAY_SETTINGS=True
  ```
  </details>
- On Windows 10 with Windows PowerShell 5.1, the integrated-main installer failed the recovery fixture as expected because it omitted the manual command. The candidate passed recovery and real batch-launch fixtures, covering the special-character path, argument delivery, child exit codes 0 and 23, and environment restoration. Candidate installer SHA256: `bb1834fe5f16ef64f5d47c4f7a0338e007536ccfa772a1c283595eecf6a91d9d`; fixture SHA256: `f19c1824d3a18a1dbd552672f63bf6cae8728ac4c977035510501d905db56bcc`. Earlier [native Windows boundary results](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/185309#issuecomment-6452969756) cover the pre-integration candidate.
- On the merged candidate, Node 24.22.1 and pnpm 12.15.0: `pnpm test test/scripts/install-ps1.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` passed 14 tests, with one Windows-only test skipped on Linux (8.32 seconds test duration). The installer sibling suite passed 41 tests, with three platform-specific skips (25.90 seconds). Targeted formatting, lint, scripts-test typecheck, and `git diff --check` passed.
- The canonical shared autoreview ran against the entire resulting PR delta from base `bb9b2fd4fcbb732371de08a71da8bf317f3965c1` to the candidate tree committed as `f1bf6180b2d646fbd41bec93585d921d3daf1fce`: scoped clean at P0–P2, with no actionable findings. The pr-simplify and test-audit passes retained the existing shape and its distinct behavioral tests.
- [CI for the pushed head](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40594938010) reports `openclaw/ci-gate` success; the [Windows installer job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/40594938051/job/122508675321) also passed. CodeQL reported a neutral warning that 18 main-branch configurations were unavailable for comparison.

Remaining proof gaps: a newer stable-release upgrade was unavailable for this comparison, and the synthetic configuration and one workspace file do not cover all real user data. The interactive run stopped before authentication. The original silent failure and Codex activation remain unproved.

Human contributor credit: DonnieFi; preserved in the commit co-author trailers.
