issues.title: [Bug]: Discord plaintext approvals can be answered by an allowlisted peer bot
issues.body:
### Affected component

channel

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

With `listen_to_bots = true`, an allowlisted peer **bot** can resolve the agent's pending tool approvals on Discord by posting a plaintext approval reply (`<token> yes` / `<token> always`) in the prompt's channel.

The plaintext path (`DiscordChannel::resolve_approval_reply`) authorizes the responder only with `is_user_allowed(responder)` plus the destination binding added in #9574. A bot that the operator allowlisted so the agent can *talk* to it (`external_peers` in a Discord peer group) therefore also passes the approval check, because the Discord author's `bot` flag is not considered. Discord component approvals don't have this gap, since only a human can click a component.

### Expected behavior

Allowlisting a bot as a conversational peer should not make it an approver. A plaintext approval reply whose Discord author is a bot should be `Rejected`, exactly like a non-allowlisted responder: the pending approval is kept and the message is not forwarded to the agent. Allowlisted human responders keep working unchanged.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure a Discord channel with `listen_to_bots = true` and a peer group whose `external_peers` contains another bot's user ID plus a human operator.
2. Trigger a supervised tool call so ZeroClaw posts an approval prompt with a token.
3. Have the other bot post `<token> yes` in the same channel.
4. The approval resolves as an operator approval.

Unit-level reproduction on current master (run on 99bd353c7): construct `DiscordChannel` with that bot ID in the peer resolver and `listen_to_bots = true`, register a pending approval for destination `c1`, and call `resolve_approval_reply("<token> yes", "<bot-id>", "c1")`. It returns `Resolved`, and the approval receiver gets `Approve`.

### Impact

Two agents sharing a Discord channel (a configuration `listen_to_bots` exists for) can approve each other's tool calls. One agent's model output then stands in for the human-in-the-loop approval, defeating supervised mode for that channel. It requires the operator to have allowlisted the other bot, so it is a tightening of an existing trust boundary rather than an unauthenticated bypass.

### Logs / stack traces

N/A (authorization logic; no error is produced).

### ZeroClaw version

master @ 99bd353c7 (version 0.8.7 on master); same code in release v0.8.6

### Rust version

1.97.1

### Operating system

Linux aarch64 (Raspberry Pi OS)

### Regression?

No, first-time setup

### Pre-flight checks

- [x] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

Related: #9387 / #9574 (responder and destination binding for Telegram, Slack, Lark and Matrix). Slack's `allow_bots` text-approval path likely has the same shape and is out of scope here.

issues.title: [Feature]: Add /load-session to resume a Code session by name or UUID

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

issues.body:
### Summary

Add a `/load-session <name|uuid>` slash command to ZeroCode's Code (ACP) pane that resumes a previously persisted session by display name or session UUID.

### Problem statement

The only way to resume an earlier Code session from inside ZeroCode is the `Ctrl+S` session picker, which lists every persisted ACP session for the pane and requires scrolling to the right row. That is slow when there are many sessions, it cannot be driven from the input bar, and a session ID copied from logs, a PR description, or another terminal cannot be pasted to jump straight to that session.

Other session lifecycle actions already have slash commands (`/new`, `/new-session`, `/restart-session`, `/change-directory`), so resuming a known session is the odd one out.

### Proposed solution

Add a ZeroCode-local slash command, `/load-session`, owned by the input bar's `LOCAL_COMMANDS` table (like `/change-directory` and `/restart-session`):

- `/load-session <uuid>`: look up the session in the pane's own store (`session/list-acp` for Code panes) by exact `session_id`, then attach it through the existing `switch_to_session_entry` path used by the `Ctrl+S` picker. If the session is already tracked in this pane, focus it rather than attaching it again.
- `/load-session <name>`: match against the session list's `name` field. Exact match wins. An unambiguous case-insensitive match or unique UUID prefix is accepted. If more than one session matches, open the existing session picker filtered to the candidates instead of guessing.
- `/load-session` with no argument opens the existing session picker, mirroring `/model` and `/model-provider`.
- No match, an ambiguous match, a store error, or the per-pane session cap produces a localized info notice through ZeroCode's Fluent catalogue. It never silently starts a new session.

The daemon already implements `session/load` / `session/resume`, and ZeroCode already has the attach path, so no new RPC is required for UUID lookup.

**Dependency:** `handle_session_list_acp` currently returns `name: None` for every ACP session ("ACP sessions don't carry a user-set display name today"). Lookup by name in the Code pane only becomes useful once ACP sessions carry names, which is tracked by #10285. UUID lookup and the no-argument picker can land on their own. Name matching should read the same list `name` field so it starts working when #10285 lands, with no second name source.

### Non-goals / out of scope

- Adding session naming or renaming (tracked in #10285).
- Loading a session across panes or stores, for example resuming a Chat session in a Code pane or the reverse. Each pane only searches its own store.
- Loading sessions owned by another principal. Existing owner-visibility filtering in `session/list-acp` and the authorization in `session/load` stay unchanged.
- Restoring open sessions automatically on ZeroCode restart (see #11727).
- Fuzzy or substring search beyond the exact, case-insensitive, and unique-prefix rules above.

### Alternatives considered

- **Keep `Ctrl+S` only:** works, but it can't take a pasted ID and gets slow as the session count grows.
- **CLI flag such as `zerocode --session <id>`:** useful for startup, but it doesn't help mid-session. Could be added later on the same lookup helper.
- **Make it a shared `zeroclaw-commands` builtin:** resuming by ID depends on each surface's own session store and attach semantics, so a ZeroCode-local command fits better for now.

### Acceptance criteria

- `/load-session <uuid>` in a Code pane attaches the matching persisted ACP session with its restored transcript, using the same path as the `Ctrl+S` picker.
- If the target session is already tracked in this pane, the command focuses it and does not attach a duplicate.
- `/load-session` with no argument opens the existing session picker.
- Ambiguous matches open a filtered picker. No-match and error cases show a localized notice and do not create a session.
- The per-pane session cap is enforced the same way as for picker-driven attach.
- The command appears in `/help` and slash-command completion. All user-facing text uses ZeroCode Fluent keys.
- Unit tests cover parsing, exact UUID, unique prefix, case-insensitive name, ambiguous, not-found, already-tracked, and cap-reached cases.

### Architecture impact

- `apps/zerocode/src/input_bar.rs`: new `SlashCommandId` / `LOCAL_COMMANDS` entry and parse arm.
- `apps/zerocode/src/chat.rs`: command handler, session lookup helper, reuse of `switch_to_session_entry` and the `SessionOverlay::List` picker.
- `apps/zerocode/locales/`: new Fluent strings.
- Daemon RPC (`session/list-acp`, `session/load`): no changes expected.

### Risk and rollback

Low to medium. This is a client-only command layered on existing list and attach paths, and it doesn't touch session persistence or authorization. The main risk is resolving the wrong session on a loose match, which the exact-first, ambiguity-opens-picker rule addresses. Rollback is reverting the single ZeroCode PR.

### Expected routing

Ordinary feature triage

### Next decision surface

Ordinary triage is enough. Name lookup in the Code pane is sequenced behind #10285.

### Breaking change?

No

### Data hygiene checks

- [X] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [X] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

issues.title: [Feature]: Honor runtime-profile thinking levels for OpenAI
issues.body:
### Summary

Honor each runtime profile's existing thinking level when building native OpenAI reasoning requests.

### Problem statement

Two agents sharing an OpenAI provider cannot select different native reasoning efforts through their runtime profiles. The selected profile's thinking configuration reaches the turn layer, but OpenAI request construction reads the provider-wide effort resolved from `runtime.reasoning_effort`. Profile prompting and temperature adjustments can still apply; the missing behavior is native OpenAI effort.

Source inspection against master `5d4b18d335780af8bf15979b2f45e541f91c5eb9` identifies these boundaries:

- [Runtime profile resolution](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/5d4b18d335780af8bf15979b2f45e541f91c5eb9/crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs).
- [Turn thinking resolution](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/5d4b18d335780af8bf15979b2f45e541f91c5eb9/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/thinking.rs) and [provider request contract](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/5d4b18d335780af8bf15979b2f45e541f91c5eb9/crates/zeroclaw-api/src/model_provider.rs).
- [Global provider options](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/5d4b18d335780af8bf15979b2f45e541f91c5eb9/crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/lib.rs) and [OpenAI Responses requests](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/5d4b18d335780af8bf15979b2f45e541f91c5eb9/crates/zeroclaw-providers/src/openai.rs).

Reproduction to cover in regression tests: configure two runtime profiles with `native_thinking = true`, select `low` and `high` respectively, bind two agents to those profiles and the same reasoning-capable OpenAI model, and set a conflicting global effort. Capture the outgoing requests: each should use its profile's effort. This report is based on source inspection; no live-provider reproduction has been run.

### Proposed solution

Keep `native_thinking = true` as the opt-in. Resolve the existing inline override, then session override, then runtime-profile default. Carry that neutral ZeroClaw level with the request independently of token-budget parameters, and map it at the selected OpenAI model/endpoint boundary. The opted-in request setting overrides global effort; otherwise existing global/default behavior applies.

Map `off` to `none` where supported, otherwise the lowest supported effort. Map `minimal`, `low`, `medium` and `high` to the matching effort, or the next supported higher effort capped at the model maximum. Map `max` to the highest supported effort. Use verified capabilities, with separate treatment of subscription endpoints. Unknown/non-reasoning models retain existing gating and global/default behavior, with diagnostics explaining an unmapped request.

Apply this consistently to Responses, Chat Completions, streaming, tools, fallbacks and existing OpenAI Codex subscription requests. Preserve explicit raw-body override precedence and current bounded compatibility retries. Record requested/effective effort and the selected provider/model in diagnostics.

### Non-goals / out of scope

New native thinking support for other providers, new configuration keys, changing global accepted effort values, authentication changes, broad runtime extraction, or deployment.

This differs from #10705, which requests accepting literal `max` in global `runtime.reasoning_effort`. That issue is related, not resolved by this proposal.
https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/10705

### Alternatives considered

- A global effort cannot express two profiles sharing one provider.
- Fixing provider construction alone misses per-turn overrides and model fallbacks.
- Provider-specific profile strings would bind runtime policy to one backend instead of mapping the existing ZeroClaw levels.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Two profiles sharing an OpenAI endpoint produce their own requested efforts despite a conflicting global effort.
- [ ] All six ZeroClaw levels work independently of a native token budget; native opt-out preserves global/default behavior.
- [ ] Model-specific mappings, unsupported/unknown cases and subscription distinctions are tested.
- [ ] Streaming, tools, request reconstruction and fallback attempts preserve and correctly map the selected level.
- [ ] CLI, channels, Agent/RPC and delegates use the appropriate profile/session policy; concurrent turns remain isolated.
- [ ] Cache reuse cannot hide a changed explicit effort.
- [ ] Existing other-provider budgets, fallback accounting, attribution and replay guarantees remain compatible.
- [ ] Configuration survives save/reload without a new key or migration; behavior and Rust API compatibility changes are documented.

### Architecture impact

Canonical level and request data belong in `zeroclaw-api`, configuration re-exports preserve the existing schema, and model/wire mapping belongs in `zeroclaw-providers`. Runtime/channel changes are limited to propagating existing selected thinking policy and request-cache behavior.

Any new functionality in the transitional runtime crate requires the bounded Core Team-approved exception prescribed by its AGENTS.md, recorded with scope, destination and review condition. This request does not grant that exception. The intended destination of turn plumbing is the planned agent-loop owner in `zeroclaw-kernel`.

#### Bounded runtime exception requested

Core Team review is requested for the following proposed scope; no exception has been granted by this issue.

Paths are relative to `crates/zeroclaw-runtime`:

- `src/agent/thinking.rs`: carry the selected level independently of native token budgets.
- `src/agent/{agent,loop_}.rs` and `src/agent/turn/{mod,provider_call,stream_consume,max_iter}.rs`: propagate that request-bound level through existing turn/recovery/stream paths and bypass cached responses for explicit native-thinking overrides.
- `src/tools/delegate.rs`: use the target profile for independent delegates and preserve bounded-delegate inheritance.
- Focused regression tests in those existing owners.

**Destination:** agent-loop/request-context owner in the planned `zeroclaw-kernel` extraction. Level/request types, configuration policy and OpenAI wire mapping retain their API/config/provider owners.

**Review condition requested:** reconsider at agent-loop extraction, or before widening provider families, retained state or native-thinking policy.

**Required grant:** a separate Core Team-approved PR records the permitted scope, destination, approving authority and review condition in the [runtime exception table](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/5d4b18d335780af8bf15979b2f45e541f91c5eb9/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/AGENTS.md#exceptions). Additional runtime paths or behavior need explicit coverage. The implementation PR cannot grant itself this exception.

#### Publication artifacts and dependency

Delivery will produce three linked artifacts: this feature request, a separate implementation PR that resolves it, and a separate exception-only PR requesting the bounded runtime exception.

After implementation validation and review, publish the exception-only PR first so the implementation PR can name it with `Depends on #...`. Both PRs target `master` from separate task branches. The implementation PR links this feature request with closing semantics; the exception PR links it as related work.

Publishing either PR does not grant the exception. The implementation PR remains blocked from merging until the Core Team approves and records the exception through the separate PR.

### Risk and rollback

Incorrect mapping can cause upstream request rejection or alter token usage and latency. Verify supported efforts per model/endpoint, keep request state isolated and preserve existing retries. Disable the profile's native-thinking opt-in to recover global/default behavior, or revert the implementation commit.

### Expected routing

Needs maintainer design assessment

### Next decision surface

Publish the linked implementation and exception-only PRs. The exception PR is the Core Team decision surface; record its approval separately before the implementation PR merges.

### Breaking change?

Yes — adding a field to the public Rust `ChatRequest` requires downstream struct-literal constructors to initialize it. Preserve the `ThinkingLevel` configuration import through a re-export. Existing TOML values and configuration layout remain compatible.

### Data hygiene checks

- [x] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [x] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

issues.title: System prompt size budget is not enforced (unlimited default, warning-only check, uncapped workspace bootstrap)
issues.body:
## Summary

The `max_system_prompt_chars` runtime-profile limit does not protect agents from an oversized system prompt. Three compounding defects:

1. **Unsafe default**: `default_max_system_prompt_chars() = 0` means *unlimited* (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs` ~line 6824). Any profile that fails to resolve silently loses the cap.
2. **Warning-only enforcement**: when the assembled system prompt exceeds the budget, the runtime logs `context_floor_exceeds_budget` and **sends the request anyway** (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/turn/mod.rs` ~2463–2490). An over-budget prompt reaches the model with no truncation and no error.
3. **Uncapped workspace bootstrap**: for agents with `compact_context = false`, session bootstrap inlines workspace files into the system prompt with `bootstrap_max_chars = None` (`crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/mod.rs` ~17101). `BOOTSTRAP_MAX_CHARS` applies only when `compact_context = true`.

## Impact

A new session for an agent with a large workspace (hundreds of KB of `.md`) gets a system prompt of 100k+ tokens even with `max_system_prompt_chars = 50000` configured. The model then answers from a drowned system prompt — persona and instructions are lost, responses become generic confabulation. Observed on v0.8.6: 563K-char system prompt (~143K tokens) sent to the provider against a 50K-char configured budget; the only trace was a WARN.

A hot-reload of the config racing session creation makes profile resolution more likely to fall back (cap = 0), which is how the unlimited default surfaces in practice.

## Expected behavior

- A non-zero safe default for the cap.
- Over-budget prompt = hard stop: the turn fails with a clear error (or an emergency compaction/bootstrap-trim is attempted first), and the request is **not** sent to the provider.
- Workspace bootstrap respects a character budget regardless of `compact_context`.
- One resolution path: the budget used to build the prompt and the budget checked before the provider call must come from the same config snapshot.

## Repro (abstract)

1. Configure an agent profile with `compact_context = false` and `max_system_prompt_chars = 50000`; give the agent a workspace with >200KB of `.md` files.
2. Start a **new** session (e.g. a first message from a new chat).
3. Observe `llm_request` in `runtime-trace.jsonl`: `system_chars` far above the budget; WARN `context_floor_exceeds_budget` present; request still sent.

## Environment

zeroclaw 0.8.6, Windows service deployment, any model provider.

A fix with regression tests is being prepared and will be proposed as a PR referencing this issue.

issues.title: [Bug]: MCP HTTP client has no pool/keep-alive control, so a stale pooled socket loses the tool call as outcome-unknown
issues.body:
### Affected component

tools

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

The HTTP/SSE MCP client has no control over idle-connection reuse. `build_remote_http_client`
builds a bare `reqwest::Client::builder()` with no pool tuning:

`crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/mcp_transport.rs` (master 5d4b18d), lines 171-172:

```rust
fn build_remote_http_client(config: &McpServerConfig) -> Result<reqwest::Client> {
    let mut builder = reqwest::Client::builder();

    if let Some(path) = config.tls_ca_cert_path.as_deref() {
        // ...only TLS/redirect configuration follows...
```

and the transport keeps one client + one `session_id` for the process lifetime
(`mcp_transport.rs:1136-1183`).

This workspace resolves `reqwest 0.12.28` (`Cargo.lock`), whose defaults are
`pool_idle_timeout = 90 s` and `tcp_keepalive = 15 s`. Many MCP servers are far more aggressive:
uvicorn's default `timeout_keep_alive` is **5 s**, so a FastMCP/uvicorn server drops the TCP
connection after 5 idle seconds while the client keeps that socket in its pool for up to 90 s and
still considers it reusable.

When that dead socket is picked up, the request is written to a half-closed connection and fails
inside `req.send()`. Since `lifecycle.mark_outcome_unknown()` is called *before* `send()`
(`mcp_transport.rs:1256`), that failure is correctly — but permanently — classified as outcome
unknown, so `dispatch_rpc` refuses to replay it (`mcp_client.rs:683`). The tool call is lost and the
model is told the outcome is unknowable, so it cannot safely retry either.

Reproduced on a FastMCP streamable-HTTP server. Raw-socket probe on one keep-alive connection,
server at uvicorn defaults:

```
first request        -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
after 3s idle        -> 200 OK
after 6s idle        -> 200 OK
after 12s idle       -> BrokenPipeError        <- uvicorn closed it at 5s, client had not noticed
```

With `uvicorn_config={"timeout_keep_alive": 650}` on the server, the same connection survived
40 s+ of idle and the failures stopped. So the trigger is confirmable and the server-side knob is
the only mitigation available today.

`reqwest` will not retry this for us either: hyper-util's `retry_canceled_requests` only retries
when the body was provably never written, and reqwest 0.12.23+'s `retry` layer only covers HTTP/2
`GOAWAY`/`REFUSED_STREAM` and HTTP/3 timeout — an HTTP/1.1 reset after the head is on the wire is
surfaced as an error.

Runtime trace from v0.8.6 in production, first tool call after an idle gap:

```
tool failed: finance__add_transaction
  error="MCP server `finance` failed during tool call `add_transaction`;
         outcome unknown and request was not replayed"
  duration_ms=6
```

### Expected behavior

Expose the client's pool/keep-alive behaviour in `McpServerConfig` so operators can set it below
their server's idle TTL, e.g.:

```toml
[[mcp.servers]]
name = "finance"
transport = "http"
url = "http://finance-mcp:8000/mcp"
pool_idle_timeout_secs = 10   # None/0 = reqwest default (90s)
tcp_keepalive_secs = 15       # None/0 = reqwest default
```

The client cannot know every server's idle TTL, so the actionable fix is a knob plus a sane
default. A conservative default below common server values (or `pool_idle_timeout` unset but
documented) would prevent the "dead socket after idle" class of failure entirely, because a
socket discarded before it goes stale can never produce an ambiguous write.

I am **not** asking for replay of outcome-unknown requests — that rule is correct and should stay,
especially for side-effecting tools.

### Related observation (secondary, deliberately not framed as a bug)

Separately, a 404 carrying a `Mcp-Session-Id` is mapped to `StaleSession`
(`mcp_transport.rs:1263-1272`) and returns **without** `lifecycle.mark_completed()`, unlike the
adjacent non-success branch at 1273. So `dispatch_rpc` takes the outcome-unknown branch and the
request is never retried — the connection is re-handshaked, the call is not.

I see that `call_tool_recovers_stale_session_without_replaying_tool`
(`mcp_client.rs:3025-3098`) asserts this is intentional, so I am not calling it a defect. But the
rationale in that test is "the request crossed the write boundary". A 404 *response* proves the
server received and evaluated the request without executing it — the MCP 2025-06-18 spec says a
server MUST answer requests for a terminated session with 404, and that the client MUST then start
a new session via a fresh `InitializeRequest`. Responding 404 is definitionally a non-execution, so
this is the one post-write case where a retry is provably safe. Worth considering whether
`StaleSession` should mark the lifecycle completed and be treated as retryable; happy to be told
the current conservatism is deliberate for other reasons.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Serve a streamable-HTTP MCP server with uvicorn defaults (FastMCP
   `mcp.run(transport="http", ...)`), then configure ZeroClaw:

   ```toml
   [[mcp.servers]]
   name = "finance"
   transport = "http"
   url = "http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp"
   ```

2. Call any tool once so a `Mcp-Session-Id` is issued.
3. Idle for >5 s (uvicorn keep-alive) but <90 s (reqwest pool idle) — the window where the pooled
   socket is dead but still considered reusable.
4. Call a tool again.

Observed: intermittently fails with `... outcome unknown and request was not replayed`, with a very
small `duration_ms` (fail-fast on a dead socket, not a timeout). The next identical call succeeds.

### Impact

Affected users: anyone using remote HTTP/SSE MCP servers behind uvicorn/nginx-style servers whose
keep-alive is shorter than reqwest's 90 s pool window. stdio is unaffected.

Frequency: intermittent, and worse the sparser the tool usage — it needs a gap long enough to kill
the socket but short enough that the pool still holds it. In practice it shows up as "the first
tool call after a quiet period fails".

Consequence: silent data loss for side-effecting tools (`add_transaction`, bookings, payments). The
model reports "outcome unknown" and correctly refuses to retry, but the server never executed the
call, so the user's operation vanishes. There is no config workaround on the client side today.

### Logs / stack traces

```
MCP server `finance` failed during tool call `add_transaction`; outcome unknown and request was not replayed
MCP server `host_monitor` failed during tool call `get_host_metrics`; outcome unknown and request was not replayed
```

```
2026-10-27T02:58:27.093Z  tool failed: finance__add_transaction  duration_ms=6
```

### ZeroClaw version

v0.8.6 (c473221); source reviewed against master 5d4b18d

### Rust version

n/a (running release binary; findings from source review of master)

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04 (kernel 6.8.0-136-generic)

### Regression?

Unknown

### Pre-flight checks

- [x] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

milestone.title: v0.9.0
milestone.description:
v0.9.0 prioritizes opt-in OIDC dashboard sign-in, principal isolation, schema V4 and a CLI-only build option.

The standard build keeps the working in-process dashboard. Sign-in stays off by default, preserving the existing pairing flow. Release gates are real-provider sign-in evidence; the five principal-isolation repairs (#11234, #11220, #11225, #11230, #11266, with #11198 tracked); schema V4 (#11218); and a build-time CLI-only option that omits gateway/web assets and directs dashboard users to the standard build.

Scoped dashboard chat has a November 3 go/no-go, with sign-in alone as the fallback. November 10 is the earliest target, subject to the gates, not a committed date.

Standalone zeroclaw-gw, full gateway IPC route/parity work, cross-process webhook handling and two-process desktop packaging move to v0.9.x. Channel listeners remain in core under existing documented exceptions. These deferrals do not complete the remaining gateway roadmap.

Source of truth: #7432 (https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/7432), current release allocation. Existing implementation trackers keep their detailed work. Feature acceptance, current-head review/CI, recorded placement decisions and the v0.8.7-tag hold on breaking work remain in force.

issues.body:
### Affected component

tools

### Severity

S1 - workflow blocked

### Current behavior

When an MCP server over HTTP or SSE becomes briefly unreachable during a tool call (container
restart, systemd restart, proxy reload, laptop sleep), ZeroClaw makes exactly one reset +
re-handshake attempt, scheduled at the instant of failure while the dependency is still down.
When that attempt fails, `RecoveryBarrier::poison()` sets an AtomicBool that nothing in the
tree ever clears. Every subsequent request on that `McpServer` fails closed in
`wait_recovery_ready` with

  MCP server `<name>` is unavailable: a prior request's outcome became unknown and recovery
  failed; not writing on an unrecovered session

without touching the network, even after the MCP server is fully healthy again. Because `SharedMcpTransportConn::health_check` defaults to `true` and neither HttpTransport nor
SseTransport overrides it, the poisoned connection reports healthy to `kill_dead_connections` / `reconcile_heartbeat_mcp_registry`, so it is never rebuilt. 

_Recovery requires restarting the ZeroClaw process._

Three coupled causes, all in crates/zeroclaw-tools/src (line numbers at v0.8.5 == master a6937df):
  A. mcp_client.rs:233 poison() is terminal — 11 occurrences of `poisoned` in the file, only
     :196 (init false) and :234 (store true) write it; no store(false)/swap/compare_exchange.
  B. mcp_transport.rs:452 health_check() defaults true; only StdioTransport (:1123) overrides.
  C. mcp_transport.rs:1256 (HTTP) and :2030 (SSE) call mark_outcome_unknown() BEFORE
     req.send(), so a DNS/connect/TLS failure that never reached the server is classified
     outcome-unknown and takes the poison-capable path (dispatch_rpc checks
     outcome_unknown_epoch() at mcp_client.rs:683 before the MAX_RECONNECT_ATTEMPTS branch
     at :696; that branch also only retries errors that downcast to McpTransportError, :695).

Regression: v0.8.3 has no poison flag; RecoveryBarrier was introduced by #9418 (commit
1e99541d, between v0.8.3 and v0.8.4), which fixed the stdio-only issue #9186 — HTTP/SSE
inherited the permanent latch without stdio's health_check override. The struct comment (mcp_client.rs:178-180) documents the permanent latch as intentional; this report argues the latch should scope to the session, not the connection — see Expected behavior.

### Expected behavior

Failing the one ambiguous request is correct and the no-replay rule could remain as is. But a failed re-handshake should leave the connection in "needs re-handshake before use", not "dead forever": a later request (or a timer) should attempt reset + handshake again, with bounded retries and backoff, instead of failing closed for the process lifetime.  A re-handshake produces a new session; the old session's ambiguity does not carry into it.

On success `reestablish` already calls `finish()` and clears the recovery state (mcp_client.rs:614); on failure it latches forever. Same session ambiguity in both branches, opposite treatment.

Additionally: 
(1) a request that failed to connect (reqwest `is_connect()`) was never sent and should take the existing bounded pre-write retry path, not the outcome-unknown path; 
(2) `McpServer::health_check()` should report a poisoned barrier as dead so the existing registry rebuild machinery can act.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# --- Deterministic (no network, no Docker; ~1 s once built) ----------------
1. git clone https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw && cd zeroclaw && git checkout v0.8.5
# Paste the test `connection_recovers_after_one_failed_recovery` from the first comment
# at the end of `mod tests` in crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/mcp_client.rs, then:
cargo test -p zeroclaw-tools --lib mcp_client::tests::connection_recovers_after_one_failed_recovery
# Expected: pass.  Actual: fails at the first assertion —
#   connection stayed poisoned after the server recovered: Some(MCP server `flaky` error
#   during tool call `anything`  Caused by: MCP server `flaky` is unavailable: a prior
#   request's outcome became unknown and recovery failed; not writing on an unrecovered session
# The 43 existing mcp_client:: tests still pass; only this one fails. A second test in the
# first comment (§4b-ii) reaches the same state through the real dispatch_rpc path with the
# HTTP serial gate installed, and fails the same way.

# --- Verify by reading (no build) ---------------------------------------------------------
grep -n "poisoned" crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/mcp_client.rs        # 11 lines; writes only at :196, :234
grep -n "fn health_check" crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/mcp_transport.rs  # 5 hits; the only SharedMcpTransportConn impls are :452 (default, true) and :1123 (stdio)
sed -n '1256,1258p' crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/mcp_transport.rs    # mark_outcome_unknown precedes .send()

# --- Application Steps to Reproduce (captured in production trace; timing-dependent) -----------
1. Configure an MCP server with transport = "http".
2. Start an agent turn that calls a tool on it.
3. While a call is in flight: docker restart <mcp-container>  (or systemctl restart, or kill
     a supervised process — anything that makes the endpoint unreachable for > ~50 ms).
4. Wait until the server is healthy again, then make further tool calls in the same turn.

Notice:  Every later call fails with duration_ms: 0 and exactly one  "mcp_client: asynchronous recovery failed after outcome-unknown request" ERROR record appears at the moment of poisoning.
```

### Impact

**Affected users:** anyone running an MCP server over HTTP or SSE whose MCP Service could become unavailable during a call ( can restart, loose connectivty, etc.). while ZeroClaw is up — i.e. any Docker Compose / systemd / supervised deployment.

**Frequency**: every time an MCP request is in flight during a restart lasting more than a few tens of milliseconds. The recovery attempt fires immediately (spawn_recovery detaches the task with no delay), so it runs while the dependency is still down and reliably loses.

**Consequence**: silent, permanent (process-lifetime) loss of that MCP server. In the observed occurrence the agent misdiagnosed a healthy server as down ("Health probes also fail ... so it's the MCP server itself"), abandoned its work cycle, and the turn was recorded outcome: success; from the source, the heartbeat tick then calls mark_component_ok("heartbeat") (daemon/mod.rs:2109) and record_success (:2256). One ERROR log line is the only signal produced. Stdio transports are affected within a turn but StdioTransport overrides health_check, the daemon reconciler rebuilds them on the next pass; HTTP/SSE are never rebuilt.

### Logs / stack traces

```text
\Production, v0.8.5, scheduled heartbeat, 2026-09-06, trace 9b9526b7-cd5c-477c-a8a6-0b5075ad00f0.
Four records, verbatim except for the two redactions noted; duration_ms is the daemon's own.

{"@timestamp":"2026-09-06T19:01:30.382Z","attributes":{"_file":"crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/tool_execution.rs","_line":325,"error":"MCP server `gitea_agent` failed during tool call `list_issues`; outcome unknown and request was not replayed","input":{"labels":["<label>"],"owner":"<org>","repo":"<repo>","state":"open"},"output":"","tool":"gitea_agent__list_issues","tool_call_id":"call_1h8qmn8o"},"event":{"action":"fail","category":"tool","outcome":"failure"},"message":"tool failed: gitea_agent__list_issues","zeroclaw":{"duration_ms":2}}
{"@timestamp":"2026-09-06T19:01:30.403Z","attributes":{"_file":"crates/zeroclaw-tools/src/mcp_client.rs","_line":530,"error":"MCP server `gitea_agent` failed to re-handshake during recovery: HTTP request to MCP server failed: error sending request for url (http://gitea-mcp:3001/mcp): client error (Connect): dns error: failed to lookup address information: Name or service not known","operation":"tool call `list_issues`"},"event":{"action":"reconnect","category":"internal","outcome":"failure"},"message":"mcp_client: asynchronous recovery failed after outcome-unknown request","severity_text":"ERROR"}
{"@timestamp":"2026-09-06T19:01:32.399Z","attributes":{"_file":"crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/tool_execution.rs","_line":325,"error":"MCP server `gitea_agent` error during tool call `list_issues`","tool":"gitea_agent__list_issues"},"event":{"action":"fail","category":"tool","outcome":"failure"},"zeroclaw":{"duration_ms":0}}
{"@timestamp":"2026-09-06T19:01:54.809Z","attributes":{"_file":"crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/turn/mod.rs","_line":1110,"iteration":7,"text":"Heartbeat check could not complete — the Gitea MCP server is erroring, so I cannot verify board state this cycle.\n\n**Raw errors (verbatim):**\n- `gitea_agent__list_issues` (labels=[\"<label>\"], <org>/<repo>, open) → `MCP server gitea_agent failed during tool call list_issues; outcome unknown and request was not replayed` on first try, then `MCP server gitea_agent error during tool call list_issues` on retry.\n- Health probes also fail: `get_me` and `get_gitea_mcp_server_version` both return the same MCP error — so it's the MCP server itself, not the query.\n\n**My reading:** the MCP transport for this office is down or degraded, not an empty board.","trace_id":"9b9526b7-cd5c-477c-a8a6-0b5075ad00f0"},"event":{"action":"complete","category":"agent","outcome":"success"},"message":"turn_final_response"}

Note the two signals: the first record carries the dispatch_rpc:688 wrapper ("failed during
... outcome unknown and request was not replayed"), which is what every real HTTP send
failure produces under cause C; the third carries the :719-721 wrapper ("error during tool
call"), reachable for HTTP only from the barrier bail or from an actual server reply — and it
```

issues.title: [Bug]: OpenAI Codex stream-decode fallback retries without streaming, which the default ChatGPT endpoint always rejects
issues.body:
### Affected component

provider

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

When a streaming OpenAI Codex response cannot be decoded, `OpenAiCodexModelProvider::send_responses_request` retries the same request once with `stream: false` (added in #6668). On the default ChatGPT Codex endpoint (`https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses`, OAuth / subscription auth), that retry can never succeed: the backend rejects non-streaming requests with

```
400 Bad Request: {"detail":"Stream must be set to true"}
```

`reliable.rs` then classifies the 400 as a non-retryable client error, and the channel shows the generic "selected model provider rejected the request". The real cause, a truncated stream, is hidden behind a misleading request-shape error.

Observed on 2026-10-27 in a Discord channel turn (alias using `gpt-6-luna`, `requires_openai_auth = true`). Full sequence for one occurrence (17:40 UTC) from `runtime-trace.jsonl`, metadata only:

1. `ERROR openai_codex: empty SSE stream payload`. The payload contained only `event: response.created` with `status: in_progress` and no output, terminal, or error event; the stream ended about 9 s after the request, well inside `timeout_secs = 600`.
2. `WARN OpenAI Codex streaming response decode failed, retrying without streaming`
3. `ERROR providers: API error`, status 400, `{"detail":"Stream must be set to true"}`
4. `WARN Non-retryable error, moving on` → `channel_message_error`

The same channel error appeared twice more in the next 25 minutes, but the rotating runtime trace no longer held those entries when checked, so the 400 is only confirmed for the occurrence above.

The existing tests (`codex_retries_non_streaming_when_stream_decode_fails`, `..._malformed_frame_after_text`) pass because the mock server accepts `stream: false`. They model a custom endpoint, not the default ChatGPT backend.

### Expected behavior

On the default ChatGPT Codex endpoint, a stream that ends without output should be retried once **as a stream**. If that also fails, the error should name the streaming failure, not a 400 from a request the backend never supports. Custom endpoints (`provider_api_url`, where #6668's non-streaming recovery may be valid) keep the current behavior.

### Steps to reproduce

Live reproduction depends on the backend truncating a stream, which is intermittent. Deterministic reproduction with the existing mock: configure the provider as the default endpoint (OAuth profile, not the custom-endpoint API-key mode), reply to the first request with an SSE body holding only `response.created` (`status: in_progress`), and observe that the retry request carries `stream: false`. Against the real backend that request returns the 400 above.

### Impact

Every transient truncated stream on the subscription route becomes a hard turn failure with a misleading error message. In our case all three channel errors came while the agent was replying to a longer message from a peer bot. That correlation is noted, but it is far too small a sample to establish why the backend truncates the stream. This report is about the recovery path, not the truncation.

### Logs / stack traces

See the sequence above. Payload contents and conversation text intentionally omitted.

### ZeroClaw version

master @ 99bd353c7 (fallback since #6668); observed on a build from 96c052753

### Rust version

1.97.1

### Operating system

Linux aarch64 (Raspberry Pi OS)

### Regression?

No, first-time setup

### Pre-flight checks

- [x] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [x] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

Related: #6668 (introduced the non-streaming recovery), #6074.

issues.body:
### Task

Shorten the Release Stable `Build Desktop App (macOS Universal)` job, which now gates publishing and runs close to its 180-minute timeout, and add enough margin that a slow runner cannot block a release.

### Context

`publish` needs `build-desktop`, so the GitHub Release cannot be created until the macOS universal desktop job finishes. With #11347 the bundled `zeroclaw` sidecar builds the `dist` selection, which now includes the plugin host and Cranelift.

In the v0.8.6 Release Stable run [39095722409](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/39095722409):

- `Stage bundled kernel sidecar (universal)` took **108 minutes**. It builds the sidecar for both `aarch64-apple-darwin` and `x86_64-apple-darwin` on one runner, with the release profile (`opt-level = "z"`, fat LTO, one codegen unit).
- The job's timeout is 180 minutes. It was the last job before the `github-releases` gate.
- The CLI `aarch64-apple-darwin` build took 90 minutes and `x86_64-apple-darwin` 66 minutes.

In the v0.8.5 run [33946673896](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/33946673896), the same desktop job took 42 minutes, with a 33-minute sidecar step, and the CLI `aarch64-apple-darwin` build took 43 minutes.

The desktop job's duration was not measured before the v0.8.6 release; the CLI archive smoke does not cover desktop bundles.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The macOS universal desktop job finishes with a clear margin under its timeout on a Stable or manual cross-platform run, and the run is linked here.
- [ ] The desktop job no longer adds time on top of the slowest CLI macOS build before `publish` can start, or the remaining gap is measured and accepted here.
- [ ] Whatever route is chosen keeps the shipped sidecar's feature set and signing unchanged, or states the difference.

### Likely files or areas

- `.github/workflows/release-stable-manual.yml` (`build-desktop`, `publish` needs)
- `scripts/desktop/prepare-kernel.sh`
- `.github/workflows/cross-platform-build-manual.yml` (to rehearse the change)

Possible routes, to compare:

1. Reuse the binaries the CLI `aarch64-apple-darwin` and `x86_64-apple-darwin` legs already build and combine them with `lipo`, instead of rebuilding both in the desktop job. The sidecar adds `embedded-web` on macOS, so check whether the CLI legs can carry it or the desktop needs its own build.
2. Build per-architecture sidecars on two runners in parallel, then combine.
3. A larger macOS runner for this job.
4. As a stopgap, a higher timeout for the job.

### Contributor fit

maintainer-scoped task, not yet ready for pickup labels

### Mentor, reviewer, or contact

@JordanTheJet. Review by `.github/**` CODEOWNERS.

### Risk notes

The desktop job signs and notarizes the dmg. Any change to how the sidecar is produced must keep the binary that is signed identical in features to what the release notes describe. Related: #11829 (Cranelift under the hardened runtime).

### Task

Remove the SHA-256 assertion over `release-stable-manual.yml` from `immutable_stable_release_recipe_has_real_command_and_failure_baselines` in `tests/architecture/release_workflow.rs`. Keep the semantic assertions. Add a named assertion only where the digest protects something that matters and no other assertion covers.

### Context

The test is at `tests/architecture/release_workflow.rs:581` on #11347's head `f39ffd4791`. It reads the Stable workflow, removes the arm64 build-memory block, and cuts out the one reviewed `Build release` step. It then compares a SHA-256 of everything else with a literal (lines 602 to 605). A change to any other byte in the file fails the test, and the failure shows only two hashes.

Most changes to that file are routine. Of the last 15 commits on master that touched `release-stable-manual.yml`, seven would have failed this test:

- five action-version bumps: #10598, #10500, #9920 and #9752 from Dependabot, plus #9856
- the `macos-14` to `macos-15` runner move, #11522
- the 1.98.0 toolchain bump, #9527

Each author would have had to find this test and recompute the hash, with nothing to say what the hash guards. The Dependabot PRs would have stayed red until a maintainer pushed to them.

The semantic checks already pin what matters:

- `assert_arm64_build_memory` checks the arm64 memory handling.
- `assert_release_caller` checks the `Build release` step's inputs.
- The matrix loop checks each target's linker and `use_cross` settings.
- The recipe runs check the command and failure traces for all ten targets.
- A separate test checks that the shared body inverts the input adapters back to the immutable body.
- Other tests in the same file assert the `needs` of `publish` (including `plugin-smoke` and `crates-preflight`) and of `docker` (including `plugin-smoke`).

`OLD_RELEASE_RECIPE_SHA256`, in the same test, pins a constant inside the test file, not the workflow. It can stay.

Raised in the #11347 review.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The whole-file digest assertion is removed.
- [ ] The PR lists what the digest covered, and each part either has a named assertion or is stated as intentionally unpinned.
- [ ] Changing a `uses:` pin outside the `Build release` step, as Dependabot does, no longer fails the test. Shown on the PR.
- [ ] Mutation checks still fail a test: removing `plugin-smoke` from `publish`'s `needs`, removing it from `docker`'s `needs`, and removing the arm64 memory step.

### Likely files or areas

- `tests/architecture/release_workflow.rs`

### Contributor fit

maintainer-scoped task, not yet ready for pickup labels

### Mentor, reviewer, or contact

@JordanTheJet. Review by `tests/**` CODEOWNERS (@JordanTheJet, @Audacity88).

### Risk notes

The digest is a blunt guard against unreviewed edits to a publishing workflow. Without it, that guard is the named assertions plus CODEOWNERS review of `.github/**`. The risk is a semantic gap, and the mutation checks above cover the main ones. Until this lands, every PR that touches the Stable workflow has to update the literal, including the `macos-15` runner fix.

issues.body:
### Task

Find out whether the plugin host works inside the signed and notarized macOS desktop app. If it does not, add the hardened-runtime entitlement that Cranelift needs and sign the bundled `zeroclaw` sidecar with it. Until this is confirmed, nothing should tell desktop users that plugins work.

### Context

**The desktop app now carries the plugin host.** Release Stable's `build-desktop` job builds the app's bundled `zeroclaw` with `scripts/desktop/prepare-kernel.sh --target universal-apple-darwin --features embedded-web`. That script resolves the `dist` selection for each target. With #11221 and #11347, `dist` includes `plugins-wasm-cranelift` on both macOS targets. So the sidecar in the dmg carries the plugin host and the Cranelift compiler.

**Nothing in the signing setup allows JIT.** The repo has no entitlements file. Neither `apps/tauri/tauri.conf.json` nor the `apps/tauri/tauri.bundled.conf.json` overlay has a `bundle.macOS` section, so Tauri signs the bundle with its defaults. Notarization requires the hardened runtime. Under the hardened runtime, a process cannot make anonymous memory executable unless it is signed with `com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit` (for `MAP_JIT` mappings) or `com.apple.security.cs.allow-unsigned-executable-memory`. Cranelift compiles each plugin to machine code in memory and then runs it.

**This is reasoning, not a reproduction.** Nobody has run `zeroclaw plugin install` inside a notarized dmg yet. Two things need checking: which entitlement Wasmtime's code memory needs on macOS, and whether Tauri signs `externalBin` sidecars with the app's entitlements.

**The plugin smoke does not cover it.** #11347's `plugin-smoke` job runs the CLI archives on native runners. It does not test the desktop bundle. The macOS CLI archives are not signed with the hardened runtime either, so their smoke pass says nothing about the notarized app. The Linux and Windows desktop bundles build their sidecar the same way and are not smoke-tested either, but they have no equivalent signing restriction.

**Why it matters.** On builds with the plugin host, `zeroclaw status`, `/api/plugins` and the dashboard report the plugin host as available. If the reasoning holds, a macOS desktop user is shown plugins as available, and loading one fails.

Raised in the #11347 review.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On a signed and notarized dmg from a release or release candidate, the bundled `zeroclaw` installs and loads a registry package. The `redact-text` tool needs no account, so it is a good test. The result is recorded here with the macOS version and chip.
- [ ] If that fails: an entitlements file with the narrowest entitlement that works is added and wired through the Tauri config so the sidecar is signed with it. Then the check above passes and notarization still succeeds.
- [ ] Until the first item passes, no release note or doc says the desktop app runs plugins.
- [ ] Optional: a desktop release check that runs `plugin install` against the signed sidecar, so this cannot regress silently.

### Likely files or areas

- `apps/tauri/tauri.conf.json`, `apps/tauri/tauri.bundled.conf.json`
- a new entitlements file under `apps/tauri/`
- `scripts/desktop/prepare-kernel.sh`
- `.github/workflows/release-stable-manual.yml` (`build-desktop`)

### Contributor fit

maintainer-scoped task, not yet ready for pickup labels

### Mentor, reviewer, or contact

@JordanTheJet. Review by `apps/tauri/**` CODEOWNERS (@JordanTheJet, @Audacity88), and `.github/**` CODEOWNERS for any workflow change.

### Risk notes

- `allow-unsigned-executable-memory` is broader than `allow-jit`. Use `allow-jit` if Wasmtime works with it.
- An entitlement loosens the hardened runtime for the whole binary it signs. Give it to the sidecar only, unless the app shell needs it too.
- A signing change can break notarization. Check the notarization result on the first release run after the change.

issues.body:
### Affected component

config/onboarding

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

With a daemon running, `zeroclaw config set` of a plugin instance's settings (`plugins.entries.<key>.config.<name>`) or its egress grant (`plugins.entries.<key>.egress_hosts`) rewrites `config.toml` and reports success, but the running daemon never sees the change. Nothing says so.

Seen with the Discord channel plugin: after removing `*.discord.gg` from the instance's grant and restarting (gateway refused, as expected), I put the grant back on the running daemon:

```text
$ zeroclaw config set --no-interactive plugins.entries.<key>.egress_hosts ["*.discord.gg","discord.com"]
plugins.entries.<key>.egress_hosts updated.
```

The plugin kept being refused once a minute for the next five minutes:

```text
08:40:45.998Z WARN discord: gateway connect failed {... "raw": "{\"error\":\"destination-denied\",\"host\":\"gateway.discord.gg\",\"resume\":false}"}
08:40:45.998Z ERROR discord: gateway connection refused by the host; retrying every minute {... "raw": "{\"reason\":\"egress_denied\"}"}
... (same pair at 08:41:47, 08:42:52, 08:43:54, 08:44:56)
```

`POST /admin/reload` (same PID) applied it, and the gateway was READY about 3 s later.

Why:

- `config set` sends only agent paths to the daemon (`src/main.rs:11721`). Every other path is written with `set_prop_persistent` and `save_dirty` (`src/main.rs:11763-11764`). The daemon does not watch the file; it re-reads it only on reload or restart (`src/main.rs:9391-9394`).
- The plugin host is built to apply such edits live. Egress is resolved from the daemon's live config on every request (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/tools/mod.rs:933-952`), and plugin config and secrets on every call (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/tools/mod.rs:1001-1045`). The orchestrator passes the live handle to plugin channels (`crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/mod.rs:17164-17170`). The plugin guide promises that a config plus credential rotation "is visible together on the next operation without daemon reload or channel reconstruction" (`docs/book/src/plugins/writing-a-channel-plugin.md:350-357`), and the Discord package's README says an edit "applies without a restart".
- The daemon already has a `config/set` RPC that publishes a new live revision (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs:9263`). The CLI uses it only for `agents.*`.

`plugin install --channel-alias`, `plugin bind` and `plugin info` do say it ("A running daemon picks up plugin.<alias> after a restart or reload.", `src/main.rs:4734-4738`). `config set` prints only `updated.`

### Expected behavior

When a daemon owns the config, `config set` of `plugins.entries.*` goes through the daemon's `config/set`, as agent paths do, so the next egress check or `config.get` / `secrets.get` call sees the new value. If the CLI keeps writing those paths offline, it should at least say that a running daemon picks the change up after `POST /admin/reload` or a restart.

Note for whoever picks this up: routing through the daemon makes a grant or a public setting apply live, but not every credential. 10 of the 12 channel packages in the registry read their credential once in `configure()` and keep it (for example `load_config()` in zeroclaw-plugins `plugins/telegram/src/lib.rs`), so for them a rotated token still needs the instance rebuilt, which a reload does. Discord and Matrix read it at each use.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
zeroclaw plugin install discord --channel-alias main --egress declared
# set bot_token, channel_ids, the agent's channels and the peer group as the Discord docs describe
zeroclaw config set --no-interactive plugins.entries.<key>.egress_hosts '["discord.com"]'
zeroclaw daemon
# gateway connect refused once a minute (expected: *.discord.gg is not granted)

# in another terminal, with the daemon still running:
zeroclaw config set --no-interactive plugins.entries.<key>.egress_hosts '["*.discord.gg","discord.com"]'
# prints "updated."; the daemon keeps refusing the gateway every minute
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:<gateway-port>/admin/reload
# the gateway reaches READY within a few seconds
```

### Impact

Any operator who edits a plugin instance from the CLI while the daemon runs: grants, channel filters, tokens. The command reports success and the daemon keeps the old value until something reloads it, so it looks like the plugin ignored the change.

### ZeroClaw version

v0.8.6 release-candidate build (61a2c95); code references are to current master

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04 (WSL2)

### Regression?

No, first-time setup

### Related

#11329 (its acceptance template's "Grant restored" row says "without a restart" and names no way to apply the grant)

issues.body:
### Summary

Create `data_dir` with an owner-only mode, and at startup detect a data root that other local users can write to. Then either tighten it or refuse it with an actionable remedy, using one trust rule everywhere the daemon keeps state.

### Problem statement

`data_dir` (`<install>/data` by default) holds state whose integrity matters:

- `daemon.sock`, the local RPC endpoint;
- `control_plane.db`, `sessions/acp-sessions.db`, `memory/` and `state/`;
- `cron/`, the scheduled jobs;
- `tls/`, `relay/`;
- `config-lifecycle.lock`.

If the directory itself is writable by another user, that user can unlink and replace any entry in it, even when the entry is 0600 or 0644. Replacing a database or the socket is enough to tamper with agent state or impersonate the daemon to local clients.

Today:

- Config loading creates the directory with a plain `create_dir_all` (`crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs`, "Failed to create data directory"), so its mode follows the process umask: 0775 under umask 0002, 0777 under umask 0000.
- The daemon's IPC setup (`prepare_parent` in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/local.rs`) chmods the socket's parent, `data_dir` by default, to 0700 on a best-effort basis. `require_trusted_lock_dir` then vets the endpoint's lock directory: owned by the current user or root, and not group- or other-writable unless the sticky bit is set. Its error says how to fix it: `chmod go-w` or `+t`, or point `ZEROCLAW_SOCKET` at a private directory.
- The config lifecycle lock added in #10621 checks the data directory separately, with a different rule (no sticky-bit allowance) and no remedy. Its handling of umask-created directories is tracked in the lifecycle-directory umask issue. In v0.8.5 and earlier, nothing checked the data root at all.

So the guarantee depends on which command ran first, under which umask, and on whether the daemon ever reached its IPC setup.

### Proposed solution

1. **Create owner-only.** Every path that creates `data_dir` (config loading, the lifecycle lock, the IPC endpoint) uses `DirBuilder::new().recursive(true).mode(0o700)` on Unix, so a new data root does not depend on the umask.
2. **One trust rule.** Factor the IPC endpoint's rule into a shared helper and apply it to the data root: owned by the current user (or root), and not group- or other-writable unless sticky. Apply it once at startup, before anything reads state from the directory.
3. **Existing permissive roots.** For a directory the current user owns, choose between:
   - (a) tightening it with `chmod go-w` and logging a notice naming the old and new modes; or
   - (b) refusing with the remedy text.

   (a) suits upgrades from v0.8.5, where `data/` may be 0775 through no fault of the operator. (b) is the stricter default for shared hosts. For a directory owned by another user, always refuse.
4. **Surface it.** `zeroclaw doctor` reports the data root's owner, mode and verdict.

### Non-goals / out of scope

- Agent workspaces, `shared/` and skills directories; they can follow the same helper later.
- Filesystems that cannot represent Unix permissions (WSL `/mnt/c`, CIFS, FAT); see the runtime-directory lock fallback issue.
- Windows ACLs (the checks are Unix-only today).

### Alternatives considered

- **Check only the lock directory:** leaves databases and the socket replaceable.
- **Refuse every permissive root:** turns v0.8.5 installs with a 0775 `data/` into startup failures, which is what the umask issue reports.
- **Rely on the IPC chmod alone:** it is best-effort, runs only in the daemon, and runs after other startup steps.

### Acceptance criteria

- A fresh data root is 0700 under umask 0000, 0002 and 0022.
- A pre-existing 0775 root owned by the current user is handled as decided (tightened with a notice, or refused with the remedy), and a regression covers both without depending on the test host's umask.
- A root owned by another user is refused; a sticky shared directory is accepted, matching the IPC rule.
- The IPC endpoint, the lifecycle lock and the data-root check share one helper and one message.
- `zeroclaw doctor` shows the verdict.

### Architecture impact

`zeroclaw-config` (data-root creation), `zeroclaw-runtime` (`live_config_authority`, `rpc/local`), `zeroclaw-infra` if the helper belongs there, and `zeroclaw doctor`. No config keys, schema or wire changes.

### Risk and rollback

The risk is refusing to start, or changing permissions on hosts that deliberately share a data root through a group. Mitigations: never act on directories owned by another user, keep the sticky-bit allowance, and log every change. Rollback is a revert; no data migration.

### Expected routing

Needs maintainer design assessment

### Next decision surface

Tighten or refuse for existing permissive roots (step 3), decided together with the lifecycle-directory umask fix.

### Breaking change?

No

### Data hygiene checks

- [x] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [x] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

issues.body:
### Summary

Suppress repeated plugin egress refusal records per instance and host, so a plugin that keeps retrying a refused destination does not write a WARN record on every attempt.

### Problem statement

Every refused plugin egress attempt writes a persisted WARN record (`plugin_egress_denied`, or `plugin_egress_connection_limit` for a full connection budget). `wasi:http` does this today, and #11304 extends it to raw sockets and WebSockets. A channel plugin that redials on every poll therefore writes one record per poll for as long as its grant is wrong, and the operator's log fills with copies of one message.

Each record is bounded and the log writer drops records rather than blocking, so this is noise and disk churn, not a memory risk.

### Proposed solution

Suppress repeats in the shared reporter (`crates/zeroclaw-plugins/src/egress_report.rs`, added by #11304):

- Record the first refusal for a given instance, transport, host, and `error_key` as today, remedy included.
- Count further identical refusals inside a window instead of recording each one, and emit one summary record per window with the count.
- Start over when the instance's grant changes or after a quiet period, so a grant that is fixed and later broken again is reported again.
- Keep the suppression state bounded (a capped map with eviction, or per-store state that ends with the instance), since hosts are guest-chosen.

### Non-goals / out of scope

- What the guest sees: each refused attempt still returns its typed error.
- The policy decision, and which refusals are recorded at all (timeouts, DNS failures, and TLS setup failures after authorization stay unrecorded, as today).
- Limiting the guest's connect attempts themselves; the per-call host-call budget and the plugin's own backoff already bound those.

### Alternatives considered

- Rely on plugins to back off: the protocol docs already ask for it, but a naive or misbehaving plugin still floods the log, and the operator cannot fix the plugin.
- Log repeats at a lower level: still one record per attempt on disk.
- One global rate limit for all refusal records: simpler, but a noisy instance would hide another instance's first refusal.

### Acceptance criteria

- A test that refuses the same connect many times in a loop sees one full record and a bounded number of summaries, for `wasi:http`, sockets, and WebSockets.
- The first record's attributes and remedy text are unchanged.
- Memory used for suppression stays bounded when a guest varies the host on every attempt.

### Architecture impact

`crates/zeroclaw-plugins` only: the shared egress reporter and wherever the suppression state lives. No WIT, config, or guest-visible change.

### Risk and rollback

Risk: suppression hides a refusal the operator needs to see. Keying on instance, transport, host, and error key, resetting when the grant changes, and carrying the count in the summary keep distinct problems visible. Rollback: revert the change, which restores one record per attempt.

### Expected routing

Ordinary feature triage

### Next decision surface

Requested as a follow-up with a named owner in the review of #11304 (owner: @IftekharUddin). Revisit once #11304 merges.

### Breaking change?

No

- [x] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [x] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

issues.body:
### Affected component

runtime/daemon

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior

### Current behavior

Once a session hits `cost.daily_limit_usd`, every later turn fails, and the only way to continue is to raise the limit and restart the daemon. Restarting kills every live session. Two separate gaps cause this.

**`allow_override` does nothing.** [`CostConfig::allow_override`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d/crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs#L7393) is documented as "Allow requests to exceed budget with --override flag", but no flag, RPC method or client action reads it. Outside schema defaults and one gateway test, nothing in the tree references it. When the budget is exceeded, [`enforce_tool_loop_budget`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/agent/turn/provider_call.rs#L211) fails the turn with an error string, and ZeroCode shows it as an ordinary failed turn. The user gets no prompt and no way to continue.

**Raising the limit from ZeroCode does not reach the running tracker.** The daemon builds the process-global `CostTracker` [once at startup](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/daemon/mod.rs#L1107), and RPC turns use that handle directly ([`dispatch.rs#L6656`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs#L6656)). [`save_and_swap_config`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d/crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/dispatch.rs#L3097) swaps the live `Config` but never calls [`CostTracker::update_config`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d/crates/zeroclaw-config/src/cost/tracker.rs#L257). The tracker therefore keeps the old limits until some other path calls `get_or_init_global` with a fresh config. ACP turns do this [per turn](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d/crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/acp_server.rs#L2008); ZeroCode's RPC turns do not. The tracker's own docs say reloads apply "at the next check_budget", which holds only for those other paths.

Related: `cost.enforcement.mode` defaults to `"warn"` and accepts `"block"` and `"route_down"`, but no runtime code reads it. The budget check always blocks. That is out of scope here; I note it because it is a second advertised escape hatch that does not exist.

### Expected behavior

- When a turn would exceed a daily or monthly limit, ZeroCode shows a blocking notice in red. The notice names the period, the recorded spend and the limit, and stays up until the user acts on it.
- With `allow_override = true`, the notice offers "override and continue". This lifts enforcement for the rest of the current period in the running daemon. No restart is needed and no session is lost. The override ends when the period rolls over. With `allow_override = false`, the notice explains how to raise the limit instead.
- Changing `cost.*` through `config/set` takes effect at the next budget check on every path, RPC turns included.
- Hard-limit enforcement is unchanged for channels without an interactive client (Telegram, cron, webhooks).

The warning-threshold half of this flow is #10950. Its notice should use the same red, must-dismiss presentation.

### Steps to reproduce

```text
1. [cost] daily_limit_usd = 300, allow_override = true. Run the daemon and a ZeroCode session until recorded spend passes $300.
2. Observe: the turn fails with "Budget exceeded: $303.5080 of $300.00 Day limit". There is no prompt and no override action.
3. In ZeroCode's config editor, set cost.daily_limit_usd = 800. config.toml now shows 800.
4. Send another prompt in the same session.
5. Observe: it fails again against the $300 limit. Only a daemon restart picks up 800.
```

### Impact

A user who hits the limit mid-task has to restart the daemon, which drops every open session, including sessions with turns in flight. `allow_override` suggests a recovery path that does not exist, so the user looks for an override and does not find one.

### Logs / stack traces

Runtime trace from the dogfood daemon (revision below), local time +08:00. The reject at 06:08:57 came after `config.toml` was rewritten with `daily_limit_usd = 800` at 06:08:34:

```text
06:06:41  tool-call loop budget exceeded  current_usd=303.51 limit_usd=300.0 period=Day  channel_type=rpc
06:07:40  tool-call loop budget exceeded  current_usd=303.51 limit_usd=300.0 period=Day  channel_type=rpc
06:08:13  tool-call loop budget exceeded  current_usd=303.51 limit_usd=300.0 period=Day  channel_type=rpc
06:08:57  tool-call loop budget exceeded  current_usd=303.51 limit_usd=300.0 period=Day  channel_type=rpc
06:09:15  Received SIGINT, shutting down...
```

### ZeroClaw version

Observed on `3541e272540590f58f8a9085c800c10690fc04bb` (dogfood integration build). Source paths cited at master `e654b4b73f286201166cf574c7fe9ff342d3341d`, where the same code is present.

### Rust version

Not collected; no build for this report.

### Operating system

macOS (arm64). The paths involved are not OS-specific.

### Regression?

No. `allow_override` has never been wired.

### Pre-flight checks

- [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release. Observed on the dogfood build above; master was checked by source reading.
- [X] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.body:
### Task

Settle how the release size gate handles the next release. The x86_64 Linux `zeroclaw` binary, built with the standard distribution features, is about 0.7 MB (about 1%) under the 64 MiB hard limit that fails a release build. Decide whether to raise the limit with a recorded headroom policy, shrink the binary, or replace the absolute limit (for example with per-target limits or a growth limit against the previous release), and land that before the v0.8.6 release build.

### Context

**The gate.** Every build leg of `.github/workflows/release-stable-manual.yml` runs `scripts/ci/check_binary_size.sh` in its "Check binary size" step with `BINARY_SIZE_HARD_LIMIT: "67108864"` (64 MiB). A leg over the limit fails. Only the experimental Android leg is `continue-on-error`, and `publish` needs the build job, so one oversized x86_64 Linux binary stops the release from publishing.

**History.** At v0.8.2 the then 50 MB limit was tripped by `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` at 53,154,008 bytes. #8342 (2026-06-26) raised it to 64 MiB to "restore headroom for the 0.8.x line", attributing the growth to organic source growth with no feature or dependency change.

**Measurements.** Sizes of the `zeroclaw` binary for the two x86_64 Linux targets. The two release rows come from the "Check binary size" step of each release run. The last row comes from a manual Cross-Platform Build dispatched on the head of #11306, which merges current master and changes no Rust code; its bytes were read from the binaries the run uploaded.

| Build | Run and commit | `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` | `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| v0.8.4 release, 2026-08-02 | [30764737521](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/30764737521), `a56c345d51` | 58,323,704 | 58,400,272 |
| v0.8.5 release, 2026-09-05 | [33946673896](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/33946673896), `cb2b20a9fe` | 61,537,880 | 61,572,272 |
| master plus #11306, 2026-10-06 | [37408271392](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/37408271392), `40cb7be43e` | 66,344,920 | 66,409,584 |
| Hard limit | `BINARY_SIZE_HARD_LIMIT` | 67,108,864 | 67,108,864 |

Headroom on the last row is 763,944 bytes for gnu and 699,280 bytes for musl. The binary grew by about 3.2 MB between v0.8.4 and v0.8.5 and by about 4.8 MB in the month since, so at the recent rate the next few weeks of merges cross the limit.

Comparability: the manual workflow resolves the same feature selection (`cargo generate features --selection dist --target <triple>`) and builds with the same `cargo build --release --locked --no-default-features --features ...` command and pinned toolchain (1.98.0) as the current release workflow. Its Linux legs run on `ubuntu-latest` rather than the release workflow's `ubuntu-22.04`, and the earlier release rows used whatever toolchain was pinned at the time, so treat the trend as approximate and the last row as a close estimate of the next release build.

Other targets have more room. On the manual run: `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` 55,920,128, `arm-unknown-linux-gnueabihf` 52,534,300, `armv7-unknown-linux-gnueabihf` 52,223,004, and `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` 48,227,120. That run's macOS legs hit the workflow's 40-minute job limit; at v0.8.5, `x86_64-apple-darwin` was 51,919,432.

The advisory thresholds in `check_binary_size.sh` (a warning above 15 MB and a "target" warning above 5 MB) fire on every release build at these sizes, so they no longer signal anything.

Related: #10998 (binary-size evidence and optional-tool gating), #11306 (local size measurement and comparison tool), #11221 (gates SaaS and coding-CLI tools behind features but keeps them in the standard distribution, so it does not shrink this binary), and FND-001 section 7 (binary size tracked and reported).

### Acceptance criteria

- A decision recorded on this issue: raise the limit (new value and the headroom policy that sets it), shrink the x86_64 binary below the current limit with margin, or replace the absolute limit with another gate.
- The v0.8.6 release build's x86_64 Linux legs pass the size gate without an ad hoc override during the release.
- If the limit changes, its rationale is recorded where the gate is defined, and the advisory thresholds in `check_binary_size.sh` either mean something at current sizes or are removed.
- If the binary shrinks, before and after measurements are attached with target, profile, features, and artifact identity.

### Likely files or areas

- `.github/workflows/release-stable-manual.yml` (the "Check binary size" step)
- `scripts/ci/check_binary_size.sh`
- `Cargo.toml` (`default`, `[package.metadata.zeroclaw] dist_extra_features`)
- `docs/book/src/maintainers/release-runbook.md`

### Contributor fit

maintainer-scoped task, not yet ready for pickup labels

### Mentor, reviewer, or contact

Release maintainers; maintainer triage required.

### Risk notes

Raising the limit again without a policy repeats #8342 and leaves the next trip to whoever cuts a release. Shrinking the binary by removing features from the distribution falls under the replacement-first policy (RFC #6165) and needs its own review. Either way, a failing size gate blocks publishing, so this should be settled before the release build starts.

issues.body:
### Affected component

plugins

### Severity

S2 - degraded behavior. In `permissive` or `disabled` signature mode, a package can briefly run under the manifest of the generation it replaced.

### Current behavior

Discovery reads a package's `manifest.toml` by path (`load_manifest`), and later reads its component by path through a separate confined open (`admit_component`), both in `crates/zeroclaw-plugins/src/host.rs`. Nothing ties the two reads to the same directory generation.

Install and remove could not pair two generations this way: install publishes a new name with one rename, and remove deletes. `plugin update` (#11261, #11262) replaces a package in place: it claims the installed directory and renames the replacement onto the same name. A discovery that runs between its two reads can therefore pair the old manifest with the new component.

In `strict` mode the manifest carries a signed `wasm_sha256`, so the digest check refuses that pair. In `permissive` or `disabled` mode it can be admitted. The new code then runs, until the next discovery, with the old manifest's permissions, possibly including one the new version deliberately dropped.

Raised in the review of #11261, which states the window in its scope boundary.

### Expected behavior

Discovery opens each package directory once and reads both the manifest and the component through that one handle, as install and recovery admission already do (`admit_open_directory` and `admit_component_in`). A rename that lands between the two reads then changes neither, because both come from the generation that was opened.

### Steps to reproduce

Read from the code; not reproduced:

1. Install a package and run a host that discovers it, such as the daemon building a tool set.
2. In another process, run `zeroclaw plugin update <name>` so that its publish lands after discovery has read `manifest.toml` and before it reads the component.

Operators in `permissive` or `disabled` mode who update a plugin while the daemon builds tool sets. The window is the time between two reads in one discovery pass.

#11261 on top of #11236 (neither merged yet)

All
